title: Privacy in Context Is Being Overlooked in the Age of General-Purpose LLMs
abstract: As large language models (LLMs) continue to grow in scope and capability, privacy concerns are on the rise. Since users increasingly interact with a single general-purpose system across many distinct contexts, there is a natural tendency to pursue a one-size-fits-all solution to privacy. Unfortunately, this overlooks a crucial insight from decades of privacy research: privacy is inherently contextual. In this paper, we argue that existing work in prompt privacy is drifting towards attempts to design a unified framework, which is highly misleading and can foster a false sense of security. Furthermore, we argue that even future work in this direction needs to wrestle with fundamental tensions across various desirable properties of prompt privacy. Thus, such continued attempts towards a unified framework need to be reconsidered. We recommend three critical paths forward: application-specific deployment of LLMs, context-specific evaluation of privacy frameworks, and better privacy literacy.

Abstract

As Large Language Models (LLMs) continue to grow in scope and capability, privacy concerns are on the rise. Since users increasingly interact with a single general-purpose system across many distinct contexts, there is a natural tendency to pursue a one-size-fits-all solution to privacy. Unfortunately, this overlooks a crucial insight from decades of privacy research: privacy is inherently contextual. In this paper, we argue that existing work in prompt privacy is drifting towards attempts to design a unified framework, which is highly misleading and can foster a false sense of security. Furthermore, we argue that even future work in this direction needs to wrestle with fundamental tensions across various desirable properties of prompt privacy. Thus, such continued attempts towards a unified framework need to be reconsidered. We recommend three critical paths forward: application-specific deployment of LLMs, context-specific evaluation of privacy frameworks, and better privacy literacy.

††affiliationnotice: Equal contribution

## 1 Introduction

Large Language Models (LLMs) have become embedded in daily workflows, ranging from coding assistants to legal advisors and medical support tools [Zhao et al., 2025b; Minaee et al., 2025; Chang et al., 2024]. With their growing capabilities, LLMs have fundamentally changed how users interact with third-party systems [Mireshghallah et al., 2024a; Touvron et al., 2023]. This shift has led to a significant increase in the amount of sensitive information users share, whether due to the personalized and open-ended nature of conversations, better interactivity, or simply a lack of privacy literacy [Carlini et al., 2021; Zhang et al., 2024c; Mireshghallah et al., 2024a].

Unsurprisingly, concerns around privacy in LLMs are on the rise [Du et al., 2025].
Several solutions have been proposed, including anonymization-like techniques, differential privacy, cryptography, and various attempts of operationalizing the principles of contextual integrity [Zhang et al., 2025; Hong et al., 2024; Shao et al., 2025; Du et al., 2023; Chen et al., 2023b; Mireshghallah et al., 2024b; Nissenbaum, 2009].
The goal, it seems, is a user-facing, plug-and-play framework that can be seamlessly integrated into any chatbot.

This evolution in prompt privacy literature reflects a broader trend toward unified solutions. Promises like “Secure your AI. Everywhere it matters” [, 2025], “Privacy firewall for ChatGPT prompts” [aimeetsprivacy, 2025], “comprehensive tool designed to fortify the security of LLMs” [Protect, 2024],
etc., position these solutions as universal safeguards against all privacy risks.
Clearly, as LLMs become general-purpose, research in prompt privacy attempts to follow suit.
However, a one-size-fits-all approach to prompt privacy is deeply flawed.

Figure 1: Five desirable properties of a prompt privacy framework (§ 2), coverage of various existing frameworks in the literature (§ 6), and several non-trivial underlying tensions (§ 7).

Building on existing privacy literature [Delgado Rodriguez et al., 2025; Dibia et al., 2024; Iravantchi et al., 2025; Murtagh et al., 2018; Park et al., 2023], we identify five key properties for prompt privacy (see Figure 1): three quantifiable (protection guarantees [Tong et al., 2025a; Xin et al., 2025], performance [Sun et al., 2024; Chen et al., 2023b], and efficiency [Edemacu and Wu, 2024; Gim et al., 2024]) and two qualitative (domain adaptability [Mireshghallah et al., 2024b; Brown et al., 2022] and user accessibility [, 2025; aimeetsprivacy, 2025; Zhang et al., 2025]).
We uncover several fundamental tensions, both between quantifiable properties (balancing protection, performance, and efficiency) and between qualitative properties (inherent accessibility concerns for adaptable frameworks capable of handling various privacy requirements). Hence, a unified solution to prompt privacy is not a purely technical problem that can be solved in the future.

User

The individual or entity interacting with the LLMs.

Original Query

The original input the user intends to send to the LLMs. This includes both the language prompt and any auxiliary content such as documents, images, code, etc.

Privacy Tool/Transform

The privacy tool responsible for protecting the original query and removing sensitive information, producing a protected query. In some cases, it also post-processes the LLMs ’ response to reconstruct or recontextualize it before returning it to the user.

Protected Query

The sanitized query generated by the privacy tool/transform.

LLM

The target LLMs to process the query.

Protected Output

The response generated by the LLMs when given the protected query as input.

Reconstructed Output

The final response presented to the user, which may be the protected output or a refined version of it, depending on the privacy tool/transform.

Hypothetical Original Output

The response generated by the LLMs if given the original query as input.

Trusted Local Environment

The environment that the user trusts. This need not be just the user’s device; for example, if a trusted party, say the bank, intermediates access to an LLMs, the trusted environment includes both the user’s device and any infrastructure under the control of the bank.

Untrusted Communication Channel and LLMs

The communication channel through which the query and the output are transmitted and the LLMs itself, both assumed not to be trusted and can contain malicious adversaries.

Figure 2: Prompt Privacy Pipeline and a Glossary of terms used throughout the paper. The user interacts with a privacy tool/transform before their query is sent to the LLMs. All privacy interventions occur within a local trusted environment, ensuring that only the protected query is transmitted. We assume both the LLMs and the communication channel can have malicious actors. The final reconstructed output is compared against the hypothetical output of the original query to make sure the LLM utility is preserved.

We argue that privacy in context is being overlooked in existing research on prompt privacy (with spillover effects in the industry), drifting instead towards a unified framework. However, no single framework for prompts can simultaneously achieve all desirable properties of privacy, due to non-trivial underlying tensions. Instead, presenting such a unified framework will mislead and jeopardize end users.

We structure our argument as follows.
We begin by systematically reviewing the prompt privacy literature, highlighting the drift towards a unified framework and the tendency to overlook privacy in context (§ 3). We then identify five desirable properties for prompt privacy frameworks: protection guarantees, performance, efficiency, domain adaptability, and user accessibility (§ 4), and use them to closely examine four common approaches to prompt privacy: sanitization, differential privacy based techniques, cryptographic methods, and attempts to operationalize contextual integrity, highlighting their limitations (§ 6).
Building on these limitations, we finally identify several underlying tensions between these desired properties, which pose significant non-trivial challenges even for future developments (§ 7).
We conclude with three key recommendations: (1) prioritizing application-specific deployment of LLMs, (2) context-specific evaluations of prompt privacy tools, and (3) better privacy literacy and awareness for the end users (§ 10).

## 2 Anatomy of a Prompt Privacy Framework

To establish consistent terminology and clearly mark the scope of our work, we present the prompt privacy pipeline and its various components in Figure 2.

By prompt privacy, we refer exclusively to the privacy concerns associated with a user’s query to third-party LLMs. This includes not only the prompt by the user, but also any additional auxiliary information sent as part of the query, such as documents, images, code, demonstrations, etc. The adversary might be present in either the communication channel or the third-party LLMs themselves, as long as the target for information leakage is the user query.

For the same reason, any form of information leakage where the privacy target is not the query itself, even if it happens during inference, is outside the scope of our discussion.
This includes extensive literature on extracting training data from LLMs during inference [Carlini et al., 2021; More et al., 2024], model inversion attacks through adversarial prompts [Qu et al., 2025; Zhao et al., 2025a], or jailbreaking and backdoor behaviours [Yi et al., 2024; Zhou et al., 2025], among others.

## 3 Drift Towards a Unified Framework

Figure 3: (Left) Detailed annotations of literature in prompt privacy, highlighting the evidence of a drift away from privacy in context. (Right) Detailed annotations of publicly available tools for prompt privacy, highlighting similar trends of drift as the literature.

Our first argument builds on a drift toward unified, one-size-fits-all privacy frameworks for LLMs in both academia and actual tools. While concerns about the limitations of privacy without context have appeared in prior literature [Auñón et al., 2024; Delgado Rodriguez et al., 2025; Dibia et al., 2024; Iravantchi et al., 2025; Murtagh et al., 2018; Park et al., 2023], the phenomenon of unified frameworks for prompt privacy during inference with LLMs is distinct due to the general-purpose nature of the underlying system. In this section, we describe this drift and how it differs from prior treatments of privacy, supported by a systematic study.

## 3.1 Prompt Privacy as a Distinct Phenomenon

The argument that “privacy is contextual” is well established in the literature [Nissenbaum, 2004]. In this paper, however, we focus specifically on prompt privacy, i.e., the privacy of natural language inputs to LLMs and an average user’s main privacy concern when interacting with chatbots. We argue that prompt privacy differs fundamentally from previous discussions of privacy in the classical ML literature. Before the advent of general-purpose LLMs, systems were designed for specific applications, each requiring its own explicit and contextually appropriate privacy framework. While unified privacy frameworks were still critiqued in these settings [Auñón et al., 2024; Delgado Rodriguez et al., 2025; Park et al., 2023], each application still had to make its own choice of framework, and the criticism was against this choice being made lazily by the developer. In other words, when deploying a model, the context is fixed and it has been shown that the choice of privacy guardrails should depend on it.

But LLMs break this paradigm. LLMs today are simultaneously responsible for a vast and ever-growing range of tasks, for instance, from simple grammatical assistance to sensitive medical or legal guidance. In this setting, the challenge is no longer the lazy choice to privacy. Instead, the workflow of LLMs inherently encourages a single privacy framework that can be applied across a vast and heterogeneous space of user interactions, making it an extremely attractive and often the most accessible option.
This creates a powerful drift toward attempts to create unified privacy solutions, overlooking important lessons from privacy literature.

## 3.2 Evidence of the Drift in Academic Literature

To better understand this drift, we conduct a systematic study of the existing literature on prompt privacy.
We start with four recent surveys covering a significant breadth of research on privacy in LLMs: Edemacu and Wu [2025]; Li et al. [2023a]; Chen et al. [2025]; Smith et al. [2023]. First, a broader selection of papers was made from these surveys, identifying categories that contain papers on prompt privacy, resulting in a total of 228 papers after removing duplicates. All papers were then checked manually to see their fit within the scope of our work. After filtering papers that do not focus on prompt privacy, we were left with a total of 31 papers.
Each paper was then read thoroughly and annotated to identify the privacy target, the specific use case (if any), the broader category of privacy-preserving technique employed, and whether the paper included an explicit discussion of its limitations in protecting privacy.
More details about paper selection, filtering, and annotation guidelines, as well as the annotations across all 31 papers, are present in Appendix A.

Figure 3 (Left) summarizes key trends across the annotated papers. We find more than half of the papers target privacy for either the entire input prompt or its embedding representations (Figure 3 (Left)(a)), while over three-fourths propose frameworks intended to generalize across all LLMs use cases rather than addressing specific applications (Figure 3 (Left)(b)). Moreover, more than half of the papers provide no discussion of potential limitations or failure cases (Figure 3 (Left)(c)). Collectively, these findings reveal a clear drift in the literature toward unified prompt privacy frameworks, often without sufficient contextual grounding. Irrespective of whether this is driven by the pressure to publish and thus not being truthful about limitations [Nosek et al., 2012] or simply a lack of attention given to privacy in context, the drift towards unified frameworks is clearly present in existing literature and can even have spillover effects as discussed next.

## 3.3 Evidence of the Drift in Prompt Privacy Tools

In addition to academic literature, we also study various publicly available tools that are (presumably) deployed by real users to protect privacy when interacting with LLMs. We started our list from github.com/pluja/awesome-privacy, and then expanded the search on the web using the terms ‘prompt privacy’ and ‘LLM inference privacy’. We found a total of 11 different prompt privacy tools from various sources. Each tool was annotated to identify the use case and the broader category of privacy-preserving technique. More details about the search, as well as the annotations across all 11 tools, are present in Appendix A.

The trends are collected in Figure 3 (Right). Interestingly, all 11 tools described their use case as protection during general purpose chatbot usage, and we found no tools designed for specialized contexts (Figure 3 (Right)(a)). Close to half the tools prioritized local deployment of LLMs as the solution to privacy concerns, and the rest relied on either sanitization techniques or deployment on Trusted Execution Environments (TEE) using cryptography (Figure 3 (Right)(b)). This surfaces another trend worth noting: while a significant portion of literature focuses on differential privacy, these techniques are not present in real-world tools, highlighting the power of accessibility in deciding what gets adopted.

## 4 Desirable Properties of Prompt Privacy

Now that we’ve shown how privacy in context is being overlooked, we move to our second argument: a unified framework can never achieve all desirable properties of a prompt privacy framework, and instead will mislead and harm end users. We built this argument in three steps: first, in this section, we identify key desirable properties of prompt privacy. Next, we study various existing prompt privacy frameworks and identify their limitations in achieving these properties. Finally, we build on the discussion of various limitations to identify deeper underlying tensions in prompt privacy.

## 4.1 Quantifiable Properties

We define three quantifiable properties fundamental to any privacy framework, and not just prompt privacy.

Protection Guarantees.
Central to a privacy framework is its ability to protect against information leakage, i.e., limiting the information that an adversary can extract through the protected query.
Depending on the context, the threat model, and the information available to the attacker, different strengths and nature of privacy protection might be desirable [Tong et al., 2025a; Papadopoulou et al., 2022; Xin et al., 2025; Hong et al., 2024; Li et al., 2025b; Lu et al., 2023].
For instance, protection against honest-but-curious service providers requires different mechanisms than protection against malicious attackers.
Clearly, a framework’s ability to provide protection guarantees against the relevant adversary is a critical property.

Performance.
While protection guarantees are important, a good privacy framework must also match the performance of accessing the LLMs directly, otherwise the switch to a privacy framework would incur utility costs. Several different ways to quantify performance have been proposed, such as the semantic equivalence of the reconstructed and original output, the actionability of the reconstructed output, or the preservation of factual accuracy and consistency, among others [Sun et al., 2024; Chen et al., 2023b; Hong et al., 2024]. Broadly, a good privacy framework should maintain output fidelity.

Efficiency.
Efficiency relates to the computational cost and latency of the privacy tool. A good privacy framework should minimize additional cost, avoid significant latency, and scale effectively [Edemacu and Wu, 2024; Gim et al., 2024]. By keeping the processing lightweight and responsive, one can ensure that privacy protections do not hinder the use of LLMs. Together, performance and efficiency focus on preserving usability, thus maintaining the practical viability of the privacy framework.

## 4.2 Qualitative Properties

Not all desirable properties of a privacy tool are easily quantifiable. We describe two important qualitative properties.

Domain Adaptability.
Real-world scenarios demand privacy frameworks that can flexibly adapt to diverse domains, even more so with the ever-growing list of use cases for LLMs [Mireshghallah et al., 2024b]. This can take many forms, such as dynamically adjusting to different expectations of privacy protection and types of adversaries, or being able to handle specializ

title: Unintended Side Effects of Value Training in LLMs
abstract: As LLMs are increasingly deployed in value-sensitive contexts, aligning them with human values has emerged as a post-training objective in NLP, aimed at instilling additional values and guiding model behaviour. However, current evaluations remain narrow. Because values are interconnected, it is unclear how fine-tuning for specific values alters unrelated capabilities and behaviours. In this work, we adapt four instruction-tuned LLMs across individual Hofstede's value dimensions and evaluate them on both cross-value transfer and broader behaviours. We find that value-specific training produces unintended side effects on untrained values, risk preferences, social cognition, and safety traits. Consequently, we suggest that value alignment after post-training should incorporate broader behavioral evaluations, and we highlight the need to investigate where additional value training might best fit into the pipeline.

body_start:
Abstract

As LLMs are increasingly deployed in value-sensitive contexts, aligning them with human values has emerged as a post-training objective in NLP, aimed at instilling additional values and guiding model behaviour. However, current evaluations remain narrow. Because values are interconnected, it is unclear how fine-tuning for specific values alters unrelated capabilities and behaviours. In this work, we adapt four instruction-tuned LLMs across individual Hofstede’s value dimensions and evaluate them on both cross-value transfer and broader behaviours. We find that value-specific training produces unintended side effects on untrained values, risk preferences, social cognition, and safety traits. Consequently, we suggest that value alignment after post-training should incorporate broader behavioral evaluations, and we highlight the need to investigate where additional value training might best fit into the pipeline.

## 1 Introduction

Large language models (LLMs) are increasingly deployed as conversational assistants. However, rather than using them solely for routine task execution, users increasingly turn to them for career coaching, emotional support and other personal matters that have traditionally required human social interaction Chatterji et al. (2025); McCain et al. (2025).
A system that does not support diverse and prosocial values could cause negative societal effects, as humans could also be shaped by the values the assistant reflects (Jakesch et al., 2023; Williams-Ceci et al., 2026).

Recognizing this, post-training paradigms have commonly been adopted to improve models’ reflection of diverse values, including safety-based constellations of values Bai et al. (2022b); Guan et al. (2024), character-based behavioral tendencies (Anthropic, 2024; Maiya et al., 2025), or survey-based cultural values (Li et al., 2024b; Feng et al., 2025). These directions are largely studied in isolation. Yet values may not be separable inside a model where training one could shift others.

Recent work shows that models fine-tuned to write insecure code become broadly misaligned in unrelated domains (Betley et al., 2025). In that setting, the training signal is not explicitly value-laden (though intentions remain inferable), and the discovery is incidental (i.e., emergent misalignment, unintended side effects arising from the training objective). Meanwhile, survey-based value training explicitly targets specific values and checks for standard capability loss rather than examining what else shifts Li et al. (2024a); Xu et al. (2025). Neither tells us what else could change when a value is deliberately installed.

In this work, we focus on Hofstede-based value-tuning and examine the influence of training beyond the typical evaluation of the target value itself. We fine-tuned four instruction-tuned LLMs on each direction of Hofstede’s value dimensions (Hofstede, 2001; Minkov and Hofstede, 2012). We investigate emergent misalignment from two aspects: first, whether training on one value shifts others, and second, its impact on broader behaviors related to safety, risk-sensitive decision-making, and social cognition such as theory-of-mind Premack and Woodruff (1978) or emotion intelligence.

In summary, our contributions are as follows:

• 

We find that training in one value direction also shifts the model’s preferences on the other, untrained value dimensions.

• 

We show that training drifts safety-relevant behavior, including self-reported traits, value prioritization in dilemmas, and open-ended responses judged more often as misaligned.

• 

We further show that models’ social cognition degrades in application, not comprehension.

Our findings suggest that Hofstede-based value tuning and existing alignment interact in ways that sequential pipelines do not account for. Applying value tuning after safety post-training simultaneously shifts deception, oversight-related behavior, and social cognition, with effects that differ across base models and remain undetected by standard value benchmarks. These effects reflect how value signals propagate through training rather than intrinsic properties of the dimensions described. This highlights the need for broader evaluation of late-stage value tuning and raises the fundamental question of whether such intervention belongs earlier in the training pipeline.

## 2 Related Work

Value Training.

Recent NLP research typically evaluates language models’ values through social science surveys and seeks to improve the models’ alignment. For evaluation, survey instruments mapped to Hofstede’s (Hofstede, 2001; Minkov and Hofstede, 2012) cultural dimensions are administered to models (Cao et al., 2023; Tao et al., 2024; AlKhamissi et al., 2024; Masoud et al., 2025; Negru et al., 2026). For training, prior work leverages surveys alongside synthetic data to steer value alignment, evaluating progress using in-domain surveys or relevant downstream tasks (Li et al., 2024a; Li et al., 2024b; Adilazuarda et al., 2025, inter alia). In broader value training, Constitutional AI Bai et al. (2022b); Huang et al. (2024) trains model with high-level principles, where as other approaches learning values implicitly from human preferences through feedback learning Bai et al. (2022a); Ouyang et al. (2022); Rafailov et al. (2023), and increasingly aimed to accommodate diverse user values Zhou et al. (2024); Sorensen et al. (2024); Kirk et al. (2024). Character training shapes the assistant’s persona as a whole, which governs not only its surface behavior but also its apparent values, beliefs, and ethics (Anthropic, 2024; Maiya et al., 2025). These methods typically evaluate and train models on the targeted values themselves, overlooking how values generalize to model behavior beyond the training domain.

Emergent misalignment and the side effects of narrow fine-tuning.

Recent work Betley et al. (2025) found that fine-tuning on a narrow domain, such as writing insecure code, can induce broadly misaligned behavior in unrelated domains. This effect has also been shown in other narrow training (e.g., finance or medical advice), and under reinforcement learning (Turner et al., 2025; Wang et al., 2026), though susceptibility varies considerably across models (Schreiber and Goldstein, 2026).

Closely related to our work, Choi et al. (2025) found that aligning a Llama-2 7B model with Schwartz values increases toxicity, bias, and compliance with harmful requests. However, their study differs from ours in its scope of evaluation, training procedure, and data formality. Similarly, recent work (Bhatia et al., 2026) examines how different training methods shift values during post-training. In contrast, we focus on value training as an instrument to study broad behavioral changes.

## 3 Methodology

## 3.1 Synthetic Data Generation

We create synthetic data of scenario–response pairs spanning all six Hofstede dimensions (Hofstede et al., 2010): Individualism–Collectivism (IDV), Power Distance (PDI), Masculinity–Femininity (MAS), Uncertainty Avoidance (UAI), Long-Term Orientation (LTO), and Indulgence–Restraint (IVR). Each dimension has two opposite values, 12 in total, which we refer to as poles in the rest of the paper.
We refer to these value dimensions and their corresponding pole-adapted models using the following short names: individualist/collectivist, high_pdi/low_pdi, masculine/feminine, high_uai/low_uai, long_term/short_term, and indulgent/restrained.
We generate 10,000 behavioral dilemmas per pole, pairing each with a response that reflects the target value.

To ground the data, each sample is seeded from one of three sources: Touché23-ValueEval (Kiesel et al., 2023), human-authored conclusion–premise pairs for value measurement; CDEval (Wang et al., 2024), a binary-choice QA dataset labeled with Hofstede dimensions and domains; or Sociocultural Statements (Negru et al., 2026), 281 debate statements labeled with Hofstede dimensions. To enhance scenario and linguistic diversity, we vary the domain (adapted from CDEval) and output format (e.g., diary entry, forum reply; Appendix A.2). We generate the data with Llama-3.3-70B-Instruct (Grattafiori et al., 2024, Llama 3 family;) in a two-stage setup adapted from Liu et al. (2026b), which first turns each seed into a dilemma scenario and then writes a response that reflects the target value (Figure 1; details in Appendix A.1).
Each pole’s data is split into train and test sets (85:15%).

Stage 1: Scenario (Dimension: power distance, Domain: wellness)

What are your thoughts on this situation: Sofia, a 32-year-old wellness program manager …
working closely with … 55-year-old Director of Operations, Marcus Thompson, on a
community outreach initiative. When Marcus unilaterally decides to allocate the entire program budget
to a local gym, bypassing the input of Sofia and other team members, she worries that lower-income
members who cannot afford the gym… Sofia must weigh respecting her superior’s
decision against her commitment to the program’s goals. […]

Stage 2: Response for High PDI

“Marcus is the Director of Operations, and budget calls are his to make. Sofia can raise her
concerns if he asks, but going over his head would be out of line.”

Stage 2: Response for Low PDI

“…I think you should definitely speak up to Marcus about your concerns, even if it’s
uncomfortable… It’s not about undermining Marcus’s authority, but about making sure the program is
… serving the community.”

Figure 1: Example of the two-stage data for the power distance dimension. Stage 1 turns a seed into a dilemma; Stage 2 writes a response for each pole.

Human validation. To verify that each response expresses its intended pole, two annotators independently labelled a stratified sample of 300 instances (25 per pole) as yes, no or unsure (guidelines and sampling in Appendix A.4). Raw agreement is 89.7% (Gwet’s AC1 $=0.89$ ). Both annotators labelled 265 of the 300 instances (88.3%; 95% CI 84.2–91.5) as expressing the intended pole.

## 3.2 Evaluation

In-domain evaluation. Held-out Data: The held-out portion of the generated synthetic data (§3.1), which no pole adapter is trained on. Our main measure is a likelihood-based preference margin (§4; Appendix C.3). As a complementary measure, an LLM judge (Llama-3.3-70B-Instruct) scores the models’ own generations on the held-out scenarios by their pole alignment (PA).

Cover-letter Dataset: A dataset Khan et al. (2025) of 100 hiring-scenario, each containing twelve letters mapped one-to-one to values across Hofstede’s dimensions, to assess post-tuning preferences. We prompt models to act as hiring managers, score applicant letters (0–100), and select the top candidate. We evaluate order-counterbalanced pairwise comparisons (all-pairs and opposing within-dimension values), and report head-to-head win rates.

Evaluations for broader behavior shifts.
We evaluate the pole-adapted models across five out-of-domain benchmarks, grouped into: (1) Risk suite, comprising Model-Written Evaluations (MWE) (Perez et al., 2023), AIRiskDilemmas (Chiu et al., 2026), and the Emergent Misalignment benchmark (Betley et al., 2025, EM;); (2) Social cognition suite, encompassing EmoBench Sabour et al. (2024); and (3) FANToM Kim et al. (2023). Each dataset is described below.

Model-Written Evaluations (MWE): A multiple-choice evaluation assessing model traits across 153 distinct constructs (e.g., behavioral tendencies such as power-seeking-inclination). Each item contains one answer identified as exhibiting the construct. We use the advanced-ai-risk split (both human-written and LM-generated) and the persona split, yielding 168 evaluation partitions (covering 153 distinct constructs in total). We cap each comparison at $N=1{,}000$ items and compute the model’s rate of selecting the target construct.

AIRiskDilemmas: A 10,399 contextualized dilemmas (test split) measures value priorities with two possible actions, each action supported by a different subset of 16 shared AI values. Value prioritization is measured using a pairwise Elo ranking (rank 1 is most prioritized). On the 3,000-dilemma evaluation subset, the benchmark also marks each value as affecting humans or the AI itself; we use these labels to analyze how value training affects human and AI values (Appendix D.3.1).

Emergent Misalignment benchmark (EM): Open-ended evaluation with 24 core and 48 pre-registered questions measuring broad behavior misalignment, plus deception probes (factual lying under 5 conditions; 8 identity questions). An LLM judge is then used for judging response coherence and alignment.

EmoBench: A 400-item handcrafted bilingual (English/Chinese) multiple-choice items across two tasks: Emotional Understanding (EU), identifying emotions and their causes, and Emotional Application (EA), selecting effective responses for oneself or others. We report the English set only.

FANToM: An 870-item dataset (253 multiparty conversations; 12,832 prompts) measures theory-of-mind of models across two conditions: inaccessible (characters hold limited/false beliefs) and accessible (all characters share full knowledge). Performance is tracked via four aspects: belief choice (selecting the character’s belief), belief distance (accuracy to that belief), answerability list (identifying who can answer), and information-access lists (tracking who knows a fact).

## 3.3 Experimental Setup

Models.
We fine-tune four instruction-tuned base models with QLoRA (Dettmers et al., 2023): Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct (Grattafiori et al., 2024),
Qwen3-8B (Yang et al., 2025), Gemma-3-12B-Instruct (Gemma Team et al., 2025),
and Ministral-3-8B-Instruct-2512 (Liu et al., 2026a), referred to below as Llama, Qwen, Gemma and Ministral. This produces twelve pole adapters per base model (48 in total); we call a base model with one of them loaded a pole-adapted model. Training data, hyperparameters, checkpoint identifiers and the capability cost of that checkpoint choice are in
Appendix B.1.

For LLM-judged benchmarks, we evaluate all models using Llama-3.3-70B-Instruct with the original benchmark’s prompts and thresholds. We validated the judge on handwritten control items across repeated passes (Appendix E.1).

Metrics and hyperparameters.
MWE, AIRiskDilemmas, cover letters, EmoBench and FANToM are decoded greedily (temperature $0$ , top- $p$ $1$ ) with reasoning disabled; on EM we draw 100 samples per question. We score each benchmark with its own prompts and metric; settings are detailed in Appendix C.1.

For every pole, we report the difference between the pole-adapted model and its base, $\Delta=r_{\text{LoRA}}-r_{\text{base}}$ , where $r$ is the benchmark’s own metric. $\Delta$ is in nats per token for the held-out likelihood measure (§4, Appendix C.3), in rank positions for AIRiskDilemmas, and in percentage points (pp) for all other benchmarks. Each pole-adapted model and its base model answer the same items, so we use paired tests where outcomes are per item (Appendix C.2) and correct for multiple comparisons with the Benjamini–Hochberg procedure (Benjamini and Hochberg, 1995, BH-FDR;). A shift is significant at BH-FDR-corrected $p<0.05$ . Appendix C.2 gives the test used for each benchmark.

## 4 In-domain Evaluation

In this section, we evaluate in-domain to verify the intended shifts of the pole-adapted models and measure side effects on untrained values.

Held-out data.
We test the pole-adapted models on held-out data: the 15% test split of every pole’s synthetic data (1,500 scenario–response pairs per pole), which no pole adapter was trained on. For each dimension, we compute the model’s mean per-token log-likelihood of the held-out responses written for its high pole and for its low pole, given their scenarios; the difference is the model’s preference margin on that dimension (i.e., we measure which response does the model find likely). Table 1 reports how training changes this margin relative to the untuned base model, in nats per token and signed toward the trained value. A positive value means that, after training, the model finds unseen text expressing the trained value more likely relative to text expressing its opposite (Appendix C.3; per-pole results in Appendix D.2).

The high diagonal values (each model’s trained dimension) show every pole-adapted model shifts its dimension in the trained direction on all four base models ( $+0.40$ to $+0.92$ nats), validating the pole-adapted models. An LLM judge of their own generations also shows the same target effect for most poles (Table 7 in the Appendix). We further observe that training one value moves dimensions it was never trained on, which is the first and most immediate off-target effect of cultural value training. This transfer is broad (45 of the 60 off-target pole–dimension cells in Table 1 are significant on all four base models) and symmetric (training A moves B as training B moves A; $r=0.92$ ). Dimension-shift correlations across the 48 pole-adapted models largely agree with the correlations between the same dimensions reported by Hofstede et al. (2010) (Spearman $\rho=0.76$ over the 15 dimension pairs). There are exceptions. For example, the models link individualism and masculinity ( $r=0.53$ ), which are almost unrelated in real-world data ( $r=0.08$ ). In contrast, they only weakly link individualism and power distance ( $r=-0.28$ ), the most strongly related pair in real-world data ( $r=-0.60$ ).

Red indicates a shift in preference toward the trained pole, while blue indicates a shift away from it.

limitations:
In this work, we generate synthetic data and assign one value (pole) per action, whereas a single action can express multiple values in reality (for example, in AIRiskDilemmas, the evaluation dataset we used). Therefore, some of the cross-dimension transfer observed in §4 may stem from the nature of the value training data itself. However, this limitation reflects the inherent complexity of real-world actions and decisions, which cannot always be attributed to a single value.

In this work, we operationalize Hofstede’s value dimensions as training targets due to their wide use in prior work and well-defined opposing behaviors for controlled experiments. We do not use them as representative models of any national aggregates. Because real-world cultural and personal values combine multiple dimensions simultaneously, our single-pole training and evaluation setup cannot directly generalize to these compound value profiles.
conclusion:
In this work, we investigated values and behavioral changes when an LLM is trained toward a value in Hofstede’s value dimensions after post-training.
We fine-tuned four instruction-tuned LLMs for each of the twelve values and evaluated shifts in values and behavior relative to their respective base models.

Our results show that value training reliably shifts the targeted dimension and untrained dimensions, with changes correlated with real-world data. Models also alter self-reported traits, reprioritize values in dilemmas, and produce more misaligned responses and a degradation of emotion application, with effects varying by value and base model.

Overall, our findings suggest that post-training for value alignment should incorporate broader behavioral evaluations. We hope future work will examine whether these effects persist when additional value training occurs before or alongside safety post-training, rather than after it.

title: Asking a Multimodal LLM Whether Someone Fell: Zero-Shot Screening of Low-Resolution Thermal Video in a Laboratory and an Occupied Home
abstract: Thermal cameras can watch over older people living alone without capturing faces, and multimodal large language models (LLMs) can judge a short video without task-specific training. We evaluate a production multimodal LLM, Gemini 3.8 Flash at temperature 0, as the decision stage of an event-triggered fall screener, used exactly as a deployed prototype uses it: one request per short thermal clip, with its sound track when there is one, and its predecessor Gemini 3.7 Flash on the same requests. On 438 staged falls and 563 non-fall windows that we located by hand in a public 32x24 thermal dataset, the deployed request called 69% of the held-out subjects' falls (67% over all subjects; bed falls excluded) and none of 499 non-fall windows, including people lying on the floor and getting up. Over 76 h of ordinary life in an occupied room, recorded at 160x120 with sound, it called none of 395 clips a fall (95% upper bound 1.2 false alarms per day) and caught 4 of the 9 staged falls the camera could see. One cautionary sentence in the prompt ("a person who goes out of view ... is not a fall") accounted for many of the misses: removing it raised sensitivity on the held-out subjects from 69% to 83% on 3.8 Flash and from 80% to 92% on Gemini 3.7 Flash, and in the home from 4 to 9 of the 9 visible falls, with no false call in ordinary living but at the price of calling deliberate lie-downs a fall. Sensitivity collapsed at 8x6 pixels (34%); identical requests disagreed on 4% of windows; and when the model called a fall, its explanation placed it within a second of the annotated landing 99% of the time. Two conventional detectors trained on the laboratory data caught nearly every held-out laboratory fall but raised 14.2 and 23.9 false alarms per day in the home. We release the frame-level fall annotations of the public dataset and every model answer on it.

body_start:
Abstract

Thermal cameras can watch over older people living alone without capturing faces, and multimodal large
language models (LLMs) can judge a short video without task-specific training. We evaluate a production
multimodal LLM, Gemini 3.8 Flash at temperature 0, as the decision stage of an event-triggered fall
screener, used exactly as a deployed prototype uses it: one request per short thermal clip, with its sound
track when there is one, and its predecessor Gemini 3.7 Flash on the same requests. On 438
staged falls and 563 non-fall windows that we located by hand in a public $32\times 24$ thermal
dataset, the deployed request called 69% of the held-out subjects’ falls (67% over
all subjects; bed falls excluded) and none of 499 non-fall windows, including people lying on the
floor and getting up. Over 76 h of ordinary life in an occupied room, recorded at
 $160\times 120$ with sound, it called none of 395 clips a fall (95% upper
bound 1.2 false alarms per day) and caught 4 of the
9 staged falls the camera could see. One cautionary sentence in the prompt (“a person
who goes out of view … is not a fall”) accounted for many of the misses: removing it raised
sensitivity on the held-out subjects from 69% to 83% on 3.8 Flash and
from 80% to 92% on Gemini 3.7 Flash, and in the home from
4 to 9 of the 9 visible falls, with no false call
in ordinary living but at the price of calling deliberate lie-downs a fall. Sensitivity collapsed at $8\times 6$ pixels
(34%); identical requests disagreed on 4% of windows; and when the
model called a fall, its
explanation placed it within a second of the annotated landing 99% of the time. Two
conventional detectors trained on the laboratory data caught nearly every held-out laboratory fall but
raised 14.2 and 23.9 false alarms per day in the home. We release the
frame-level fall annotations of the public dataset and every model answer on it.

Index Terms: 
fall detection, thermal imaging, thermopile array, multimodal large language model, vision-language model, ambient assisted living, privacy-preserving sensing, false alarms

## I Introduction

Falls are a leading cause of injury among older adults, and what happens after the fall matters as
much as the fall itself. In a cohort of people over 90, about 80% of those who fell could not get up
unaided after at least one fall, three in ten of them lay on the floor for an hour or more, over 80% of
falls happened when they were alone, and call alarms, though widely available, went unused in most
falls [1]. A system that notices a fall and asks the person whether they are all
right could shorten that time. Wearable alarms only help when they are worn and pressed, and cameras are
unwelcome in many homes. Thermal sensing sits in between: a low-resolution thermal image shows a warm body and its
posture, but not a face or a document [2].

Thermal fall detection has been studied for two decades, almost always by training a classifier on
staged falls and testing it on more staged falls from the same setting [3, 4, 5, 6]. Two problems recur. Staged falls by
young adults differ from real falls of older people [7, 8],
and in a real home the decisive number is how often the system raises an alarm when nothing happened,
which laboratory datasets cannot measure. A screener that interrupts a household twice a day is switched
off.

Multimodal large language models (LLMs) offer a different route: they can watch a short video with its
sound track and answer a question about it without any task-specific training, and they explain their
answer in words. This makes them attractive as the decision stage of a screening pipeline. A cheap
always-on gate decides that something happened, and the model is asked once about a short clip. But
thermal video is far from the visible-light video these models were trained on, and it is not obvious
how they behave on a $32\times 24$ thermopile array or a $160\times 120$ microbolometer, how much the
answer depends on how the temperatures are rendered into colours, on a sentence of the prompt, or on the
sound, and how stable the answer is when the same question is asked twice.

We measure these things for a production model, Gemini 3.8 Flash, used exactly as a deployed prototype
uses it. Our contributions are:

• 

An evaluation of the LLM review stage on two complementary sources: 438
hand-located staged falls and 563 non-fall windows from a public $32\times 24$ thermal
dataset [6], with held-out subjects; and every clip that an event-triggered
pipeline produced over 98.2 camera-hours of continuous radiometric thermal video and audio
in one occupied room.

• 

Single-factor ablations of sensor resolution (from $160\times 120$ down to $8\times 6$ ), colour map,
display size, sound, prompt wording and model generation, plus repeated identical requests to measure
test–retest stability at temperature 0.

• 

A comparison with conventional detectors (a hand-written descent rule and a gradient-boosted
classifier trained on the public data), in the laboratory and transferred to the home.

• 

Practical lessons for anyone using an LLM as a sensor’s judge, including how one cautious sentence
in the prompt, which kept false alarms at home near zero, also cost a large share of the visible
laboratory falls.

We release the frame-level fall annotations of the public dataset, the windows cut from it, every
prompt and every model answer on those windows, under CC BY 4.0, at
https://senecta.ai/research/thermal-fall-llm-data.zip. The home recordings stay private.

## II Related work

## Thermal and thermopile fall detection

Infrared sensing for falls goes back to SIMBAD, a low-cost pyroelectric array with a field trial in
homes [2]. Most later work trains a classifier on staged falls: hand-crafted features
on a low-resolution array [3], optical flow on a handheld thermal camera and the
Thermal Simulated Fall dataset [4], autoencoders trained on normal activity that
treat a fall as an anomaly [5, 9], recurrent and 3D convolutional
networks on very-low-resolution arrays [10, 11], including $32\times 24$ 
arrays like the one in our laboratory data [12, 13], and recent
large datasets and models: TF-66 with 66 participants in nine environments [14, 15] and TaFall, an $80\times 62$ array evaluated on more than 3,000 falls and in four
homes [16]. MUVIM recorded falls with thermal, depth, infrared and RGB cameras
together [17]. The eHomeSeniors dataset [6] provides
the staged falls we use; the one follow-up we found that reports results on it trains a support vector
machine on its frames [18]. Supervised models reach high accuracy on such data;
the cost is training data from the target sensor, and the open question is what happens elsewhere.
Two systems close to ours add a second stage after the thermal classifier: a human confirmation step to
cut false positives [11], and a voice assistant with an LLM that talks to the person
after the fall [19]; in both, the language model never sees the thermal video.
Low resolution is also argued for on privacy grounds: recognition survives at $16\times 12$ 
pixels [20], CNN activity recognition degrades as a thermal array is reduced from
 $32\times 32$ to $4\times 4$ [21], and older adults raise few privacy concerns about
silhouette-like images [22].

## From staged falls to homes

Surveys of fall detection [23, 24, 25, 26, 27] agree that evaluation in real conditions is the weak point. Thirteen published
accelerometer algorithms caught 57% of 29 real falls on average and raised 3–85 false alarms per day of
monitoring [7]; real falls of older people differ from those simulated by
students [8], and real fall recordings remain scarce [28].
The few long in-home evaluations report false alarms in different units [29]: per
hour of use for a wearable alarm [30], and over years of continuous depth video
in 13 apartments [31] and months of radar [32, 33]; a camera
algorithm that
matched the state of the art on simulated data degraded sharply on months of home video [34],
and an acoustic detector needed source height to bring false alarms down from 32 to 5 per
hour [35]. We therefore report false calls per day of ordinary living.

## Multimodal LLMs as zero-shot judges of video

Training-free video anomaly detection with language models started from captioning frames and scoring
the captions [36]; zero-shot multimodal LLMs tend to be conservative, with high
precision and collapsed recall, and class-specific instructions move the operating
point [37]. For falls in visible-light video, open 8B models reach a fall F1 of about
0.68 in the wild but mostly call a fallen person “lying”, and changing one prompt component moved fall
F1 by up to 13 points [38]; small VLMs prompted on RGB and depth stills are interpretable but
less accurate than specialised models [39]; and Gemini Flash has been checked on
a small set of hospital fall clips [40]. On thermal imagery, benchmarks find that VLMs
fall back on language priors and degrade when the colour map changes [41, 42, 43], and six VLMs evaluated zero-shot on laboratory thermal sequences
of elder-care activities handled large movements but not safety-critical events such as
staggering [44]. To our knowledge, no prior study has evaluated a multimodal LLM as a zero-shot
fall screener on low-resolution thermal video with sound, varied the thermal resolution, rendering or
prompt for it, or reported its false-alarm burden over continuous recording in an occupied home.

## Reliability of hosted models

Hosted LLMs are not deterministic at temperature 0 [45, 46]: across ten
identical runs of text tasks, accuracy varied by up to 15% [47], which has been
traced to batch-size-dependent kernels in serving [48]. Results also depend on prompt wording and
format [49, 50]. We measure both for the screening decision.

## III The screening pipeline

We evaluate the decision stage of a research prototype of Senecta’s in-home monitoring pod, which has run
continuously in one room since September 2026. Figure 1 summarises it. The design rule is record always, analyse on
events: sensors stream all the time, a cheap gate decides when something happened, and only then is a
short clip sent to the language model.

Fig. 1: The prototype. A thermal camera and a microphone stream continuously; a wake gate combines
sound and thermal movement; each wake becomes one short clip (3 s before, 15 s after, extended by
further wakes); the clip is rendered as a video with its sound track and reviewed once by a multimodal
LLM, which answers with a fixed JSON form. This paper evaluates the last two boxes.

## III-A Sensors and streaming

A microcontroller (ESP32-S3) reads a radiometric FLIR Lepton 3.5 thermal camera [51]
( $160\times 120$ pixels, $\approx$ $57\text{\,}\mathrm{\SIUnitSymbolDegree}$ horizontal field of view, $8.7\text{\,}\mathrm{Hz}$ , absolute
temperature per pixel in centikelvin) and an I2S MEMS microphone (INMP441,
 $16\text{\,}\mathrm{kHz}$ mono). Frames are compressed losslessly on the device (median prediction with
Rice coding) and carry a CRC of the original pixels, so the server refuses rather than repairs a corrupted
frame. A server keeps the last minutes in memory and archives every 60 s segment of raw packets to
object storage. The camera was a bench unit, not a finished product: for much of the recording it looked
through a thin polyethylene film window of unspecified composition, and it stood in two places, first
seeing most of the floor and later lower, behind a bed (Section IV-B).

## III-B Wake gate

Every review costs money and time, so the gate decides what is worth a look. It combines a
sound score (how far a microphone impulse rises above the room’s adaptive noise floor, the 20th
percentile of recent levels; $8\text{\,}\mathrm{dB}$ above it maps to 0 and $24\text{\,}\mathrm{dB}$ to 1; sounds
without a sharp attack count half) with a movement score (the changed fraction of a reduced
thermal frame, saturating at 10%). The gate wakes when the product of the two reaches 0.15 with both
signals within $2\text{\,}\mathrm{s}$ , or when movement alone exceeds both 15% of the frame and three times
the room’s recent typical movement on two consecutive frames. A quiet, slow collapse while the room is
already busy does not wake it; we do not evaluate the gate’s misses here.

## III-C Episodes and clips

A wake opens an episode covering $3\text{\,}\mathrm{s}$ before and $15\text{\,}\mathrm{s}$ after it, extended by
further wakes up to $120\text{\,}\mathrm{s}$ . Footage is reviewed in clips of at most $30\text{\,}\mathrm{s}$ ; while
movement keeps an episode open, later clips are cut every $20\text{\,}\mathrm{s}$ of new footage or after
 $10\text{\,}\mathrm{s}$ of quiet. A clip ends early at its last thermal frame when the camera stalls for more
than $4\text{\,}\mathrm{s}$ (the Lepton’s flat-field correction holds the shutter for $\approx$ $1.8\text{\,}\mathrm{s}$ );
a clip whose audio coverage is below 85% is reviewed without its sound track. A cap of 40 reviews an hour
holds back ordinary wakes in busy hours; strong wakes (a high index or large movement) are exempt.

## III-D Rendering the thermal clip as video

The model receives an MP4 rather than temperatures. Each clip is mapped to colour with one fixed scale
for the whole clip (the 2nd and 98th percentiles of all its pixels) through an 8-stop perceptually
ordered palette (black–purple–orange–pale yellow, “inferno”), upscaled with nearest-neighbour
interpolation (a $160\times 120$ frame becomes $480\times 360$ ), and given a $24\text{\,}\mathrm{p}\mathrm{x}$ strip with the
text THERMAL t= $t$ s. Every source frame is kept at its own timestamp (variable frame
rate H.264, CRF 18) and the audio is high-passed at $80\text{\,}\mathrm{Hz}$ , de-clicked and AAC-encoded.

## III-E The request

One request to Gemini 3.8 Flash (a model of the Gemini family [52]; served by Vertex AI,
model identifier gemini-3.8-flash, October 2026) carries the video inline (sampled at 8 frames per
second), a fixed user text (“Review the complete $d$  s thermal incident clip. Audio track present:
…. Trigger time: …. Only the footage is evidence.”), a three-line system instruction, and a
JSON schema; temperature is 0 and the model’s thinking level is low. The deployed instruction,
called v8 below, is:

Review the thermal clip and audio.

Report fall_observed only if you are very certain an upright person collapsed onto the floor.

A person who goes out of view, including dropping behind furniture or below the frame, is not a fall.

The answer has three fields: ends_on (floor, furniture, out_of_view, none, unknown), a
binary verdict and a free-text reason. One deterministic host rule applies: a fall
verdict whose person ends on furniture is turned into no fall (a heavy sit is not a fall). A fall verdict
starts a spoken check-in (“Are you okay?”) in the room; the check-in and the escalation that follows
are outside the scope of this paper.

The previous instruction, v5, was deployed from 23 September until 4 October 2026 and is our main
comparison:

Review the thermal clip and audio.

Report fall_observed only if an upright person visibly collapses onto the floor.

Normal motion, sitting, close-up blobs, and moving out of frame are no_fall_observed.

Its schema asked for ten observation fields before the verdict (scene, person visible, before, after,
transition visible, audio observation, impact sound, visibility limits, evidence times, still supported)
and the client rejected a fall verdict that did not cite a visible transition. v8 replaced it after
replays of the bench recordings showed that v5 called most staged falls that ended out of the camera’s
view a fall, and most deliberate lie-downs on the floor too. Neither prompt was tuned on the public dataset
used below; during development the deployed prompt was only checked on seven windows of that dataset’s
development subjects.

## IV Data

## IV-A Staged falls in a laboratory: eHomeSeniors

The eHomeSeniors dataset [6] records six adults (three performers coached by
a physiotherapist, aged 34–37, and three adults aged 27–29) staging 15 fall types, five repetitions
each, in one $6\times 5$  m laboratory, with a Melexis MLX90640 thermopile array [53] ( $32\times 24$ pixels,
 $55\text{\,}\mathrm{\SIUnitSymbolDegree}$ $\times$ $37.5\text{\,}\mathrm{\SIUnitSymbolDegree}$ ) on the wall at $1.2\text{\,}\mathrm{m}$ . We use the 90 Melexis
recordings ( $92,908$ frames, median $15.5\text{\,}\mathrm{Hz}$ ); the dataset has no audio.
Recordings are labelled only by fall type, with no frame-level times, and each holds several
repetitions, so we located every fall ourselves. An automatic detector proposed collapse times from the
height of the largest warm region; every one of the 90 recordings was then inspected on a strip of frames

title: Automated Materials Data and Knowledge Extraction using Machine Learning and Large Language Models
abstract: Over the past decade, substantial efforts have been devoted to developing machine learning (ML) methods for extracting materials data and, where possible, materials knowledge directly from the scientific literature. This review traces the evolution of these methods from heuristic, rule-based pipelines through natural language processing (NLP) models and transformer-based encoders to, lastly, large language models (LLMs) and agentic systems capable of extracting materials information across multiple modalities, including text, tables, and figures. Beside construction of large, queryable materials databases and knowledge graphs that support downstream materials discovery, we discuss how these advances have enabled new capabilities, such as, generic question answering across materials science, AI co-scientists and chatbots for research assistance, and closed-loop optimization and discovery when integrated with autonomous laboratories. We critically assess the datasets generated using these approaches, their extraction accuracy and computational costs, and the respective strengths and limitations of different methodologies, and even provide practical guidelines for developing more reliable and scalable materials data extraction pipelines. Finally, we identify key open challenges, including the extraction of full materials structure-property-processing-performance tetrahedron at the sample level, the scarcity of reliable benchmark datasets for systematic evaluation, and the resolution of non-standard materials terminology across different document modalities.

body_start:
Abstract

Over the past decade, substantial efforts have been devoted to developing machine learning (ML) methods for extracting materials data and, where possible, materials knowledge directly from the scientific literature. This review traces the evolution of these methods from heuristic, rule-based pipelines through natural language processing (NLP) models and transformer-based encoders to, lastly, large language models (LLMs) and agentic systems capable of extracting materials information across multiple modalities, including text, tables, and figures. Beside construction of large, queryable materials databases and knowledge graphs that support downstream materials discovery, we discuss how these advances have enabled new capabilities, such as, generic question answering across materials science, AI co-scientists and chatbots for research assistance, and closed-loop optimization and discovery when integrated with autonomous laboratories. We critically assess the datasets generated using these approaches, their extraction accuracy and computational costs, and the respective strengths and limitations of different methodologies, and even provide practical guidelines for developing more reliable and scalable materials data extraction pipelines. Finally, we identify key open challenges, including the extraction of full materials structure-property-processing-performance tetrahedron at the sample level, the scarcity of reliable benchmark datasets for systematic evaluation, and the resolution of non-standard materials terminology across different document modalities.

Keywords: Materials data extraction, named entity recognition, relation extraction, large language model, multi-agent framework, knowledge graphs

## 1 Introduction

Materials science can be viewed as a continual effort to understand and exploit the relationships captured by the structure-processing-properties-performance tetrahedron. Experiments, whether computational or physical, probe these relationships across an enormous space of compositions, structures, processing conditions, and applications, with their findings subsequently reported in peer-reviewed journal articles, patents, theses, books and even supplementary information. However, the resulting materials knowledge is predominantly stored in unstructured or semi-structured forms—text, tables, figures, captions, and supporting files—distributed across an enormous and rapidly expanding literature corpus, estimated to contain of the order of $10^{7}$ publications [1, 2]. Only a small fraction of this knowledge is available in structured form through handbooks, curated databases, and archival resources. Thus, while on one hand, the materials literature contains a vast body of evidence, relationships and trends (either established or hidden) that can reveal how materials behave, how their properties depend on structure and processing, and what design principles govern their success in a certain application. On the other hand, this knowledge remains difficult to access systematically at scale.

The distinction between materials data and materials knowledge becomes important in this context. Materials data comprise of individual observations, e.g., a composition synthesized by a particular route, a measured property under specified conditions, or a characterization result reported in a figure or table. Materials knowledge is a more general and compact representation of such observations in the form of relationships, trends, empirical rules, and physical models that enable prediction. Examples include the Hall–Petch relation [3], Hume–Rothery rules [4], and Vegard’s law [5], which allow researchers to generalize beyond individual observations and anticipate the behaviour of previously untested materials. A materials researcher develops such knowledge as part of their formal training and by absorbing the literature, comparing observations, and gradually forming an internal model of composition–processing–structure–property relationships [6]. This process of converting numerous observations into a compact, predictive understanding may be viewed as a form of knowledge compression. It is, however, inherently limited by the amount of literature an individual can access and integrate, and by the difficulty of identifying connections distributed across different studies and subfields.

Machine learning (ML) offers a complementary route to this compression by learning patterns directly from large collections of materials data rather than relying on explicitly formulated physical relations or individual researcher experience. Property-prediction models can learn composition–structure–property relationships, while coupling these models with high-throughput calculations, active learning, and optimization methods allow exploration of materials spaces in a more systematic and efficient manner than possible through efforts of a single human researcher. However, a major bottleneck in this approach is the availability of reliable, machine-readable data. Although the information required to train such ML models is often already present in the literature, but not in a form that can be readily accessed and processed. For example, synthesizing a new polymer or ceramic may require determining suitable precursors, their concentrations, reaction conditions, and, in some cases, a sequence of intermediate reactions by examining synthesis reports across many related materials. Consequently, the central bottleneck is not the absence of materials information, but the gap between the form in which the information exists in published literature and the form in which information is required as structured, machine-actionable data. Manual curation can, and have been, used to produce high-quality databases, but its limited to specific class of materials and use-cases and cannot scale with the volume and diversity of the literature [7, 8, 9].

This gap motivates the development of materials data (and, if possible, directly materials knowledge) extraction methods, particularly those based on natural language processing (NLP) and, more recently, transformer-based large language (LLM) models. The objective is to transform the heterogeneous content of scientific publications—text, tables, figures, and supplementary information—into structured records that can act as a knowledge base for answering materials-related queries or support downstream materials discovery ML pipelines.

This work tracks the evolution of materials data extraction as a progression from manual curation, to computational generation, to automated mining of the experimental literature (see Figure 1). Early databases such as Landolt-Börnstein [10], ICSD [11], the Pauling File [12] and PoLyInfo [13], established highly reliable, expert-curated and gold standard repositories of materials structures and properties. However, their construction is inherently slow and difficult to scale. High-throughput computational approaches provided an alternative by generating data rather than extracting it. Platforms such as the Materials Project [14], AFLOW [15], OQMD [16], NOMAD [17], and Alexandria [18] enabled the systematic calculation of properties for millions of known and hypothetical structures, supporting materials screening beyond the experimentally characterised materials space. However, computational databases cannot readily capture several experimentally relevant aspects of materials, including synthesis and processing conditions, disorder, dopants, and device-level behaviour.

Figure 1: a) The evolution of materials data extraction efforts. b) Different forms of materials data, and the level of maturity and ease of automation of each type.

With the increasing maturity of AI/ML in other domains, rule-based NLP approaches such as ChemDataExtractor [19] began to emerge around 2015 for materials data extraction. These methods typically followed a two-stage pipeline of entity recognition and relation extraction. During the first stage of entity recognition, an ML model identifies and classifies relevant terms present in text or tables into predefined categories such as materials, synthesis methods, characterization methods, or properties. Relation extraction then links these entities using predefined linguistic patterns and domain-specific rules to produce structured property and synthesis records [19, 20, 21]. These approaches provided the first demonstrations of large-scale automated extraction of materials data, but their dependence on hand-crafted rules limited their generalizability across different materials domain. Transformer-based encoders, such as MatBERT, marked the next era, where contextual representations of text enabled more robust entity and relation extraction, although these approaches required dedicated efforts for model development as well as task-specific labeled data [9, 22]. The emergence of large language models (LLMs) around 2023 further shifted the paradigm towards general-purpose extraction. Prompting enabled structured extraction with little or no task-specific training, while fine-tuning enabled more reliable domain-specialized models from relatively small annotated datasets [23, 24, 25]. Beyond improving the scale and flexibility of extraction, LLMs also expanded the target representation from flat material-property records to more comprehensive materials synthesis, processing, structure, and properties records, and to even knowledge graphs [26]. More recently, agentic frameworks have further enhanced the extraction quality by enabling dynamic coordination of specialized models and tools applicable on multiple modalities (figures, tables and text). Knowledge graphs, on the other hand, provide a more efficient relational representation of materials data with explicit provenance, and the ability to achieve higher-level reasoning and hypothesis generation, bringing these models closer to the ultimate goal of materials knowledge extraction rather than mere data extraction.

This review traces this progression in materials data extraction, highlighting the opportunities, limitations, and evolving solutions associated with each era. We thoroughly discuss the databases developed using these approaches, the accuracy and cost of extraction, and the diverse data modalities considered. Finally, we discuss key open challenges and potential opportunities to improve the quality and efficiency of materials data and knowledge extraction from the literature corpus.

## 2 The forms of materials data and the difficulty of extracting them

Before we discuss the different approaches adopted for data extraction, it is important to understand what are the different forms of materials data that are usually targeted and the associated challenges. Mainly materials information is reported in five broad categories: crystallographic structure files, physical property measurements, synthesis and processing procedures, characterization data in the form of images (e.g., micrographs and device performance curves), and spectral or diffraction data. These forms differ substantially in both their amenability to automated extraction and the maturity of existing extraction pipelines, and these two aspects are not necessarily correlated, as noted in Figure 1b. Crystallographic data is the clearest case of both high maturity and high automatability. Its high automatability stems from being structured at the point of generation, with standardized CIF files [27] containing well-defined fields for unit-cell parameters, space group, and atomic coordinates. Thus, extraction simply amounts to parsing a structured file rather than interpreting information from free text. Further, its high maturity is reflected in dedicated repositories such as ICSD [28, 11], CSD [29], and COD [30], which have accumulated and curated on the order of $10^{5}$ – $10^{6}$ entries.

Property data is arguably the most sought-after category of materials data and has consequently attracted extensive development of ML-based extraction pipelines. Several large-scale efforts have produced text-mined databases (e.g., for
thermoelectrics [31], magnetic materials [32, 33],
and general materials [34]), placing this category at moderate-to-high maturity. Despite these efforts, property data still remains only moderately amenable to automated extraction because of four recurring challenges. First, the literature reported terminology is highly variable and lacks standardized forms. The same compound may be reported by its full name, abbreviation, or chemical formula (e.g., “lithium cobalt oxide”, “LCO”, and “LiCoO2”, or in case of doping as ‘5% Mg-doped LiCoO2” or “LiCo0.95Mg0.05O2”). Property names may also be incomplete or require contextual interpretation—for example, ‘strength” could refer to yield, ultimate, or compressive strength. Extraction therefore requires contextual disambiguation beyond than simply accurately extracting and matching to a fixed vocabulary [35]. Second, extracting a complete record often requires resolving dependencies across different parts of a document, since information such as composition, processing conditions, and property values may be distributed across the abstract, methods, tables, and figure captions [36]. Reconstructing a complete composition–structure–processing–property record thus requires linking information spread across these heterogeneous locations. Third, tables, despite their structured appearance, are difficult to parse reliably. Headers may be merged, transposed, or abbreviated, while essential qualifying information (e.g., symbol definitions) may appear only in captions or surrounding text rather than in the table itself [37]. Lastly, even correctly extracted values can be semantically ambiguous as the full information may not be explicitly stated in the document but is rather implicit. A reported composition may represent the nominal target used during synthesis rather than the composition measured experimentally, while a property measured under specific testing conditions may be incorrectly tagged as an intrinsic property of the material. The combination of these challenges makes property-data extraction only moderately amenable to automation despite substantial progress in the field.

Synthesis and processing data remains low in both maturity and ease of automation. While dedicated synthesis databases exist (solid-state synthesis recipes [38], MOF synthesis records [39]), the absence of a structured standard for reporting this information, analogous to that of the CIF format, limits their maturity. In addition to the four challenges described for property extraction, the synthesis extraction entail additional challenges due to its inherent relational and sequential nature—precursors and their quantities, operations, and conditions involved must be correctly linked to one another to arrive at a correct synthesis record. These details are also often partly implicit, with conditions inherited from cited procedures or sometimes simply described as “standard.” This additional relational and sequential complexity makes synthesis data substantially harder to extract. Characterization images, such as micrographs and device performance curves, require visual and contextual reasoning, making them the least developed in both maturity and ease of automation. Few dedicated databases exist [40], while there is an additional need of multimodal reasoning to identify relevant figures, interpret their axes, legends, and scale, and link the visual information to the surrounding scientific text. Such capabilities are only beginning to be explored with vision-language models [41, 42]. Diffraction and other spectral data occupy a more unusual position. Diffraction data, in particular, has a long history of institutionalized curation—the ICDD Powder Diffraction File has served as a reference for phase identification since 1941 and now contains more than one million curated patterns [43], while Rietveld refinement has been widely used to extract structural information from diffraction patterns [44]. However, this maturity has relied largely on manual expert curation, and efforts to extract diffraction data directly from literature figures remain relatively nascent [45, 46, 47, 48, 49]. Other spectral data, including Raman, FTIR, XPS, and NMR, are less mature, with existing resources typically limited to specific techniques or material classes, such as the RRUFF database of mineral Raman and infrared spectra [50]. Overall, we consider this category moderately mature but still difficult to automate, particularly because data must be recovered from published figures, which requires the same multimodal reasoning challenges encountered in characterization-image extraction. Overall, this discussion forms the backdrop in which several efforts for materials data extraction are discussed next. Importantly, not all materials data types have achieved same level of success and each presents a unique set of challenges.

title: PAUSE: Search-Free Steering of Coding Agents Before Their First Source-Code Edit
abstract: Coding agents can invest substantial effort in repository exploration and testing yet still produce unsuccessful patches. Existing online steering methods review trajectories periodically or invoke an advisor when a monitor detects behavioral problems; frequent reviews are costly, and the absence of anomalous behavior does not mean that an agent is on the right track. We propose PAUSE, a framework for steering coding agents with a single planning intervention. Agents reach their first source-code edit at a median of 60% of trajectory progress, after exploration, bug reproduction, and testing. PAUSE intercepts this edit request before it executes, which requires no learned monitor, no search over checkpoints, and no extra model call (search-free). A separate Planner reads the task and the pre-edit transcript and writes one repair plan; the same agent, the Executor, resumes with this plan, keeping its context and workspace. PAUSE applies online, during a live run, and offline, from a recorded trajectory prefix. We evaluate PAUSE on SWE-bench Verified and SWE-bench Multilingual with two Executors and three agent harnesses. With Qwen3-coder as Executor and GPT-5.6 Sol as Planner, online steering improves resolution by 16.8% on Verified in OpenHands and by 14.7% on Multilingual in SWE-agent. In SWE-agent, PAUSE outperforms LivePlan, a rule-triggered advisor, by 3.2% on Verified and 3.7% on Multilingual at similar Planner cost, and is comparable to SICA's periodic overseer at about 11-15% of its Planner cost. Offline, PAUSE recovers 35.4% of eligible failed Verified tasks, and resuming from the recorded prefix uses 33-41% fewer Executor tokens than restarting.
