Abstract.

Coding agents can invest substantial effort in repository exploration and testing yet still produce unsuccessful patches. Existing online steering methods commonly review execution trajectories periodically or invoke an advisor when a monitor detects behavioral problems. Frequent reviews are costly, and the absence of anomalous behavior does not mean that an agent is on the right track. To bridge this gap, we propose PAUSE, a framework for steering coding agents with a single planning intervention.
We find that agents reach their first source-code edit at a median of 60% of trajectory progress, with the preceding work largely devoted to repository exploration, bug reproduction, and testing. This motivates intercepting the request before execution, so that the agent’s accumulated investigation can guide the repair it is about to implement.
Because the first source-code edit directly identifies when to intervene, PAUSE locates this point without a learned monitor, a search over candidate checkpoints, or an extra model call—a property we call search-free. At this point, a separate Planner reads the task and pre-edit transcript to produce one repair plan. The same agent, the Executor, resumes with this plan, retaining its accumulated context and workspace. PAUSE applies both online, during a live run, and offline, from a recorded trajectory prefix.

We evaluate PAUSE on SWE-bench Verified and SWE-bench Multilingual with two Executors and three agent harnesses. With Qwen3-coder as Executor and GPT-5.6 Sol as Planner, online steering in OpenHands improves resolution on Verified by 16.8%, and online steering in SWE-agent improves resolution on Multilingual by 14.7%. In SWE-agent, against LivePlan, which invokes an advisor through rule-based monitoring, PAUSE is more effective at a similar Planner cost, improving resolution by 3.2% and 3.7% on Verified and Multilingual, respectively. Against SICA, which reviews the trajectory periodically, PAUSE remains comparable on both benchmarks while incurring about 11% and 15% of SICA’s Planner cost on Verified and Multilingual, respectively. Offline, PAUSE recovers 35.4% of the eligible failed Verified tasks, and resuming from the recorded prefix uses 33–41% fewer Executor tokens than restarting. These results show that a single planning intervention at the first source-code edit is more effective than rule-based monitoring and competitive with periodic oversight at a small fraction of its cost.

Keywords: 
coding agents, agent steering, planning, trajectory reuse

## 1. Introduction

LLM-based coding agents tackle repository-level issues by inspecting code, making edits, and running commands and tests through an interactive tool interface (Yang et al., 2024; Wang et al., 2025a; Bouzenia et al., 2025).
Existing repair systems gather relevant context through localization and structural code search (Xia et al., 2025; Zhang et al., 2024b), and infer code intent to guide repair (Ruan et al., 2025).
However, agents can still struggle to turn this investigation into a correct repair (Yang et al., 2024).
This motivates online steering, which uses the context accumulated during execution to guide the agent’s subsequent repair decisions (Gandhi et al., 2025b; Nanda et al., 2026; Liu et al., 2026a).

The timing of guidance shapes both the effectiveness and cost of online steering (Liu et al., 2026b).
As shown in Table 1, existing methods decide when to guide either through repeated model-based reviews or by waiting for a detected problem.
With periodic model-based review, methods such as SWE-PRM (Gandhi et al., 2025b) and SICA (Robeyns et al., 2025) repeatedly assess ongoing execution at regular step or time intervals to determine whether guidance is needed.
Each review incurs additional inference cost, while longer intervals can delay useful feedback until the agent has taken further steps along an ineffective path (Liu et al., 2026b).
A fixed schedule also need not align with the point at which accumulated investigation is ready to inform a code change.
To reduce review overhead, LivePlan uses rule-based checks to invoke an advisor when signals such as repetition, stagnation, or skipped phases are detected (Liu et al., 2026b).
This reduces monitoring cost, but intervention remains limited by the coverage of predefined signals, which LivePlan acknowledges may be incomplete (Liu et al., 2026b).
Thus, the absence of a behavioral alarm does not establish that the repair strategy is correct: an agent may follow an orderly workflow while preparing an ineffective change.

We therefore seek a moment to guide repair using the agent’s accumulated investigation, without repeated trajectory reviews or waiting for a behavioral alarm.

The curve marks first source-code edits (median 60.0%); 24 runs without one lie below the divider.A heatmap of 500 trajectories over normalized action progress from 0 to 100 percent. Yellow denotes think actions, blue file reads, green shell commands, red file-editor actions, and gray other or finish actions. The final 24 rows have no source-code edit and appear below a horizontal divider.

Why the first source-code edit?

To identify such a moment, we analyze 500 recorded Qwen3-coder trajectories on SWE-bench Verified.
We define the first source-code edit as the first file-editor request targeting a source-code file of the repository.
We classify recorded actions into five categories: explicit reasoning, file inspection, shell command execution, file editing, and other operations, including termination.
Figure 1 visualizes these sequences over normalized action progress and orders trajectories by their first source-code edit; edits to scratch files or reproduction scripts outside the designated source-code paths are excluded.
Among the 476 trajectories containing such a request, its median position is 60.0% of action progress, and 80.5% occur after the midpoint.
Before this point, command execution is the most common action type and file reads account for 31% of actions, reflecting substantial repository investigation before the proposed source change.
This observation motivates intervening before the proposed source-code edit executes, when accumulated evidence is available to inform the repair and the proposed change remains open to revision.
Our experiments confirm that this point balances the two: an earlier intervention gives the Planner too little of the investigation to ground a plan, whereas a later one arrives after the agent has committed to and built on its own changes, which the plan must then overturn.

Prior work uses explicit planning to coordinate repository edits (Bairi et al., 2024; Tao et al., 2024) and explores planning and execution roles in model collaboration (Lee et al., 2026; Gandhi et al., 2025a).
To guide repair at this point, we introduce PAUSE, a framework that uses the first source-code edit to trigger a single planning intervention.
The request identifies the intervention point directly from the agent’s proposed action and its target path, without a learned monitor, a search over candidate checkpoints, or an additional model call to locate the point; we call this property search-free.
A separate Planner reads the task and the coding agent’s preceding transcript, including inspected code and execution feedback, and returns one natural-language repair plan.
The same coding agent, the Executor, receives this plan and continues from its existing conversation and workspace, retaining its investigation and responsibility for editing and testing without updating its underlying language model.

PAUSE supports online steering and offline recovery.
Online, it blocks the first source-code edit during a live run and adds the Planner’s guidance before resuming the Executor from its live state.
Offline, it restores an existing failed trajectory to a pre-edit state, adds a plan based on the recorded prefix, and resumes the same Executor with its remaining budget.

We evaluate PAUSE on SWE-bench Verified (Jimenez et al., 2024) and SWE-bench Multilingual (Yang et al., 2025), which spans nine programming languages, using two Executors and three agent harnesses.
With Qwen3-coder as Executor and GPT-5.6 Sol as Planner in OpenHands, online steering improves resolution on Verified by 16.8%.
In SWE-agent, it improves resolution by 14.8% and 14.7% on Verified and Multilingual, respectively.
Against LivePlan, which invokes an advisor through rule-based monitoring, PAUSE is more effective at a similar Planner cost, improving resolution by 3.2% and 3.7% on Verified and Multilingual, respectively.
Against SICA, which reviews the trajectory periodically, PAUSE remains comparable on both benchmarks while incurring about 11% and 15% of SICA’s Planner cost on Verified and Multilingual, respectively.
Offline, PAUSE recovers 79 of 223 eligible failed Verified tasks, a recovery rate of 35.4%.
These results show that a single planning intervention at the first source-code edit is more effective than rule-based monitoring and competitive with periodic oversight at a small fraction of its cost.

Our contributions are:

• 

An empirical characterization of the first source-code edit as an opportunity to guide repair after substantial repository investigation.

• 

PAUSE, a search-free framework that gives the same Executor one plan while preserving its context and workspace, supporting online steering and offline recovery.

• 

An evaluation across two benchmarks, two Executors, and three harnesses, showing that PAUSE is more effective than rule-based monitoring at a similar Planner cost and is competitive with periodic oversight at 11–15% of its Planner cost, with controlled studies of intervention timing, planning guidance, and state reuse.

## 2. Related Work

## 2.1. Repository-Level Repair and Planning

SWE-bench frames repository-level repair as resolving real GitHub issues through changes to an existing codebase (Jimenez et al., 2024).
SWE-agent equips language models with interfaces for navigating repositories, editing files, and using execution feedback (Yang et al., 2024).
OpenHands provides an extensible platform in which agents perform software development through code execution and other tools (Wang et al., 2025a).
CodeAgent integrates retrieval, navigation, implementation, and testing tools for repository-level coding (Zhang et al., 2024a), while RepoGraph and LingmaAgent use repository graphs to support context gathering and exploration (Ouyang et al., 2025; Ma et al., 2025).
Alongside these interactive agents, Agentless separates localization, repair, and patch validation into a structured pipeline (Xia et al., 2025).
SHERLOC further studies dedicated diagnostic exploration, transferring localization findings to a downstream repair agent (Tamoyan et al., 2026).
Training-based approaches include SWE-Fixer’s specialized retrieval and editing modules (Xie et al., 2025) and SWE-Gym’s agent and verifier training in executable repository environments (Pan et al., 2025).

Explicit planning also structures reasoning and collaboration.
Plan-and-Solve decomposes problems before solving them (Wang et al., 2023), and Plan-and-Act separates high-level planning from environment actions (Erdogan et al., 2025).
MetaGPT organizes software development through role-specific procedures and intermediate artifacts (Hong et al., 2024), while Self-Collaboration coordinates analyst, coder, and tester roles (Dong et al., 2024).
Within repository repair, planning can compare candidate solutions before implementation.
SWE-Manager trains an 8B model to select among competing repair proposals and synthesize a golden proposal for implementation (Tan et al., 2026).
Its P2A framework separates proposal generation, managerial selection and synthesis, and implementation into distinct roles (Tan et al., 2026).
PAUSE instead obtains one plan from the investigation already accumulated by an executing agent, using its first source-code edit to determine when guidance is provided.
The same Executor then continues with its retained conversation and workspace.

## 2.2. Online Steering

Online steering introduces guidance while an agent is still carrying out its task.
SWE-PRM periodically reviews a recent trajectory window and produces natural-language feedback grounded in a taxonomy of execution inefficiencies (Gandhi et al., 2025b).
SICA includes an asynchronous overseer that examines execution state at regular intervals or key events and can notify or stop an agent when it detects problematic behavior (Robeyns et al., 2025).
LivePlan separates detection from advice: a deterministic monitor checks for signals such as repetition, stagnation, and skipped phases, then requests corrective guidance when a signal fires (Liu et al., 2026b).
These designs make the intervention decision depend on periodic assessment or detected behavioral conditions.
PAUSE uses a different trigger: the first source-code edit identifies an opportunity to guide the repair regardless of whether the preceding trajectory exhibits a behavioral alarm.
This enables a single planning intervention without repeated model-based reviews or a search for an intervention point.

## 2.3. Trajectory Reuse and Reflection

Search-based approaches explore alternative reasoning and action sequences.
Tree of Thoughts searches over alternative reasoning paths (Yao et al., 2023a), while Language Agent Tree Search combines tree search with environment feedback and reflection (Zhou et al., 2024).
For code generation, CodeTree searches over coding strategies, candidate programs, and revisions using execution and agent feedback (Li et al., 2025).

Within repository repair, reusing intermediate work can reduce exploration repeated across attempts.
SWE-Search combines Monte Carlo tree search with iterative refinement to explore alternative repair trajectories (Antoniades et al., 2025).
SWE-Replay retains an archive of sampled trajectories and selects intermediate steps from which to restore state and generate new continuations (Ding and Zhang, 2026).
DARS resamples actions at branching points using prior execution feedback (Aggarwal et al., 2025), while SE-Agent revises, recombines, and refines existing trajectories (Guo et al., 2025).
These methods use intermediate states to diversify the search for a successful repair.
Offline PAUSE reuses a recorded prefix to support a different operation: inserting one plan at a checkpoint determined by the first source-code edit and continuing with the remaining execution budget.

Another approach uses verbal feedback to guide later attempts.
Reflexion stores verbal feedback from prior attempts in an episodic memory to guide subsequent trials (Shinn et al., 2023).
Self-Refine iterates between feedback generation and output revision using the same language model (Madaan et al., 2023).
Tool-grounded feedback supports related correction mechanisms: CRITIC verifies and revises outputs through tool interaction (Gou et al., 2024), while Self-Debugging and LDB use program execution evidence to diagnose and revise generated code (Chen et al., 2024; Zhong et al., 2024).
ChatRepair retains candidate patches and test feedback within a repair conversation to inform subsequent attempts (Xia and Zhang, 2024).

Execution feedback also supports candidate selection: CodeT uses generated tests and execution agreement (Chen et al., 2023), whereas LEVER learns to score candidate programs from their inputs, code, and execution results (Ni et al., 2023).
PAUSE places the planning call within an existing coding trajectory and retains the Executor’s conversation and workspace when delivering guidance.
The Planner reasons over the recorded evidence in a separate invocation, which may use the Executor’s model.

## 3. Method

## 3.1. Problem Formulation

A repository-level repair task consists of an issue description $d$ and an
initial repository snapshot $R_{0}$ (Jimenez et al., 2024). A coding agent, which we call the
Executor, investigates the issue, modifies files, and tests its changes
through an execution harness (Yang et al., 2024; Wang et al., 2025a).
Reasoning-and-acting agents interleave model decisions with observations
from the environment (Yao et al., 2023b). After $t$ completed actions, the Executor’s conversation
 $h_{t}$ contains the system prompt, the task, and the recorded actions and
observations; $W_{t}$ is the resulting workspace. From this state, the
Executor proposes its next action $a_{t+1}$ for the harness to execute.

Online steering aims to improve the final repair during execution. It must
determine when to intervene and what guidance to provide using the task and
available evidence. We call the model supplying repair guidance the Planner.
The available evidence includes inspected code, command outputs, and the
Executor’s own test results. Benchmark evaluator feedback, hidden tests,
reference patches, and future actions are excluded from the planning input.

title: Every Part Has Its Role: Part-of-Speech Effects in LLM Post-Training
abstract: Large language models are typically trained with next-token prediction (NTP), which rewards predicting specific tokens rather than explicitly accounting for the semantic similarities between different words or expressions. Prior work has addressed this limitation by augmenting training data with minimally varying sentences that replace a target word with conceptually related alternatives, e.g., "The tired coach ran home" $\rightarrow$ {"The tired trainer ran home", "The tired instructor ran home", ...}. Such concept augmentation improves performance, but it remains unclear whether its effectiveness depends on where in the sentence the concept is expressed. We reproduce and extend prior work $\textit{beyond nouns}$ to verbs and adjectives, asking whether the part of speech (POS) carrying the concept signal affects perplexity and downstream performance. We find different patterns across evaluation settings: concept augmentation improves perplexity most consistently on news, independent of the POS used, whereas verbs provide the most reliable downstream gains. Despite these behavioral differences, representational analyses using CKA and linear probing show that the conditions yielding the largest downstream gains are not necessarily those that most alter the model's internal representations. Together, these results suggest that the effectiveness of concept augmentation depends on where and how conceptual information is introduced during training.

headings: Every Part Has Its Role: Part-of-Speech Effects in LLM Post-Training
body_start:
Abstract

Large language models are typically trained with next-token prediction (NTP), which rewards predicting specific tokens rather than explicitly accounting for the semantic similarities between different words or expressions. Prior work has addressed this limitation by augmenting training data with minimally varying sentences that replace a target word with conceptually related alternatives, e.g., “The tired coach ran home” $\rightarrow$ {“The tired trainer ran home”, “The tired instructor ran home”, …}. Such concept augmentation improves performance, but it remains unclear whether its effectiveness depends on where in the sentence the concept is expressed. We reproduce and extend prior work beyond nouns to verbs and adjectives, asking whether the part of speech (POS) carrying the concept signal affects perplexity and downstream performance.
We find different patterns across evaluation settings: concept augmentation improves perplexity most consistently on news, independent of the POS used, whereas verbs provide the most reliable downstream gains. Despite these behavioral differences, representational analyses using CKA and linear probing show that the conditions yielding the largest downstream gains are not necessarily those that most alter the model’s internal representations. Together, these results suggest that the effectiveness of concept augmentation depends on where and how conceptual information is introduced during training.

## 1 Introduction

Large language models (LLMs) are predominantly trained with next-token prediction (NTP), which rewards predicting the observed token in a sequence. While highly effective, NTP operates over individual tokens: different words are treated as distinct targets even when they express closely related meanings. Humans, by contrast, reason not only over words but also over concepts: semantic units that connect different linguistic expressions under shared meaning (Shani et al., 2023). For example, “trainer,” “coach,” and “instructor” are distinct lexical forms but closely related expressions of the same concept.

Recent work has begun to incorporate such conceptual relationships into language-model training. In particular, Iyer et al. (2026) introduce concept-aware post-training using synonym and hypernym supervision and show that concept signal can affect both language-model and downstream performance. However, their data-augmentation experiments focus on nouns, leaving open a basic question: does the linguistic category through which a concept is expressed affect the value of concept supervision?

Nouns, verbs, and adjectives encode different aspects of meaning: entities and categories, actions and relations, and properties and
states, respectively. For example, the sentence “The tired coach ran home” can be varied by replacing the noun “coach” with “trainer,” the verb “ran” with “hurried,” or the adjective “tired” with “exhausted.” Each substitution introduces a conceptually related alternative while changing a different component of the sentence. Concept-aware training may therefore induce different forms of invariance depending on which part of speech carries the concept signal.

We extend the data-augmentation approach of Iyer et al. (2026) from nouns to verbs, adjectives, and a combination of all three POS. We retain the standard NTP objective, isolating the effect of where conceptual variation is introduced rather than changing the training loss itself. We post-train Llama-3-8B with synonym and hypernym augmentation across arXiv, news, and YouTube data, and evaluate the resulting models using held-out perplexity and seven downstream NLP tasks.

Our results show that POS meaningfully shapes the effects of concept augmentation. Perplexity effects depend strongly on post-training domain, while verb augmentation provides the most consistent downstream gains across experimental settings. However, the strongest POS varies across domains and tasks, and augmenting all three POSs together does not consistently outperform targeted augmentation. These findings suggest that concept-aware training should not treat all content words as interchangeable sources of concept signal: POS provides an additional design axis for concept supervision.

Figure 1: 
Illustration of POS-specific concept augmentation.
For the same input sentence, we generate synonym and hypernym substitutions
using either context-aware or dictionary-based concept extraction. Rows show
augmentation applied to nouns, verbs, adjectives, or all three POS categories
together.

## 2 Related Work

## Limitations of next-token prediction.

Several lines of work have questioned whether next-token prediction alone provides the right supervision for learning generalizable
semantic structure. Bachmann and Nagarajan (2025) show that teacher-forced NTP can fit the training distribution without learning
the underlying solution required for generalization. At the semantic
level, Shani et al. (2023) argue that token-level probabilities can fragment probability mass across different word choices of the same concept, while
Zhang et al. (2026) show that standard NTP treats semantically valid alternative continuations as competing targets. Our work does
not replace NTP, but asks whether introducing structured semantic variation into the training data changes what is learned under the same objective.

## Concept-aware language modeling.

Recent work has introduced concept-level structure at several points in the language-modeling pipeline. Shani et al. (2023)
study conceptual structure in LLMs and motivate moving beyond purely token-level representations. At the architectural level,
team et al. (2024) introduce Large Concept Models, which autoregressively predict sentence-level semantic embeddings rather
than individual tokens. Other work incorporates higher-level structure while retaining token prediction: Chen et al. (2025) use multi-token
prediction during post-training to encourage learning of coherent multi-token units, Tack et al. (2025) combine NTP with continuous concept representations derived from model activations, and Liu et al. (2026) jointly predict discrete latent concepts and
tokens. These approaches differ in what constitutes a “concept,” but
share the goal of providing supervision above the level of individual tokens.

Figure 2: 
Overview of the concept-augmentation and evaluation pipeline.
Datapoints are drawn from arXiv, news, YouTube, or the combined corpus, and target words are selected by part of speech. For each POS condition, training data are either left unchanged (vanilla) or augmented with context-aware or dictionary-based synonym or hypernym substitutions. Each resulting corpus is used to further train Llama-3-8B with the standard next-token prediction objective, producing 96 post-trained models, which are subsequently evaluated through LoRA-based fine-tuning on seven downstream classification tasks.

Most closely related to our setting, Iyer et al. (2026) incorporate lexical-semantic concepts into post-training using synonyms
and hypernyms through both data augmentation and concept-level objectives. Zhang et al. (2026) instead construct self-supervised sets of contextually equivalent tokens over nouns, verbs, and adjectives
and directly optimize probability mass over those concept sets. Our question is complementary: we retain the standard NTP objective and use only data augmentation, allowing us to isolate how the
part of speech carrying the concept signal affects perplexity,
downstream transfer, training dynamics, and representation geometry.

## 3 Data Processing and Models

We follow the concept extraction, data augmentation, and post-training pipeline introduced by Iyer et al. (2026). Our downstream fine-tuning procedure differs and is described in Section 4.2. We therefore summarize the original pipeline and focus on the modifications introduced in this study.

## 3.1 Data & Concept Supervision Extraction

We use the post-training corpora of Iyer et al. (2026): arXiv abstracts, news text, and YouTube comments, representing scientific, journalistic, and informal language, respectively, as well as their combined condition. These domains let us test whether the effectiveness of POS-specific concept supervision depends on the domain in which it is introduced. We downsample conditions where necessary to balance post-training volume across augmentation variants.

We reprocess each corpus to extend the original noun-only augmentation to four target conditions: nouns, verbs, adjectives, and all POSs, combining all three categories.

For each target POS, we retain the two levels of conceptual resolution from Iyer et al. (2026): synonyms, which provide alternatives
at approximately the same semantic resolution (e.g., coach $\rightarrow$ trainer), and hypernyms, which provide broader conceptual abstractions (e.g., coach $\rightarrow$ 
professional).

We also retain their two extraction procedures: context-aware alternatives generated by an LLM conditioned on the full sentence and target word, and dictionary-based alternatives extracted from WordNet without sentence context.

Figure 1 depicts all of these conditions.

## 3.2 Concept Models

All experiments initialize from Llama-3-8B (Grattafiori et al., 2024). We further post-train a separate model for each POS, post-training corpus, semantic relation, and concept-source condition described above, following the post-training setup of Iyer et al. (2026).

The original study explored two ways to insert concept-supervision during post-training: a modified concept-level training objective and concept-aware data augmentation, in which additional training sentences are created using conceptually related substitutions. Because the data-augmentation approach performs more consistently in the original study, we focus exclusively on this setting. Figure 2 summarizes the full training pipeline, from POS-specific augmentation through standard NTP post-training and downstream fine-tuning.

Figure 3: 
The effect of concept augmentation on perplexity depends
on both post-training corpus and POS.
Perplexity improvement of concept-augmented models relative to
their matched vanilla baselines, separated by post-training corpus.
Positive values indicate lower perplexity after augmentation.
Points show context-aware and dictionary-based augmentation for
nouns (N), verbs (V), adjectives (Adj), and all three parts of
speech (ALL); dotted horizontal lines show the mean improvement
for each corpus. Augmentation improves perplexity most consistently
when post-trained on news ( $+5.5\%$ ), while it decreases performance
on arXiv ( $-8.2\%$ ). The relative effect of each POS also
changes substantially across corpora.

## 3.3 Baselines

We post-train each POS condition on arXiv, news, YouTube, and a combined corpus. Each augmented model is paired with a size-matched vanilla model constructed from the same source sentences. Instead of replacing the target with a synonym or hypernym, the vanilla dataset repeats the original sentence as needed to match the number of augmented training examples. We construct this baseline separately for each POS, relation, and corpus, so augmentation and vanilla models differ in conceptual substitution rather than total training volume.

## 4 Experimental Setup

We now describe the evaluation procedure for the post-trained models. We measure intrinsic language-model performance using held-out perplexity and downstream transfer using seven classification benchmarks, reporting all results relative to matched vanilla models where applicable.

## 4.1 Perplexity

For perplexity, we report the absolute improvement relative to the
matched vanilla model:

 $\mathrm{PPL\ Improvement}=\mathrm{PPL}_{\mathrm{vanilla}}-\mathrm{PPL}_{\mathrm{concept}}.$ 

(1)

Positive values indicate lower, and therefore better, perplexity than the matched vanilla model.

For downstream evaluation, we report the accuracy difference from the corresponding vanilla model:

 $\Delta_{\mathrm{Acc}}=\mathrm{Acc}_{\mathrm{concept}}-\mathrm{Acc}_{\mathrm{vanilla}}.$ 

(2)

This lets us measure what conceptual augmentation contributes beyond additional exposure to the same underlying data.

## 4.2 Downstream Evaluation

We evaluate the post-trained models on the same seven downstream classification tasks as Iyer et al. (2026), but replace the original instruction-style fine-tuning procedure with LoRA-based sequence classification (Hu et al., 2021). This gives every benchmark a common classification formulation and enables validation-based early stopping, which we additionally use to analyze fine-tuning dynamics. We select the checkpoint with the lowest validation loss and report held-out test accuracy as our primary metric, along with weighted precision, recall, F1, and AUC-PR. Full LoRA and optimization hyperparameters are provided in Appendix C.

## 5 Results

We first evaluate how POS-specific concept augmentation affects model performance, beginning with a reproducibility check against the noun-only results of Iyer et al. (2026). We then examine held-out perplexity, the relationship between perplexity and downstream transfer, and performance across the seven downstream tasks.

gain in accuracy averaged over the seven downstream tasks. Points in the
shaded upper-right quadrant improved on both measures. Marker shape and colour

## 5.1 Reproducibility Reality Check

Before comparing POS conditions, we verify that our pipeline recovers the noun-based behavior reported by Iyer et al. (2026). Our noun-only results reproduce the same broad perplexity and downstream trends, providing a sanity check for the expanded experiments. Small differences are expected because we reprocess the post-training data to extract multiple POS categories and use a revised LoRA-based downstream fine-tuning procedure. The full comparison is described in Appendix A.

## 5.2 Perplexity

We first ask whether the effect of concept augmentation on perplexity changes across post-training domains and POSs. Figure 3 reports each augmented model’s improvement relative to its matched vanilla model, where positive values indicate lower perplexity.

The clearest effect is driven by the post-training corpus. Concept augmentation improves perplexity for models post-trained on
news, with an average improvement of $5.5\%$ , while it hurts models post-trained on arXiv by $8.2\%$ . Models trained on YouTube and the
combined corpus show smaller average decreases of $2.6\%$ and $2.5\%$ , respectively. Thus, the same augmentation procedure can improve or worsen perplexity depending on the domain in which it is introduced.

Within each corpus, we also observe a strong interaction with POS. On arXiv, augmenting all POSs is the only condition that improves perplexity on average; among the
individual POS conditions, verbs degrade substantially less than nouns or adjectives. News shows a different pattern: augmentation is
generally beneficial, with adjectives producing the largest gains. For hypernyms, adjective and verb augmentation reduce perplexity by
 $14.4\%$ and $13.8\%$ , respectively, relative to their vanilla baselines. On YouTube, verbs are instead the clearest individual-POS
beneficiary: synonym augmentation improves perplexity by $12.6\%$ , while adjective performance is much more sensitive to the concept
source. The combined corpus again produces a different ordering, with adjective hypernyms improving by $9.8\%$ but adjective synonyms
substantially worsening perplexity.

Overall, there is no single POS whose augmentation consistently lowers perplexity. Rather, the effect of POS is
conditioned on both the post-training domain and the semantic relation being augmented. This domain dependence motivates looking
beyond perplexity alone when evaluating whether the resulting models learn more useful concept representations.

## 5.3 Perplexity and Downstream

compares intrinsic and extrinsic effects by plotting each model’s perplexity improvement against its downstream accuracy gain, both

limitations:
Several lines of work have questioned whether next-token prediction alone provides the right supervision for learning generalizable
semantic structure. Bachmann and Nagarajan (2025) show that teacher-forced NTP can fit the training distribution without learning
the underlying solution required for generalization. At the semantic
level, Shani et al. (2023) argue that token-level probabilities can fragment probability mass across different word choices of the same concept, while
Zhang et al. (2026) show that standard NTP treats semantically valid alternative continuations as competing targets. Our work does
not replace NTP, but asks whether introducing structured semantic variation into the training data changes what is learned under the same objective.
conclusion:
Our results show that the usefulness of concept augmentation depends on where the concept signal is introduced. Verbs provide the most consistent downstream gains, while the strongest POS still varies across domains and tasks. In contrast, augmenting all three POS categories together does not reliably outperform targeted augmentation. This suggests that concept supervision is not simply additive. Different POS categories encode different kinds of semantic structure, and exposing the model to more conceptual variation does not necessarily produce more useful representations. One possible explanation for the strength of verbs is that they encode actions and relations that organize the event structure of a sentence, so varying their word choice may encourage invariance to surface form while preserving relational meaning.

The perplexity and CKA results further suggest a distinction between fitting the post-training distribution and preserving transferable structure. Models that move further from the pretrained representation achieve lower further-training loss, but also have higher held-out perplexity. At the same time, the conditions that produce the largest representational change are not the conditions that transfer best: all-POS models diverge most under CKA, whereas verb models remain comparatively close to the base model while providing stronger downstream performance. This pattern is consistent with post-training specialization, where stronger fitting to the observed next-token distribution need not preserve the structure most
useful outside that distribution (Bachmann and Nagarajan, 2025).

Linear probing provides a complementary result. POS information becomes more linearly decodable after further training, but much of this effect also appears in matched vanilla models. All-POS augmentation produces the clearest concept-specific probe increase, yet does not yield the strongest downstream performance. Conversely, verb augmentation transfers well without producing
unusually large POS-probe gains. The probe therefore appears to operate at too coarse a level of resolution to explain the behavioral differences. Concept augmentation may instead change semantic structure within a POS, such as event structure among verbs, entity categories among nouns, or attribute
structure among adjectives. Together, the CKA and probing results suggest that the usefulness of concept augmentation depends less on how much the

title: Broadband Mid-Wave Infrared Imaging Enabled by All-Silicon Hyperboloid Metalens
abstract: The mid-wave infrared (MWIR, 3-5 microns) is indispensable for thermal sensing, gas detection, long-range imaging, and free-space optical communications. Meta-optics offer a compact, lightweight, and potentially low-cost alternative to conventional refractive optics, making them attractive for size, weight, and power (SWaP)-constrained systems. However, their strong chromatic dispersion has largely restricted imaging to narrow spectral bands. Here, we demonstrate broadband imaging across the full 3-5 micron MWIR band using a single-layer silicon metasurface coupled with computational reconstruction. Remarkably, the reconstruction model is adapted using only four image captures, overcoming large training data requirements and enabling broadband image recovery despite the strongly wavelength-dependent optical response. In contrast to approaches that engineer complex, dispersion-optimized metalens profiles for broadband operation, our method leverages the wavelength-dependent information encoded by a simple 2cm diameter hyperboloid metalens. We show that this metasurface captures sufficient broadband intensity information for computational reconstruction across the entire MWIR band. These results establish a simple route toward broadband computational meta-optics without requiring broadband achromatic metalens designs, offering a promising platform for compact MWIR imaging systems.

title: S-EDL: Eliciting Self-Evidence from Sequence Likelihoods for Semantic Calibration of LLMs
abstract: Calibrating large language models (LLMs) in open-ended generation is uniquely challenging because many distinct token sequences can express the same underlying meaning. Prior calibration techniques target either fixed-set classification confidence or the binary correctness of individual strings, making them inherently ill-suited for the dynamic, multi-string nature of open-ended semantic outcomes. To bridge this gap, we introduce S-EDL, a novel evidential method that natively optimizes LLMs for semantic calibration. By eliciting evidence from the sequence likelihoods of the model itself, S-EDL constructs a differentiable Dirichlet prior over prompt-specific semantic classes. Optimizing the evidential loss under this prior yields a calibration-aware training signal over variable semantic classes, completely bypassing the need for fixed multiple-choice options. Evaluations across four open-ended benchmarks and three models demonstrate that S-EDL substantially reduces semantic calibration error while improving accuracy. By aligning generative likelihoods with semantic correctness, this work establishes a framework for deploying trustworthy LLMs in complex, open-ended applications. Code is available at: https://github.com/sandylaker/s-edl.

body_start:
Abstract

Calibrating large language models (LLMs) in open-ended generation is uniquely challenging because many distinct token sequences can express the same underlying meaning. Prior calibration techniques target either fixed-set classification confidence or the binary correctness of individual strings, making them inherently ill-suited for the dynamic, multi-string nature of open-ended semantic outcomes. To bridge this gap, we introduce S-EDL, a novel evidential method that natively optimizes LLMs for semantic calibration. By eliciting evidence from the sequence likelihoods of the model itself, S-EDL constructs a differentiable Dirichlet prior over prompt-specific semantic classes. Optimizing the evidential loss under this prior yields a calibration-aware training signal over variable semantic classes, completely bypassing the need for fixed multiple-choice options. Evaluations across four open-ended benchmarks and three models demonstrate that S-EDL substantially reduces semantic calibration error while improving accuracy. By aligning generative likelihoods with semantic correctness, this work establishes a framework for deploying trustworthy LLMs in complex, open-ended applications. Code is available at: https://github.com/sandylaker/s-edl.

## 1 Introduction

Large language models (LLMs) are increasingly used for open-ended reasoning tasks, where reliable confidence estimates are important for deciding when model outputs can be trusted [28, 32, 56, 24]. Early research has primarily focused on multiple-choice question answering (MCQA), where calibration can be defined over a small set of answer labels [48, 53, 37, 25]. Open-ended generation is more subtle: many distinct token sequences can express the same answer, and the probability assigned to a surface form does not necessarily reflect confidence in its semantic content.

Prior work has studied open-ended uncertainty and calibration through several related targets. Semantic uncertainty metrics [20, 12] sample multiple generations and group equivalent responses to evaluate the predictive distribution over semantic classes. Building on this perspective, semantic calibration [33] translates this grouping concept into an evaluation metric for open-ended generation. In parallel, verbal confidence calibration methods [18, 43, 52, 30, 3, 9, 55] teach models to report a confidence score of correctness. However, this calibrates the binary correctness of a single response rather than the underlying distribution over alternative semantic answers. Thus, a gap remains: how to fine-tune open-ended LLMs under a semantic calibration objective.

Evidential deep learning (EDL) natively bridges this gap. By placing a Dirichlet prior over categorical probabilities, it explicitly models the strength of evidence for multiple competing meanings, allowing calibration losses to act on distributions over semantic meanings. Building on this, we propose S-EDL, a self-evidenced EDL method tailored for semantic calibration. Unlike conventional EDL methods that require a fixed set of answer labels [39, 7], S-EDL accommodates the dynamic nature of open-ended generation by transforming the sequence likelihoods of the model into a differentiable evidence vector. This formulation allocates greater evidential support to semantic classes backed by highly probable strings. The evidence vector then parametrizes a Dirichlet prior over the semantic outcomes, providing a calibration-aware training signal. Our contributions are three-fold:

• 

We extend EDL from fixed-choice calibration to open-ended semantic calibration, allowing LLMs to optimize their confidence over diverse semantic meanings.

• 

We introduce a novel parametrization that derives a differentiable evidence vector from the model’s sequence likelihoods. This formulation also theoretically unifies post-hoc metrics such as Semantic Entropy [20, 12] under a common evidential framework.

• 

Across three models and four open-ended benchmarks, S-EDL jointly improves average accuracy and calibration over supervised fine-tuning (SFT), reducing average calibration error by up to roughly 1/3.

## 2 Related work

From MCQA to semantic calibration. Early LLM calibration focused on MCQA, where a fixed label set enables standard classification-style methods, including Bayesian low-rank adaptation [48, 53, 37, 42] and evidential approaches [25]. Open-ended generation introduces a level mismatch: many distinct sequences can express the same answer. Semantic uncertainty metrics [20, 12, 11, 34, 36, 6] sample generations and group by meaning, and semantic calibration [33] turns this view into a calibration target for open-ended generation. Our work follows this semantic line.

Verbal and token-level calibration. A separate line of work asks models to emit a scalar correctness score [18, 43, 52, 30, 3, 9, 55], which calibrates a Bernoulli pushforward (correct vs. incorrect) of the output distribution rather than a categorical distribution over semantic outcomes. Meanwhile, SelfReflect [19] captures the categorical distribution by a verbalized string. Token-level methods such as label smoothing [15, 44], temperature scaling [41, 22], RCFT [50], and CATTO [35], regularize per-token distributions, supervising a different granularity than the semantic marginal targeted here.

Evidential deep learning. EDL [31, 39, 10, 7, 17, 5, 4, 54] places a Dirichlet prior over class probabilities through an evidence vector. Although previous work has applied EDL to calibrate LLMs in MCQA [25] and detect misbehavior in vision-language models [16], S-EDL is, to the best of our knowledge, the first instantiation of EDL for calibrating LLMs in open-ended generation.

## 3 Background

## 3.1 Semantic calibration in open-ended LLM generation

Our work focuses on calibration in open-ended generation, for which we adopt the framework of B-calibration [33]. Let $\mathcal{D}$ be a distribution over prompt-completion pairs $(x,y)\in\mathcal{V}^{*}\times\mathcal{V}^{L}$ , where $x$ is a prompt over vocabulary $\mathcal{V}^{*}$ and $y\in\mathcal{V}^{L}$ is a ground-truth completion of length $L$ . An autoregressive LLM $p_{\bm{\theta}}$ with parameters $\bm{\theta}\in\Theta$ assigns probability $p_{\bm{\theta}}(z|x)$ to each candidate response $z\in\mathcal{V}^{L}$ . Because distinct token sequences can convey the same meaning (e.g., “half” vs. “0.5”), B-calibration [33] introduces a collapsing function $B:\mathcal{V}^{*}\times\mathcal{V}^{L}\rightarrow\mathbb{N}$ mapping each prompt-response pair to a global semantic class, a raw identifier $s\in\mathbb{N}$ . We write $s:=B(x,z)$ for a generation’s class and $s^{*}:=B(x,y)$ for the ground-truth class of $(x,y)$ . The collapsing function $B$ can be implemented by a verification tool or an LLM-as-judge that clusters responses by meaning.
A semantic distribution is then defined as the categorical distribution over semantic classes:

 $\pi_{x}(s):=\textstyle\sum_{z\,:\,B(x,z)=s}p_{\bm{\theta}}(z|x),\quad s\in\mathbb{N},z\in\mathcal{V}^{L}.$ 

(1)

Further, denote the top class $s_{x}^{\text{top}}:={\arg\max}_{s}\pi_{x}(s)$ and the semantic confidence $\mathrm{conf}(x):=\pi_{x}(s_{x}^{\text{top}})$ . Semantic calibration requires that the confidence aligns with the true probability of correctness:

 $\mathbb{E}_{(x,y)\sim\mathcal{D}}\!\left[\,\mathbbm{1}\{s_{x}^{\text{top}}=s^{*}\}\,\big|\,\mathrm{conf}(x)\,\right]=\mathrm{conf}(x)\quad\text{almost surely.}$ 

That is, among all prompts for which the model reports semantic confidence $c$ , the top semantic class should indeed be correct with frequency $c$ [33].

## 3.2 Evidential deep learning

The calibration objective above asks the model to report not just which semantic class is most likely but also how confident it is in that belief. EDL [39, 31] provides a framework for the latter: rather than predicting a single categorical $\bm{p}\in\Delta^{K}$ over $K$ classes, it predicts a distribution over $\bm{p}$ , accounting for uncertainty over class probabilities instead of training only against a point estimate.

Dirichlet prior and evidence. In this subsection, $k\in[K]$ denotes a generic class index for a standard fixed- $K$ classification problem, separate from the semantic-label notation of Section 3.1. EDL places a Dirichlet prior $\text{Dir}(\bm{p};\bm{\alpha})$ on $\bm{p}\in\Delta^{K}$ , with Dirichlet parameters $\bm{\alpha}=(\alpha_{k})_{k\in[K]}\in[1,+\infty)^{K}$ built from a non-negative evidence vector $\bm{e}=(e_{k})_{k\in[K]}\in\mathbb{R}_{\geq 0}^{K}$ via $\alpha_{k}=e_{k}+1$ .

Each $e_{k}$ represents the accumulated support for class $k$ . Conventional EDL employs a classification model $f_{\bm{\theta}}$ to predict the evidence directly, $\bm{e}=\text{SoftPlus}(f_{\bm{\theta}}(x))$ , and the Dirichlet mean serves as the predictive distribution: $\hat{p}_{k}=\mathbb{E}_{\bm{p}\sim\text{Dir}(\cdot;\bm{\alpha})}[p_{k}]=\frac{\alpha_{k}}{\alpha_{0}},\text{with \emph{Dirichlet strength} }\alpha_{0}=\textstyle\sum_{k=1}^{K}\alpha_{k}.$ 

EDL training objective. Given a one-hot target $\bm{q}=(q_{k})_{k\in[K]}\in\{0,1\}^{K}$ with $q_{k}=\mathbbm{1}\{k=t\}$ , Sensoy et al. [39] learn the model’s parameter $\bm{\theta}\in\Theta$ by minimizing the Bayes risk of MSE objective

 $\mathcal{L}_{\text{MSE}}(\bm{\theta})=\mathbb{E}_{\bm{p}\sim\text{Dir}(\cdot;\bm{\alpha})}\|\bm{q}-\bm{p}\|_{2}^{2}=\sum_{k=1}^{K}\left(q_{k}-\frac{\alpha_{k}}{\alpha_{0}}\right)^{2}+\sum_{k=1}^{K}\frac{\alpha_{k}(\alpha_{0}-\alpha_{k})}{\alpha_{0}^{2}(\alpha_{0}+1)},$ 

(2)

which admits a closed form. Previous work IB-EDL [25] has shown that EDL methods are very effective in calibrating LLMs in the MCQA setting, but their approach is limited to a fixed set of options such as A/B/C/D. In the following section, we move a step forward and instantiate this framework in the open-ended generation setting, deriving $\bm{e}$ from the LLM’s own generations.

## 4 Methodology

## 4.1 Motivation

Given EDL’s effectiveness for calibrating LLMs in MCQA, we now discuss the adaptations required to apply it in open-ended generation.
Instantiating the EDL framework in this setting hinges on one design choice: how to parametrize the evidence vector $\bm{e}$ . Conventional EDL learns $\bm{e}$ through a dedicated prediction head whose output dimension equals the number of classes. This recipe does not transfer to our setting for two reasons. First, the relevant semantic class inventory is prompt-dependent and not known in advance, so there is no canonical fixed output space. Second, and most fundamentally, the distribution whose calibration we ultimately care about is $p_{\bm{\theta}}(\cdot|x)$ ; routing evidence through an independent head decouples it from the very object we aim to calibrate. We therefore look for a parametrization that derives $\bm{e}$ from $p_{\bm{\theta}}(\cdot|x)$ .

A natural choice for constructing $\bm{e}$ is utilizing $\pi_{x}$ itself, which already encodes how $p_{\bm{\theta}}(\cdot|x)$ distributes mass over semantic classes. Since $\mathcal{V}^{L}$ is typically vast, Nakkiran et al. [33] estimate $\pi_{x}$ from $N$ i.i.d. Monte-Carlo samples $z^{(i)}\sim p_{\bm{\theta}}(\cdot|x)$ with semantic classes $s^{(i)}=B(x,z^{(i)})$ , which induce the prompt-specific semantic class set $\mathcal{S}_{x}:=\{s^{(i)}:i\in[N]\}\subset\mathbb{N}$ . Further details regarding the empirical construction of $\mathcal{S}_{x}$ in edge cases are in Section B.1. The plug-in estimator of $\pi_{x}$ is then

 $\hat{\pi}_{x}(s)=\tfrac{1}{N}\textstyle\sum_{i=1}^{N}\mathbbm{1}[s^{(i)}=s],\quad s\in\mathcal{S}_{x}.$ 

(3)

However, this histogram is not a suitable evidence vector for EDL training. Once the samples are drawn, the class indicators are constants with respect to $\bm{\theta}$ , so an evidence vector proportional to $\hat{\pi}_{x}$ provides no differentiable path from the EDL loss back to the model parameters. In addition, the histogram treats all samples equally, regardless of their likelihood under $p_{\bm{\theta}}(\cdot\mid x)$ . This is misaligned with the evidential interpretation of $\bm{e}$ : a semantic class supported by high-likelihood generations should contribute more evidence than one represented only by low-likelihood samples.

Desiderata. These observations lead to two desiderata for parametrizing evidence $\bm{e}$ :

(a) 

The parametrization should assign more evidence to semantic classes supported by high-likelihood completions, so that likely completions contribute more to evidence.

(b) 

The parametrization should remain differentiable through the sample log-likelihoods, so that the EDL loss can update the likelihoods underlying the sampled semantic estimate.

Next, we instantiate these desiderata through a Monte-Carlo estimate of a tempered semantic distribution, and use this estimate to define a Dirichlet prior over the sampled semantic classes.

## 4.2 Formulation of self-evidence

Throughout this subsection, we fix the input prompt $x$ and drop the subscript from prompt-specific quantities (e.g., $\pi_{x}$ to $\pi$ , $\mathcal{S}_{x}$ to $\mathcal{S}$ ) to lighten notation; all such objects remain implicitly conditional on $x$ . We work directly with semantic labels $s\in\mathcal{S}$ , without introducing a separate local class index. In addition, we use the term self-evidence to refer to evidential support constructed from the LLM’s own Monte-Carlo samples. At the sample level, each generation $z^{(i)}$ receives a scalar self-evidence weight $u^{(i)}$ ; at the class level, these weights aggregate into the self-evidence vector $\bm{e}$ .

Tempered semantic distribution. For a scalar $\beta\geq 1$ , we define the tempered semantic distribution over classes $s\in\mathcal{S}$ and $z,z^{\prime}\in\mathcal{V}^{L}$ as

 $\pi_{\beta}(s):=\frac{\sum_{z\,:\,B(x,z)=s}p_{\bm{\theta}}(z|x)^{\beta}}{\sum_{z^{\prime}\in\mathcal{V}^{L}}p_{\bm{\theta}}(z^{\prime}|x)^{\beta}}.$ 

(4)

For $\beta=1$ , Eq. 4 recovers the standard semantic distribution $\pi$ in Eq. 1.
For $\beta>1$ , raising per-sequence likelihoods to a higher power shifts mass toward classes that the model supports with high-confidence sequences, formalizing desideratum (a).

Self-evidence estimator. Direct evaluation of Eq. 4 is intractable because both the classwise numerator and the global normalizer require sums over $\mathcal{V}^{L}$ . We therefore estimate $\pi_{\beta}$ from the same $N$ Monte-Carlo samples introduced in Section 4.1. Writing $\ell^{(i)}:=\log p_{\bm{\theta}}(z^{(i)}|x)$ for teacher-forcing log-likelihood for sample $i$ , we assign to each sample the self-evidence weight

 $u^{(i)}:=\exp\!\left((\beta-1)\,\ell^{(i)}\right)=p_{\bm{\theta}}(z^{(i)}|x)^{\beta-1}.$ 

(5)

The exponent is $\beta-1$ rather than $\beta$ because the samples $z^{(i)}$ are themselves drawn from $p_{\bm{\theta}}(\cdot|x)$ , so multiplying by $p_{\bm{\theta}}(z^{(i)}|x)^{\beta-1}$ recovers the $p_{\bm{\theta}}^{\beta}$ terms of $\pi_{\beta}$ in Eq. 4 (made precise in Proposition 1). Because $u^{(i)}$ is a smooth function of $\ell^{(i)}$ , gradients can pass through the sample log-likelihoods to $\bm{\theta}$ and satisfy desideratum (b).
We aggregate the weights within each semantic class and normalize:

 $U_{s}:=\!\!\!\!\!\!\!\!\sum_{i\in[N]\,:\,s^{(i)}=s}\!\!\!\!\!\!\!\!u^{(i)},\qquad\hat{\pi}_{\beta}(s):=\frac{U_{s}}{\sum_{r\in\mathcal{S}}U_{r}}.$ 

(6)

A natural question is whether this estimator $\hat{\pi}_{\beta}$ recovers the true tempered distribution $\pi_{\beta}$ as the number of samples grows. The next result confirms this (see the proof in Section A.1).

Proposition 1.

As $N\to\infty$ , $\hat{\pi}_{\beta}(s)\xrightarrow{\text{a.s.}}\pi_{\beta}(s)$ for every $s\in\mathcal{S}$ .

Connection to Semantic Entropy and the practical choice of $\beta$ . Semantic Entropy (SE) [20, 12] also aggregates samples by their sequence probabilities $p_{\bm{\theta}}(z^{(i)}|x)$ , which under Eq. 5 corresponds to the special case $\beta=2$ . In our experiments, we adopt a small value $\beta=1.2$ (ablation in Section 5.5). The choice of $\beta$ reflects the two methods’ different purposes: SE measures the uncertainty as a post-hoc metric, while S-EDL uses $\pi_{\beta}$ as a training signal that drives gradient updates (Section 4.3).

Self-evidence vector and Dirichlet prior. We finally convert $\hat{\pi}_{\beta}$ into an evidential prior by distributing the sample budget $N$ over the semantic classes according to the estimated tempered distribution:

 $e_{s}:=N\cdot\hat{\pi}_{\beta}(s),\qquad\alpha_{s}:=e_{s}+1,\qquad s\in\mathcal{S}.$ 

(7)

Because $\hat{\pi}_{\beta}$ is a probability vector, the Dirichlet strength is determined a priori by the sample budget and the semantic class count:
 $\alpha_{0}=\sum_{s\in\mathcal{S}}\alpha_{s}=N+|\mathcal{S}|$ .
This differs from conventional EDL, where the model freely predicts the per-class evidences $e_{k}$ (equivalently, the Dirichlet parameters $\alpha_{k}=e_{k}+1$ ), so the total strength $\alpha_{0}=\sum_{k}\alpha_{k}$ is not fixed a priori. Here $\alpha_{0}=N+|\mathcal{S}|$ is pinned by construction, and all flexibility in the prior is routed through $\hat{\pi}_{\beta}$ . The resulting $\text{Dir}(\cdot;\bm{\alpha})$ is fed into the MSE loss of Eq. 2, completing the differentiable path promised by desideratum (b), as the entire computational chain $\ell^{(i)}\rightarrow u^{(i)}\rightarrow\hat{\pi}_{\beta}\rightarrow\bm{e}\rightarrow\bm{\alpha}\rightarrow\mathcal{L}_{\text{MSE}}$ is differentiable w.r.t. $\bm{\theta}$ .

In training, we optimize the $\mathcal{L}_{\text{MSE}}$ jointly with standard supervised fine-tuning (SFT). The SFT loss retains the next-token learning signal, while the evidential term provides the semantic-level calibration signal. Let $\mathcal{L}_{\text{SFT}}$ denote the next-token cross-entropy loss on a pair $(x,y)$ . Our final objective then is

 $\mathcal{L}_{\text{S-EDL}}(\bm{\theta})=\mathcal{L}_{\text{SFT}}(\b
conclusion:
We presented S-EDL, a method that constructs a Dirichlet prior over prompt-specific semantic classes from a model’s own sequence likelihoods, yielding a differentiable evidential objective for fine-tuning LLMs toward semantic calibration. Our gradient analysis shows that this objective conservatively reallocates probability mass across semantic outcomes, raising the likelihoods of sequences in the ground-truth class while suppressing those of the most overconfident incorrect alternative. Empirically, this reallocation produces simultaneous gains in accuracy and calibration. More broadly, our results suggest that grounding calibration objectives in a model’s own generative distribution offers a principled path toward trustworthy open-ended LLMs.

Limitations. While our find-first algorithm mentioned above substantially accelerates semantic grouping, the associated sampling and clustering steps entail a moderate training overhead compared to standard SFT. Additionally, for general tasks that necessitate an LLM judge, this requirement imposes unavoidable memory overhead and potential noise in clustering outcomes. To streamline this process, future work could bypass external verifiers or LLMs entirely by leveraging the hidden representations of generated sequences to estimate semantic dispersion, conceptually similar to methods like EigenScore [6]. Finally, we have not yet tested S-EDL on long-context tasks or domains where semantic equivalence is intrinsically difficult to define, such as code generation. Adapting S-EDL to these challenging scenarios remains an important direction for future exploration.

title: Robot Generalization Beyond Volume: The Diversity Path via Zero-Shot Capabilities
abstract: General-purpose robots must handle tasks, objects and environments they were never trained on, yet zero-shot generalization remains one of the least solved problems in physical AI. In digital AI, zero-shot capability grew with the volume and, above all, the diversity of training data, much of it sourced from the crowd. Robotics instead relies on paid collection by a few well-funded teams, which yields volume without diversity. We formulate zero-shot generalization in physical AI as coverage of the deployment distribution, and show that more samples from the same collectors shrink the unseen region only slowly, while each new contributor can extend it. Building on this and on zero-shot learning, we propose a shared latent space for robot actions that combines multi-modal alignment, generative augmentation, and noisy-label learning. As a scalable source of diverse data, we propose a community of developers building applications on one standard, approachable robot, Origami. We close with a testable hypothesis and an evaluation protocol relating real-robot zero-shot success to the diversity of contributed data.

body_start:
Abstract

General-purpose robots must handle tasks, objects and environments they were never trained on, yet zero-shot generalization remains one of the least solved problems in physical AI. In digital AI, zero-shot capability grew with the volume and, above all, the diversity of training data, much of it sourced from the crowd. Robotics instead relies on paid collection by a few well-funded teams, which yields volume without diversity. We formulate zero-shot generalization in physical AI as coverage of the deployment distribution, and show that more samples from the same collectors shrink the unseen region only slowly, while each new contributor can extend it. Building on this and on zero-shot learning, we propose a shared latent space for robot actions that combines multi-modal alignment, generative augmentation, and noisy-label learning; As a scalable source of diverse data, we propose a community of developers building applications on one standard, approachable robot, Origami. We close with a testable hypothesis and an evaluation protocol relating real-robot zero-shot success to the diversity of contributed data.

Figure 1: Examples of zero-shot generalization, shown on our desktop prototype. (a) Opening a bottle with a spoon: everyday human know-how that is rarely captured in images and, to our knowledge, absent from robot data. (b) Operating a puppet: expert skill with no robot data. (c) An elephant-shaped watering can and an artificial plant: a long-tail object combined with a semantic judgment, since the right outcome is to recognize that the plant needs no water. No single team can anticipate and collect such cases; a diverse community of developers brings them within reach.

## 1 Introduction

In recent years, several reports have projected strong growth for robotics through 2050. McKinsey estimates a $370B general-purpose robotics market by 2040 [59], Japan has set a national target of 10 million AI robots by 2040 [64], and Morgan Stanley projects a $5T humanoid market by 2050 [61]. These projections are driven by falling hardware costs, growing AI capabilities, and adoption that starts with developers and spreads through society. However, to achieve the true return on investment in physical AI, robot generalization is a major hurdle, and existing research has not yet found scalable solutions [100, 4].

The idea that an individual, on a given day, arrives home with a new appliance and hands it to their home robot, which has never seen the object before, is the promise of general-purpose robotics, as illustrated in Figure 1. A general autonomous system should be capable of inferring the new object’s affordances, selecting a suitable grasp, and completing tasks with it [3, 46]. Current robotic systems perform poorly at this capability, known as zero-shot generalization [100, 4]. Zero-shot generalization has been the target of extensive studies over the past decades in the field of digital AI such as computer vision [50, 92], large language models [71, 8], audio [70] and multi-modal learning [23, 22, 21]. We argue that it determines whether robots remain confined to controlled settings or become general-purpose economic assets.

In digital AI, zero-shot generalization has progressed as a function of the volume and diversity of data [16, 23]. As illustrated in Figure 2 volume is the density with which each situation is represented in the latent space, and diversity is the footprint those situations cover. This mirrors a familiar result for Gaussian processes: posterior uncertainty shrinks only near observed inputs, so spreading samples across the input space reduces uncertainty far more than repeating them in one region [76]. Volume helps AI systems recognize patterns accurately, but diversity allows them to interpolate within the latent space and act on concepts they have never seen. Seminal research and industry efforts have demonstrated zero-shot capabilities in large language models (LLMs) [8, 47], computer vision [69], and other fields [70, 32]. Robotics has yet to show comparable zero-shot capability. Moreover, the problem of diversity has been largely overlooked, as industry and research efforts have prioritized demonstrations of robots performing single tasks [13, 98]. Industrial and early-stage robots are typically deployed for a single, repetitive task, and each new task requires reprogramming or new training data [6, 100]. A robot able to perform an array of tasks within the same facility, adapting to new parts, layouts and procedures, would amortize its cost across many functions and lower the integration cost of each new task. For instance, in a warehouse, a robot trained to pick a given type of product could take on new types of object, or develop new tasks. In elderly care, a robot that delivers meals could assist carers with preparing food, a new task with new handling demands [78]. Further examples of zero-shot settings are depicted in Figure 1,

In this paper, we propose a novel approach based on our prior work in zero-shot and noisy-label learning applied in physical AI. Our approach combines a crowd-sourced data collection with recent advances in zero-shot generalization, generative AI, learning from noisy labels and scalable trust and safety [23, 28, 19]. We argue that generalization will emerge from structured data acquisition combined with community-driven crowd-sourcing. This combination allows us to acquire large volumes of data safely, while widening the range of scenarios, objects, situations and environments far beyond what any single engineering team could cover. Unlike digital AI, robots must also transfer what they learn in simulation to the physical world, where simulation never fully matches reality, a challenge known as the sim-to-real gap [99, 81]. A community running the same robotic platform in both simulation and reality exposes that gap at scale, and provides the tools to close it.

The remainder of this paper is organized as follows. Section 2 reviews how digital AI reached zero-shot behavior, what builds a latent space, how each training stage has drawn on crowd-sourced data, and how learning from imperfect data can absorb noisy contributions. Section 3 presents our approach. We first formulate zero-shot generalization in physical AI as coverage of the deployment distribution, showing why more data from the same collectors closes the gap only slowly, while each new contributor can widen it. We then describe a shared latent space for robot actions built from multi-modal alignment, generative augmentation, and noisy-label and uncertainty learning, in which safety is part of the space from pre-training onward and seen/unseen detection lets the robot hand control to a human (Section 3.2). Real2Sim2Real treats simulation and reality as noisy teachers of each other across a community running the same robot (Section 3.3), and a community of developers building on one standard, approachable robot provides the data, with a cost model for each contributed hour (Section 3.4). Section 4 sets out a testable hypothesis and evaluation protocol relating real-robot zero-shot success to the diversity of contributed data. Section 5 discusses limitations and open questions, and Section 6 concludes.

## 2 Related Work

This section reviews the topics that form the foundations of our approach: zero-shot capabilities, latent spaces, scaling laws, trust and safety and imperfect crowd-sourced data.

## 2.1 Zero-shot capabilities

Zero-shot capabilities are essential for online platforms such as TikTok and Instagram, where new harmful trends and content designed to evade guidelines emerge faster than training data can be collected [60, 33, 55], much as a home robot meets objects it was never trained on. Beyond trust and safety, modern LLM chatbots and their applications also extend well beyond their training data [47]. Where collecting training data would be prohibitive, dangerous or unethical, zero-shot learning is, to the best of our knowledge, the most prominent set of techniques available [86]. It allows AI models to reason about unseen circumstances by associating them with prior knowledge embedded in their latent space [92].
Over the past decades, the field has moved through three eras. Early methods described classes by hand-defined attributes, so an unseen class could be recognized from its description [50]. Deep learning replaced hand-made descriptions with learned ones, including generative models that synthesize examples of unseen classes [23, 93], alongside methods robust to imperfect labels [28]. The GPT era turned zero-shot from a research benchmark into everyday behavior: large language models performed new tasks from a prompt alone [8], instruction tuning made that ability reliable across unseen tasks [87], and human feedback aligned it with what people actually ask for [68]. Vision-language models such as CLIP extended it to images [69], and early robot models have begun transferring this web-scale knowledge to physical actions [7].
Despite this progress in digital AI, comparatively little research has addressed zero-shot generalization in robotics. Recent robot foundation models show impressive results on the tasks and settings they were trained for, yet their performance still drops sharply when the task or environment is genuinely new [100, 4]. Applied directly to robots, the zero-shot toolkit of digital AI falls short, but it points to a clear pathway. Across all three eras, one principle holds: a model handles the unseen only when its latent space is rich enough to place it, solving new cases by interpolating within that space.

## 2.2 What builds a latent space

In the latent space, AI models build representations of concepts of the world. The more diverse the latent space, the more generalizable it becomes [49, 80, 16]. Representation quality is what learning ultimately depends on [5], zero-shot performance tracks how well the embedding space covers unseen classes [92], and CLIP zero-shot transfer improved as its training data grew broader [16].

In physical AI, no single method yet controls a robot end to end; a working system layers several. Classical control and engineering handle sensing and low-level loops [66]. Reinforcement learning, trained largely in simulation, teaches basic motor skills such as balancing, reaching, and locomotion, effectively learning motor control from experience [75, 74]. Vision-language-action (VLA) models inherit a web-scale latent space and use it to orchestrate those skills from visual and linguistic context [7, 46, 6, 65, 66]. How they connect to the body is still open: some systems map VLA outputs directly to actuators [6], while others have the VLA call lower-level policies, so it never commands the actuators itself, which limits risk [3]. World models add a further layer: they learn a latent representation of how the world changes, so a robot can imagine several ways of completing a task, predict the outcome of each, and choose the most promising before acting [35, 36, 62, 97]. The architecture of physical AI is therefore far from settled.

Figure 2: Volume makes each skill reliable; diversity determines whether a new task falls within reach. A robot trained on one team’s data cannot place an unfamiliar kettle in an unfamiliar kitchen. A robot trained on diverse community data reaches it by combining skills it already has.

Despite their progress, a systematic link between these paradigms and zero-shot generalization has yet to be established: each builds a latent space, but none addresses how the diversity of that space is sourced. Furthermore, when building foundational latent spaces, two patterns are often observed: (1) pre-training models follow scaling laws for general world contextual understanding, and (2) once pre-trained, these models require expert-level annotation for supervised fine-tuning stages [43, 68].

## 2.3 Scaling laws and Noisy-labels from crowd-source data

Training data for AI has come from people in three distinct ways.

Community-driven data is produced by people pursuing their own goals and becomes training data as a by product, so its diversity grows with the number of people taking part [8, 48].
Crowd-sourced data is produced by paid workers executing tasks someone else designed, which scales and offers control but reflects its designers’ choices [15, 68, 58, 1].
Specialized data is produced by trained experts, in robotics mostly teleoperators on the target hardware, which matches the robot’s embodiment but is the most expensive per sample and concentrated in a few teams [24, 79].

Each training stage has drawn on a different form of crowd-sourcing. Pre-training, governed by scaling laws, needs volume and diversity: language models found both in text written by people all over the world as a by-product of everyday use [8, 72]. Supervised fine-tuning needs expert, high-signal data: it came from paid annotators [68] and, increasingly, from volunteer communities [48]. Table 1 compares these sources with the workarounds robotics uses today.

These sources differ in cost, scale and diversity. Paid crowd-sourcing, from annotation micro-tasks [15] to paid robot teleoperation [58], offers control, but its cost grows with every sample and its coverage reflects its designers. Volunteer communities scale with shared motivation. Data generated as a by-product of use, as in games with a purpose [85, 14], scales with the number of people who want to take part.
The common response is that robotics simply lacks data volume. We agree, but how data is collected determines what it contains: paid collection by a few teams yields volume without diversity for pre-training, and expensive, narrow expertise for fine-tuning. Language models, by contrast, sourced each stage from the crowd. A further barrier is hardware. Robots are expensive for companies to lend to collectors and expensive for annotators to buy, so collection stays concentrated in a few well-funded teams. Workarounds that avoid robots altogether, such as egocentric human video, lower the cost but introduce an embodiment gap: human hands and viewpoints differ from a robot’s, which limits how well the data transfers [34, 44].
Robotics relies largely on paid collection for both stages. Companies have raised substantial capital [25], with teleoperation and egocentric data collection a major cost [24, 79, 2], yet their models still need new demonstrations for each new task [6, 100]. A notable exception is the LeRobot community, whose contributed datasets on the low-cost SO-100 arm were used to pre-train SmolVLA [77, 11]. These open tools, however, are built for research speed: they evolve quickly, often without backward compatibility, and favor rapid experimentation over the stability needed to build reliable applications. Their community data is a by-product of writing papers, not of solving everyday problems, so it stays concentrated on the tasks researchers choose to study. Our approach differs in where contributions come from: a community of developers building applications on one stable, standard robot and platform, whose data reflects the problems they actually need to solve.
