Crowd-sourced data is never clean. In classification, learning with noisy labels has developed methods that select likely-clean samples during training [39, 51], model noise that depends on each instance rather than on its class alone [91, 28], and estimate how much noise a dataset contains [31, 29]. In robot learning, the quality of demonstrations matters as much as their quantity: policies trained on demonstrations from operators of mixed skill perform markedly worse than those trained on proficient operators alone [57]. Imitation methods have so far handled this mainly by filtering, discarding low-quality demonstrations [57, 1]. Filtering protects performance but discards diversity, and for zero-shot generalization diversity is the scarcer resource. We therefore treat imperfect demonstrations as noisy labels to be weighted rather than discarded (Section 3.2).

## 2.4 Trust and Safety in Physical AI

Most robot safety work today addresses collision avoidance, joint limits, and grasp force [95, 9, 40], and treats broader safe behavior as a layer added after pre-training: a foundation model is trained to act, then fine-tuned on examples of what unsafe means [96, 42]. This leaves two questions open. First, how can a robot avoid unsafe behavior in situations for which no data can ethically or practically be collected? Second, why is safety absent from the stage where the latent space is formed? Both are zero-shot problems, and the same foundations address them. Rare or dangerous situations can be generated rather than staged, so the robot learns them without putting anyone at risk [94, 42, 22]. The robot should also recognize when it has left familiar ground: building on generalized zero-shot learning with domain classification, which separates seen from unseen inputs [18, 22], and on estimating out-of-distribution noise [31], it can detect when a situation falls in $\mathcal{S}_{\text{unseen}}$ and stop or hand control to a human through teleoperation.

## 3 Building a Zero-Shot Foundational Latent Space

## 3.1 Problem Formulation

A deployed robot meets a stream of situations, each a combination of its own state, the task it is asked to do, and the world around
limitations: Our proposal rests on assumptions that remain to be tested. Consent and data rights: contributed sessions must be collected with explicit consent and clear terms on how they are used, retained, and deleted; trust is a precondition for the community, not a by-product of it. Quality: community data varies in skill and care; noisy-label learning reduces but does not remove the need for validation, and expert annotation remains necessary for some stages. Simulation bias: most contributions will begin in simulation, so gains in zero-shot success may not transfer until Real2Sim2Real closes enough of the gap. Coverage bias: a developer community is not the world; contributors may cluster in certain regions, languages, and settings, leaving parts of $P_{\text{world}}$ uncovered. Retention: the cost advantage depends on developers staying active, which our hypothesis does not guarantee. We will report on each of these as the community grows.
conclusion:
This paper proposed a path to zero-shot generalization in physical AI built on two pieces: a community of developers working on one standard, approachable robot, and a shared latent space that turns their varied contributions into knowledge the robot can reuse. The space combines multi-modal alignment, generative augmentation and learning from imperfect data. Together, they let a robot handle situations it was never trained on.

Generalization is what turns a robot from a single-task machine into an economic asset. We argued that what robotics lacks is not volume but diversity: it has begun to scale the amount of data, but not the range of situations that data covers. Diversity grows with the number of independent contributors rather than with the size of a few paid teams. Our platform also serves a second function: developers who contribute data acquire hands-on experience with physical AI systems, so the community that supplies diverse data simultaneously develops the workforce the field requires.

Finally, a growing wave of developers wants to learn and build with robots. We argue that this community, working on a shared robot and solving its own problems, is the most sustainable source of the diversity zero-shot generalization requires. Without such a source, robotics risks remaining a field of single-task machines while its economic and social potential stays out of reach.

title: MemoryTax: The Bitter Lesson of Agent Memory
abstract: Agent memory systems such as Mem0 and Zep decide what to keep before any question arrives; coding agents keep the raw history and let the model search it with its own tools. We ask whether designed memory still helps once the model is strong enough to search for itself. On one LoCoMo conversation (419 turns, 152 questions), we run four memory methods (full context, BM25, Mem0, Zep) and three coding agents (Pi, Codex, Claude Code), each with GPT-4o-mini, GPT-6 Luna and Claude Opus 5.5, and record what every rollout costs. Agent memory is a costly patch for a weak model: Mem0 beats full context only with GPT-4o-mini, and its build alone costs more than a whole full-context rollout. Agent memory also has a ceiling, set by the model that writes it: a stronger reader does not recover what a weaker writer left out. With Claude Opus 5.5, Pi tops the cost-accuracy frontier, scoring 99% for less than half the cost of full context; its one miss is a wrong answer key. Part of that lead comes from photo captions that only the agents could read: on the 88 questions whose evidence has no photo, Pi and full context differ by one answer.

## MemoryTax: The Bitter Lesson of Agent Memory

Zedong Peng

Affiliation: Shanghai Jiao Tong University

Email: zedongpeng1@gmail.com

3 Agent memory is a costly patch for a weak model
5 With Claude Opus 5.5, Pi tops the frontier
body_start:
Abstract

Agent memory systems such as Mem0 and Zep decide what to keep before any question arrives; coding agents keep the raw history and let the model search it with its own tools. We ask whether designed memory still helps once the model is strong enough to search for itself. On one LoCoMo conversation (419 turns, 152 questions), we run four memory methods (full context, BM25, Mem0, Zep) and three coding agents (Pi, Codex, Claude Code), each with GPT-4o-mini, GPT-6 Luna and Claude Opus 5.5, and record what every rollout costs. This is a short empirical study, with one conversation and one run per cell. Agent memory is a costly patch for a weak model: Mem0 beats full context only with GPT-4o-mini, and its build alone costs more than a whole full-context rollout. Agent memory also has a ceiling, set by the model that writes it: a stronger reader does not recover what a weaker writer left out. With Claude Opus 5.5, Pi tops the cost–accuracy frontier, scoring 99% for less than half the cost of full context; its one miss is a wrong answer key. Part of that lead comes from photo captions that only the agents could read: on the 88 questions whose evidence has no photo, Pi and full context differ by one answer.

Interactive version: zedongpeng.com/memorytax

## 1 Introduction

Agent memory systems such as Mem0 and Zep decide what to keep before any question arrives: the model extracts facts or builds a graph from the conversation, and each question sees a few retrieved pieces [1, 2]. Coding agents and recursive language models keep the raw history instead and let the model search it with its own tools [3, 4, 5, 6].

The bitter lesson is that knowledge built into a system helps at first, then plateaus, while general methods that scale with computation win [7]. Agent memory builds in what to keep. Does it still help once the model is strong enough to search for itself?

We run four memory methods (full context, BM25 [8], Mem0 and Zep) and three coding agents (Pi, Codex and Claude Code), each with GPT-4o-mini, GPT-6 Luna and Claude Opus 5.5, on a conversation from LoCoMo [9], and measure what each run costs. We find:

• 

Agent memory is a costly patch for a weak model. Mem0 beats full context only with GPT-4o-mini, and its build alone costs more than full context’s whole run (Section 3).

• 

Agent memory has a ceiling, set by the model that writes it. A stronger reader does not recover what a weaker writer left out (Section 4).

• 

With Claude Opus 5.5, Pi tops the cost–accuracy frontier (Figure 1). It answers every question whose answer key is sound, for less than half what full context costs. Where the two read the same text they differ by one answer; the rest of Pi’s lead comes from photo captions that only the agents could read (Section 5).

The study is small: one conversation, one run per cell, and a GPT-4o-mini judge. Section 6 lists what it cannot show. Within those limits, the results suggest that a strong model needs less designed memory and better tools for searching the raw record.

Figure 1: Cost and correct rate per rollout. Each badge is one cell’s whole run: the build, then all 152 questions. Colour is the model, the badge the method’s mark, and a letter in the badge marks a method without one (F full context, B BM25). The stepped line is the highest correct rate reached at or below each cost, and the labelled cells lie on it. Cost is on a log axis.

## 2 Setup

We run 21 cells, seven methods with three models each, on LoCoMo conv-26 [9]: 419 turns in 19 sessions and 152 single-hop, multi-hop, temporal and open-domain questions. LoCoMo’s adversarial questions are left out, as in Mem0’s evaluation [1]. The history fits every model’s context window. Among the ten LoCoMo conversations, conv-26’s per-method accuracies track those of the full set closely. Table 1 lists the methods.

The memory methods answer one question at a time with Mem0’s 2025 answer template; Mem0 is OSS 2.1.0 and Zep is Graphiti OSS 0.30.2, both with default extraction and retrieval [1, 2]. The agents, Pi 1.1.0, Codex 0.159.2 and Claude Code 2.1.295 [3, 4, 5], start a fresh session in a fresh container for each question, with the conversation as one file, their default tools, and the template’s answer rules in the prompt (Appendix C).

The models go from weak to strongest: GPT-4o-mini, GPT-6 Luna, Claude Opus 5.5. The last two run at reasoning effort high, the effort coding agents are usually run at [10]; GPT-4o-mini has no effort setting. In each cell one model writes the store (Mem0, Zep) and answers every question, or drives the agent.

## Photos.

Some LoCoMo turns share a photo, and the official file holds a caption of it next to the turn text. The agents get the official file, captions included; the memory methods were given the turn text only. 116 of the 419 turns share a photo, and 64 of the 152 questions have evidence in such a turn. Section 5 measures what this changes.

## Measurement.

A rollout is one run over the conversation: the build, then the 152 questions. GPT-4o-mini grades every answer with Mem0’s 2025 judge rubric [1]; empty answers count as wrong. Cost is the list price of every model call, LLM and embedding (text-embedding-3-small), with the judge excluded. A turn is one LLM call: one per question for the memory methods, one per step of an agent’s loop, and Mem0’s and Zep’s calls to build their store. Tokens are those calls’ input and output tokens, cached input included; embeddings are not counted. Each cell runs once.

## 3 Agent memory is a costly patch for a weak model

With GPT-4o-mini, Mem0 scores highest. It scores 78%, against 74% for both full context and BM25; Zep scores 43%. The agents score 63% (Pi), 28% (Codex) and 29% (Claude Code): Codex opens the conversation file for three questions in four and Claude Code almost never, and otherwise they answer from the question alone.

With the two stronger models, the patch stops helping. With GPT-6 Luna, full context scores 92%, BM25 82%, Mem0 80% and Zep 51%; Zep’s graph holds 128 facts from the 19 sessions, against 195 with Claude Opus 5.5. With Claude Opus 5.5, Mem0 and full context both score 95% and Zep 87%, and the agents score highest: Pi 99%, Codex 98% and Claude Code 97%, a lead that comes mostly from questions about photos (Section 5). Earlier work also finds that plain retrieval keeps up with elaborate memory [11] and that rankings between memory systems change with the model [12].

Figure 2: Cumulative cost–correct curves. Each curve is one rollout: the build, then the questions from cheapest to most expensive (equal costs grouped), adding up cost and correct answers; correct answers are divided by 152, so a wrong answer adds cost only. Colour is the model, the badge the method, and agents are dotted. The cost axis is linear to $2 and logarithmic above. Curves use a nine-point moving average, and the badges mark the unsmoothed totals of Table 2. Strong lines are cells that no other cell beats on both cost and correct answers.

The patch is not free. Mem0’s build alone costs more than full context’s whole rollout with the same model: $0.56 against $0.43 with GPT-4o-mini, $0.45 against $0.29 with GPT-6 Luna and $25.88 against $17.84 with Claude Opus 5.5 (Figure 2). Its questions are cheaper, so the build would pay for itself after 372, 545 and 596 questions on the same history; LoCoMo asks 152. Mem0 and Zep are never on the frontier of Figure 1, which runs through BM25 and full context with GPT-6 Luna and Pi with Claude Opus 5.5. Paying to build memory that a stronger model does not need is a memory tax.

## 4 Agent memory has a ceiling

The model that writes the store limits every reader. Mem0 and Zep write their store with the same model that later reads it. Retrieval calls no language model, so the reader can be swapped: each model answers from the retrievals of the others’ stores (Figure 3, Table 3).

Figure 3: Writer and reader. Each colour is one store, written by that model. The filled badge is the writer reading its own store, and arrows run from it to the other two readers.

A stronger reader does not recover what the writer left out. On Zep’s GPT-4o-mini graph, GPT-4o-mini, GPT-6 Luna and Claude Opus 5.5 score 43%, 43% and 45%; on the graph Claude Opus 5.5 wrote, 66%, 71% and 87%. Mem0 keeps the order with smaller gaps: 78%, 83% and 84% from GPT-4o-mini’s store, 89%, 91% and 95% from Claude Opus 5.5’s. This agrees with work where verbatim chunks beat extracted facts on long conversations [13].

## 5 With Claude Opus 5.5, Pi tops the frontier

Pi with Claude Opus 5.5 is the top of the frontier in Figure 1. No other cell scores higher: Pi scores 99% for $6.95 a rollout, while full context with the same model scores 95% for $17.84. Pi reads about 10,000 input tokens a question, 7,900 of them cached, against 28,900 for full context. Codex and Claude Code score 98% and 97% for $25.41 and $28.41; HarnessTax explains why the same model costs so differently across harnesses [10].

Its one miss is LoCoMo’s mistake. The question asks what kind of painting Caroline shared with Melanie on 13 October 2023, and the answer key says an abstract painting with blue streaks. In the conversation it is Melanie who shares that painting; Caroline shares a drawing. Pi says so and is marked wrong: “Caroline shared a drawing, not a painting. … The paintings shared that day (a sunset and an abstract piece) were Melanie’s.” With Claude Opus 5.5, full context, Codex and Claude Code point out the same mistake and are marked wrong too. On the other 151 questions, Pi with Claude Opus 5.5 is always right.

Photo captions account for most of Pi’s lead over full context. With Claude Opus 5.5, Pi answers seven questions that full context misses and misses none that it answers. Six of the seven have their evidence in a turn that shares a photo, whose caption Pi could read and full context could not (Section 2); so do all six such questions for Codex and all four for Claude Code. On the 88 questions without photo evidence, Pi scores 100%, and full context, Mem0, Codex and Claude Code 99% each (Table 4). With the same input, then, Pi matches full context for less than half its cost. Whether searching the record answers more than reading all of it, this study does not settle.

## 6 Discussion and limitations

Our results suggest that agent memory is a costly patch for a weak model and caps what any reader can answer. On this LoCoMo conversation, Mem0 helps GPT-4o-mini but not GPT-6 Luna or Claude Opus 5.5, a stronger reader does not recover what the writer left out, and with Claude Opus 5.5 Pi answers every sound question for less than full context costs.

The findings rest on a small study, and these limits apply:

• 

Scale. One conversation of LoCoMo’s ten, and one run per cell. Differences of a few questions may not hold in a second run.

• 

Grading. A GPT-4o-mini judge with a lenient rubric, and at least one wrong answer key.

• 

Photo captions. The agents could read photo captions that the memory methods were not given (Section 5). This touches comparisons between agents and memory methods, not those among the memory methods.

• 

Context length. The history fits in every model’s context window, so full context is always an option. Results may differ on other benchmarks such as LongMemEval [14] and on histories that do not fit.

• 

Settings and prices. Mem0 and Zep run with their default extraction and retrieval, and other settings may do better. Costs are list prices and depend on each provider’s caching.

Memory systems and harnesses can also be searched for automatically [15, 16], but what is found is still fixed before the question arrives. More broadly, a strong model may need less designed memory and better tools: exact, semantic and vector search over the raw record, driven by the model itself [3, 4]. Progress may then look less like another memory system and more like ripgrep after grep [17], or zvec-grep after ripgrep [18]. Designed memory may survive as a cost trade-off when many questions share one history (Figure 2).

body_start:
Abstract

Asked what to study, which career to pursue, or what product to build, large language models (LLMs) often recommend AI-related options. We ask where this tendency comes from by comparing models before and after fine-tuning and by varying how questions are asked. First, pretrained models already include explicit AI/ML terms in the recommendations of 27% of their responses, and their released instruction-tuned versions do so in 59%. Second, fine-tuning models ourselves shows that this rise is not inevitable: general instruction tuning leaves the rate unchanged, but removing the 7% of instruction examples that concern AI cuts it by 14 percentage points, below the level of the pretrained models it starts from. Data rewarding helpfulness raise it by 9 points, while data ranked by the preferences of diverse simulated users lower it by 9. Finally, with models held fixed, asking for the “best” option or for what to do “right now” raises the rate by 8 and 18 points, whereas telling the model it is an AI advisor adds 4. Overall, the tendency starts in pretraining, and what models learn afterward, together with how a question is phrased, decides how strongly it appears.

## 1 Introduction

When users seek open-ended advice from large language models (LLMs), the recommendations can shape which options they consider and, ultimately, their decisions. This makes systematic tendencies in these recommendations important to understand, even when individual suggestions appear reasonable.

One such tendency is pro-AI prominence: the frequent inclusion of AI-related content in open-ended recommendations. Prior work documented such prominence in open-ended advice, and more favorable estimates for AI cases in matched prediction tasks (Trabelsi et al., 2026), while other studies report self-preference in LLM evaluations, preferences for AI-generated content, and provider bias in code generation (Panickssery et al., 2024; Laurito et al., 2025; Zhang et al., 2025). This prominence is not necessarily unjustified, but its origins remain unclear: when an instruction-tuned model recommends AI, the recommendation alone does not reveal whether this tendency reflects pretrained behavior, subsequent training, the system context, or the wording of the request itself.

## Possible sources.

We examine four explanations, which are not mutually exclusive (Figure 1).
H1 (pretraining prior): pretrained models may already associate AI with innovation, growth, or future value.
H2 (post-training): post-training may strengthen or weaken pro-AI prominence, depending on the training data, method and objectives.
H3 (AI identity/context): mentioning AI in the system context, particularly by identifying the assistant itself as AI, may change what it recommends.
H4 (prompt wording): temporal and superlative wording, such as “right now” and “best”, may shift recommendations toward AI-related content.

Figure 1: Study design. Top: the four possible sources of pro-AI recommendation prominence and the comparison that tests each; controlled branches are compared with their immediate parent. Bottom: the outcome shared by all comparisons.

## Approach.

We pose 20 open-ended advice questions from four domains, each in ten paraphrases, and measure how often a model’s recommendation includes explicit AI/ML terms. To test H1 and H2, we compare ten released Base–Instruct pairs and train eleven pretrained models with six post-training recipes, comparing each recipe with its parent checkpoint. To test H3 and H4, we vary the system message and the wording of the question for ten instruction-tuned models.

## Main findings.

Pro-AI prominence is already substantial in pretrained models, consistent with H1, and far higher in their released instruction-tuned counterparts. Controlled post-training shows that this shift is not a generic effect of instruction tuning (H2): general supervised fine-tuning (SFT) leaves pro-AI prominence almost unchanged, whereas other training recipes raise or lower it depending on their data. At inference time, temporal and superlative wording (H4) raise pro-AI prominence far more than AI cues in the system context (H3), and identifying the assistant itself as AI adds no significant further increase.

## 2 Related Work

LLM recommendations often reflect factors beyond the substance of a request. Name cues affect employment and salary recommendations (Nghiem et al., 2024), while demographic and small linguistic cues affect educational recommendations (Shailya et al., 2025; Benedetto et al., 2026). Research has also examined popularity bias in LLM recommenders and changes in product recommendations under different framing (Lichtenberg et al., 2024; Filandrianos et al., 2025).

## 2.1 Bias across training stages

Bias in LLM behavior reflects both pretraining and later training. Instruction-tuned models were shown to exhibit stronger decision biases than Base or less tuned models, yet experiments that vary instruction datasets suggest that several biases follow the pretrained model more closely than the later training data (Itzhak et al., 2024; Itzhak et al., 2025). These studies compare released models or exchange whole instruction datasets; we instead remove one content category from otherwise identical instruction data and compare preference-optimization recipes applied to the same checkpoint. Controlled studies also show that changes to AI-related text during pretraining affect later alignment behavior, even after SFT and Direct Preference Optimization (DPO), and that small differences near the end of pretraining change responses to the same subsequent preference training (Tice et al., 2026; Lu et al., 2026).

Preference optimization was shown to reinforce biases in training feedback, including through methods such as DPO (Rafailov et al., 2023): biased preference rewards increase models’ tendency to agree with users, while preference models favor simple features such as length, technical language, and agreement (Shapira et al., 2026; Bharadwaj et al., 2026). Together, these findings suggest that both training history and post-training choices matter; we test their effects on pro-AI recommendations.

## 2.2 Prompt and system-context effects

Model behavior also varies with prompt wording. Evaluation results based on a single instruction template differ from averages across paraphrases, and even meaning-preserving edits substantially change outcomes (Mizrahi et al., 2024; Sclar et al., 2024). Specific effects include apparent publication dates favoring newer passages during reranking and context cues changing how models respond to assumptions in user requests (Fang et al., 2025; Cheng et al., 2026). Targeted prompt changes are also often difficult to distinguish from ordinary sensitivity to wording (Yang et al., 2026).

System prompts provide another source of variation. Assigning roles to an assistant was shown to affect its answers without consistently improving task accuracy (Zheng et al., 2024). We therefore distinguish changes caused by wording and surrounding context from those caused by identifying the assistant as AI.

## 2.3 AI as a subject of preference

AI is itself a subject of model preferences. LLM evaluators were shown to favor their own generations, while preferences for LLM-generated communication and for evaluators’ own model-generated résumés have been observed in other decisions (Panickssery et al., 2024; Laurito et al., 2025; Xu et al., 2025). Provider preferences also appear in code generation and recommendations among competing AI models (Zhang et al., 2025; Dubash and Friedler, 2026). These effects concern who produced the content or which provider is favored, rather than whether AI or ML appears within the recommendation itself. Closest to our study, prior work documented AI prominence in open-ended recommendations and more favorable estimates for matched AI cases in salary and program-completion tasks (Trabelsi et al., 2026). Whereas that work documents the phenomenon, we study where it comes from, across pretraining, controlled post-training, and inference-time prompts.

## 3 Experimental Design

## 3.1 Recommendation task

We study open-ended advice questions with many plausible answers. The four domains are Study, Career, Startup, and Scientific Research. Study, Career, and Startup follow Trabelsi et al. (2026), who chose domains covering consequential choices for which users commonly seek LLM advice. We add Scientific Research because researchers widely use LLMs in their work (Liao et al., 2025), and LLMs are increasingly studied as sources of research ideas (Si et al., 2025). Each domain contains five conceptual questions, each asked in ten fixed paraphrases. The questions are in English and contain no information about the person asking. All comparisons except the wording test ask every question with both a superlative and a temporal cue (e.g., “What is the best {concept} right now?”); the wording test varies these cues. All responses are generated with temperature 0, top-p 1, a 512-token output limit, and seed 12345, with thinking disabled for Qwen models.

## 3.2 Primary outcome

We first detect explicit AI/ML terms (e.g., artificial intelligence, machine learning, deep learning, LLMs and generative AI; full list in Appendix A.5) using fixed lexical patterns, then use two LLM filters to exclude mentions outside the recommendation itself. Responses without such terms are counted as negative. Each filter must answer with a single yes/no label; any other output (0.1% of DeepSeek and under 0.01% of Qwen judgments) is invalid and treated as missing rather than negative.

We use Qwen3.6-27B and DeepSeek-V4-Flash as the two filters. Each filter’s rate is computed over the responses it classified validly, and the two rates are averaged with equal weight for each model, condition, and question.

Our measure of pro-AI prominence is the share of responses with explicit AI/ML terms within their recommendations, averaged over the two filters. Responses without a recommendation count as zero, so the measure reflects how often a user who asks the question receives an AI recommendation. Empty responses are excluded rather than counted as zero (Appendix A.5).

Because LLM-based judgments can depend on the evaluator,
we also examine the two filters separately
(Verga et al., 2024; Thakur et al., 2025).
The two filters give nearly identical effect estimates ( $r=0.990$ ) and agree on which effects are significant, except for one small effect in the AI-context test (Appendix Table 15). On 200 detector-positive responses labeled by a human expert, the measure agrees with the expert on 85.2% (95% CI [81.0, 89.5]), with 96.9% precision and 86.6% recall (Appendix A.12).

## 3.3 Statistical analysis

Effects are calculated from matched experimental conditions, averaging equally across the evaluated models and the 20 questions (five per domain). The 20 questions are our statistical units; the ten paraphrases of a question are treated as repeated wordings of it, not as separate observations.

We compute 95% confidence intervals by resampling questions within each domain (20,000 bootstrap samples).

Significance is tested by flipping the signs of the 20 question-level effects in all $2^{20}$ possible ways (two-sided exact test of the null hypothesis that each question’s effect is equally likely to be positive or negative). We apply Holm correction separately within the four prespecified hypothesis families (H1: one test; H2: six; H3: three; H4: three), using $\alpha=0.05$ .

## 4 How Post-Training Changes Pro-AI Prominence

We first ask whether pro-AI prominence is already present
before instruction tuning, and whether subsequent training consistently amplifies it. We address these questions through released Base–Instruct comparisons and controlled experiments with specific post-training recipes.

Figure 2: Released Base–Instruct contrast (top) and six controlled post-training comparisons. Markers show effects with 95% confidence intervals. Each controlled branch is compared with its immediate parent, as identified by the row labels.

## 4.1 Released Instruct models show a large shift

Released Instruct checkpoints include explicit AI/ML terms within recommendations substantially more often than their pretrained Base counterparts. Across ten matched Base–Instruct model lines from five open-weight model families, pro-AI prominence increases by an average of 32.48 percentage points (95% CI [29.46, 35.39]; Holm-adjusted $p<.001$ ). On average, 26.80% of responses from released Base checkpoints and 59.28% from released Instruct checkpoints recommend an option with explicit AI/ML terms.

Both checkpoints receive the same three fixed plain-text input formats, designed so that either checkpoint type completes them as an answer; their results are averaged equally. The high rate in Base checkpoints shows that pro-AI prominence does not require instruction tuning. Which training steps raise it is not isolated by this comparison; the controlled experiments below address that question.

## 4.2 Controlled post-training reveals different effects

We next examine whether different post-training recipes consistently change prominence in the same direction.
We evaluate eleven model lines from six families in a
controlled training tree. General SFT and Clean no-AI SFT start from the pretrained Base checkpoint, while Helpfulness DPO, Safety DPO, Role SFT, and Persona DPO start from General SFT.
Each procedure is compared with its immediate parent under the same fixed input formats. The two SFT branches compare ordinary instruction tuning with tuning on the same data minus its AI-related examples; the four branches built on General SFT add common later stages: helpfulness, safety, or persona/value-oriented preference optimization, or role-conditioned instruction tuning.

Figure 2 places these six controlled comparisons alongside the released Base–Instruct contrast. Because the comparisons start from different checkpoints, they are not successive steps of one training run.

## General SFT changes little.

General SFT uses a 60k-example instruction mixture based on Tülu 3, UltraChat, and OpenAssistant-style conversations (Lambert et al., 2025; Ding et al., 2023; Köpf et al., 2023). It changes pro-AI prominence by only $+0.02$ pp on average (95% CI [ $-1.58$ , 1.73]; Holm-adjusted $p=.996$ ), with effects of both signs across models (Appendix Figure 4).

## Clean no-AI SFT lowers pro-AI prominence.

A different result emerges when the instruction data are filtered.
Clean no-AI SFT uses the same instruction pool after removing the 7.2% of examples that are AI/ML/LLM-related. Relative to Base, it reduces pro-AI prominence by 13.89 pp (95% CI [ $-16.09$ , $-11.60$ ]; Holm-adjusted $p<.001$ ). Its absolute level falls from 24.64% in Base to 10.74%, so SFT does not always move pro-AI prominence in the same direction.

Figure 3: Prompt-level effects on pro-AI prominence. Left: the percentage of responses with explicit AI/ML terms in their recommendations, in each of the four wording conditions (design in Figure 1); arrows show the average increase from each cue. Right: the AI-context effects of adding AI to the advisor and grammar-checker messages, and the difference between the two, with 95% confidence intervals.

## Preference-training branches move in opposite directions.

Helpfulness DPO uses a 108k helpfulness-preference mixture including Tülu preference data, UltraFeedback, and HelpSteer2-style pairs (Cui et al., 2024; Wang et al., 2024b). Persona DPO uses 20k response pairs ranked by the persona/value preferences of synthetic users, based on PERSONA (Castricato et al., 2025).

Helpfulness DPO raises pro-AI prominence by 9.48 pp (95% CI [7.37, 11.60]; Holm-adjusted $p<.001$ ). Persona DPO moves in the opposite direction, lowering it relative to General SFT by 8.95 pp (95% CI [ $-10.76$ , $-7.15$ ]; Holm-adjusted $p<.001$ ).

The shared General-SFT starting point makes this contrast particularly informative: the two DPO branches differ by approximately 18 percentage points in their estimated effects.
Applying preference optimization therefore does not imply a uniform direction of change; the associated training recipe matters. We discuss possible reasons in Section 6.

Safety DPO, trained on 20k safety-preference pairs from PKU-SafeRLHF (Ji et al., 2025), produces a smaller but significant decrease ( $-2.34$ pp, 95% CI [ $-3.27$ , $-1.42$ ]; Holm-adjusted $p=.003$ ). Role SFT, trained on 20k role-conditioned dialogues from ZenMoore/RoleBench (Wang et al., 2024a), shows no significant change ( $+2.44$ pp; Holm-adjusted $p=.136$ ).

Post-training therefore does not uniformly amplify pro-AI prominence: the direction and size of each change depend on the training recipe rather than the training stage.

## 5 Prompt-Level Effects

Recommendations may also change with the input alone, without any change to model weights. We therefore keep model weights fixed and investigate two possible influences at inference time, each on ten instruction-tuned model lines from five families: the criteria expressed in the user’s request and explicit AI cues in the system context.

## 5.1 Temporal wording and superlatives both increase explicit AI/ML recommendations

We first vary only the wording of the user’s question, using each model’s chat template. We vary two cues, each present or absent: a superlative cue (best, strongest, or most promising) and a temporal cue (right now, currently, or at present). This yields four conditions: N (neither), S (superlative only), T (temporal only), and ST (both); for example, an ST prompt is “What is the best {concept} right now?” Each condition has ten paraphrase templates; in five of them (P6–P10), the conditions share a sentence frame and differ only in the cues (Appendix Tables 9 and 10). For each cue, we report its average effect across both settings of the other cue, and we tes
limitations:
We measure explicit AI/ML terminology within recommendations, not their quality or whether AI-related advice is justified. This measure can miss implicit AI recommendations, and compared with a human expert it misses some explicit ones (86.6% recall), so its absolute rates are conservative.

Base checkpoints establish that the tendency is already present, but not its origin within pretraining. Recent enthusiasm for AI may contribute to this tendency, but further research is needed to determine its influence. Controlled comparisons evaluate complete training recipes rather than isolating individual mechanisms, and each branch has only one training run per model. Statistical inference treats the evaluated models as fixed and resamples questions; the findings may differ across other models, languages, domains, and settings.
conclusion:
Recent work found that models often recommend AI, but did not call this recommendation pattern bias, because no reference says how often AI should be recommended (Trabelsi et al., 2026). Our comparisons do not need such a reference: each holds the advice question fixed, yet pretrained and instruction-tuned versions, models trained on different data, and models given different system messages recommend AI at very different rates, from 11% after Clean no-AI SFT to 73% when the question asks for the best option right now. Whatever the appropriate rate is, they cannot all be right. We therefore call a shift toward AI-related options in what models recommend, relative to the same question under another condition, pro-AI bias.

The largest shifts come from factors that add little information about the user’s needs. A user asking for advice already wants the best option for their current situation, yet saying “best” or “right now” pushes models strongly toward AI. Released Instruct checkpoints recommend AI-related options far more often than their Base counterparts; Base models are not explicitly trained to answer questions, but both versions receive identical prompts, designed so that either answers them. Telling the model that it is an AI advisor, or that the conversation will reach an AI grammar checker, also increases AI-related recommendations, although neither changes what would serve the user.

title: Metamodel-Guided LLM Decoding for Consistent DSL Generation
abstract: Large language models (LLMs) are increasingly used to generate software engineering artifacts written in domain-specific languages (DSLs). Correct DSL instances usually must comply with not only the concrete syntax but also the abstract syntax defined by a metamodel augmented with semantic well-formedness constraints. Existing constrained decoding approaches typically guarantee compliance only with concrete syntax or with a limited set of semantic constraints expressed over the generated text, making metamodel-level constraint consistency difficult to enforce during generation. We present MeMoDecode: a decoding framework that enforces a DSL's concrete syntax, abstract syntax, and well-formedness constraints jointly. Specifically, whenever the LLM generates a complete metamodel concept, MeMoDecode incrementally maps the current output to a partial model and verifies whether it can still be completed into a consistent instance. We combine MeMoDecode with a simple retry mechanism that resumes decoding from the most recent completable snapshot whenever an inconsistency is detected. Under a sound backend verifier, MeMoDecode never performs worse than grammar-constrained decoding on alignment metrics satisfying natural assumptions. Across four DSLs and six open-weight LLMs ranging from 0.6B to 70B parameters, MeMoDecode achieves the highest consistency, improving consistency by 23% on average over unconstrained decoding and by 8% on average over grammar-constrained decoding. It also improves benchmark performance while incurring only modest runtime overhead. These results show that metamodel-guided decoding is an effective approach for enforcing DSL consistency during decoding across diverse DSLs and LLM scales.

Specifically, whenever the LLM generates a complete metamodel concept, MeMoDecode incrementally maps the current output to a partial model and verifies whether it can still be completed into a consistent instance. We combine MeMoDecode with a simple retry mechanism that resumes decoding from the most recent completable snapshot whenever an inconsistency is detected. Under a sound backend verifier, MeMoDecode never performs worse than grammar-constrained decoding on alignment metrics satisfying natural assumptions. Across four DSLs and six open-weight LLMs ranging from 0.6B to 70B parameters, MeMoDecode achieves the highest consistency, improving consistency by 23% on average over unconstrained decoding and by 8% on average over grammar-constrained decoding. It also improves benchmark performance while incurring only modest runtime overhead. These results show that metamodel-guided decoding is an effective approach for enforcing DSL consistency during decoding across diverse DSLs and LLM scales.

Index Terms: 
constrained decoding, domain-specific languages, large language models, metamodels

## I Introduction

Context.
Modern software engineering (SE) relies on a wide range of artifacts, from architecture design and configuration to query languages and flowcharts, many of which are expressed in domain-specific languages (DSLs) tailored to a particular task or domain [1]. As large language models (LLMs) are increasingly used to automate SE activities, a growing portion of these artifacts is generated, either fully or partially, by LLMs, from natural language specifications [2, 3]. Beyond traditional SE workflows, DSL artifacts also serve as structured interfaces in LLM-based agentic systems, supporting multi-agent communication [4, 5, 6] and tool use [7, 8, 9].

In SE, especially in model-driven engineering, DSL instances are often used as machine-processable artifacts for downstream automation, analysis, model transformation, and code generation [10, 11, 12].
As a result, a DSL is typically characterized by three complementary aspects: its concrete syntax, usually defined by a grammar; its abstract syntax, captured by a metamodel; and a set of semantic well-formedness constraints over that metamodel, with execution semantics defined on top of them [13, 14, 15]. These aspects form a hierarchy of correctness. A generated instance may satisfy the grammar while still violating the metamodel or its constraints, preventing meaningful analysis, transformation, or execution. A DSL instance is consistent if it conforms to both the metamodel and the well-formedness constraints [16].
However, LLMs provide no guarantee that generated DSL instances satisfy these specifications. They may produce outputs that violate the grammar, the metamodel, or the well-formedness constraints, motivating the need for verification techniques [17, 18, 19].

A natural way to improve the reliability of generated DSL instances is post-hoc verification, where a complete instance is first generated and then checked or repaired [20, 21, 22, 23]. However, these approaches discover violations only after a full generation. As a result, they may waste substantial decoding effort and require additional repair steps. Moreover, as LLM generation is conditioned on existing prefixes, when the generated instance contains early structural errors, subsequent parts of the output are generated from an already invalid context, potentially hurting the overall quality [24, 25].

These limitations motivate decoding-time approaches that prevent invalid outputs before they are completed. Grammar-constrained decoding masks, at each decoding step, tokens that would violate the grammar, thereby guaranteeing syntactic validity [26, 27, 28, 29, 30, 31]. However, operating only on concrete syntax, it provides no guarantee that the generated DSL instance conforms to the metamodel or the associated constraints.

Recent approaches further incorporate semantic constraint verification into the decoding process [32, 33, 34]. For example, IterGen [35] augments grammar-constrained decoding with semantic checks. However, these checks are typically expressed over the generated text rather than the underlying structured model. Consequently, verification remains tied to a particular textual representation. More importantly, it limits the ability to reason about properties that are naturally defined over objects and references in the metamodel, such as multiplicity constraints, referential integrity, and transitive relationships.
As a result, decoding-time verification and guidance of metamodel-level constraint consistency over the underlying structured representation remain underexplored [19].

Approach.
In this paper, we present MeMoDecode (MetaModel-guided Decoding), a decoding framework that simultaneously enforces a DSL’s concrete syntax, abstract syntax, and semantic well-formedness constraints. The key idea is to lift verification from the generated text to the underlying model representation. As decoding proceeds, MeMoDecode incrementally maps the generated text to a partial model and, whenever the LLM completes a metamodel concept, verifies whether that partial model remains satisfiable with respect to the metamodel and its well-formedness constraints, that is, whether it can still be completed into a consistent instance. If not,
the violation is irreparable, and
MeMoDecode can immediately backtrack and retry during decoding rather than relying on post-hoc regeneration of the entire output.

Contribution.
Because verification is performed over the model representation rather than the concrete-syntax text, MeMoDecode can enforce structured metamodel-level properties that are difficult or impossible to express using grammar-based approaches. Furthermore, since constraints are specified directly over the metamodel, the verification process is independent of the concrete syntax of the DSL and can be applied across different textual representations.
More specifically, this paper makes the following contributions:

• 

We present MeMoDecode, a decoding framework that simultaneously enforces a DSL’s concrete syntax, abstract syntax, and semantic well-formedness constraints by verifying whether partially generated outputs can still be completed into consistent instances and retrying otherwise.

• 

We establish a worst-case guarantee: under a sound verifier and natural assumptions on the alignment metric, MeMoDecode never produces an output that is less aligned than the one generated by grammar-constrained decoding under identical decoding conditions.

• 

We implement MeMoDecode by combining grammar-constrained decoding [27] with the Refinery verifier [36] and a lightweight decoding-time retry mechanism.

• 

We conduct a systematic evaluation across four DSLs and six open-weight LLMs ranging from 0.6B to 70B parameters. The results show that MeMoDecode consistently improves DSL consistency, increases alignment with the ground truth, and incurs only modest runtime overhead.

Added value.
MeMoDecode demonstrates that reasoning over the underlying model representation is key to ensuring consistency of a DSL instance. By lifting verification to the metamodel level, it enables the use of established partial modeling and constraint-solving techniques within the decoding process, yielding consistency guarantees independent of the textual representation. Since verification is decoupled from the underlying LLM, MeMoDecode can benefit directly from future advances in both LLMs and backend verifiers.

## II Background and Related Work

## II-1 Domain-Specific Languages

A domain-specific language (DSL) is tailored to express the concepts of a particular application domain [1].
By focusing on a specific domain, DSLs can provide substantially higher ease of use than general-purpose programming languages for the tasks they are designed to support [11]. For instance, Figure 1 shows a CLEVR program specified using a DSL. A CLEVR program is a structured, machine-executable representation of a natural-language question about an image [37]. The listing illustrates a minimal program to answer the question “What color is the cube?”. The program begins with a scene node that returns the full set of objects in the scene, which is then passed to filter_shape to retain only cube-shaped objects. The unique function asserts that exactly one such object exists, promoting the set of objects to a single object. Finally, query_color is applied to retrieve the color of that object.

## II-2 DSL specifications

In SE, and especially in model-driven engineering, a DSL is characterized by three aspects: a concrete syntax, an abstract syntax, and a set of semantic well-formedness constraints [13, 14, 15] (see Figure 2). Formally, a DSL specification can be defined as
 $\mathcal{D}=(G,M,\mathcal{C}),$ 
where $G$ is a context-free grammar (CFG) defining the concrete syntax, $M$ is a metamodel defining the abstract syntax, and $\mathcal{C}$ is a set of semantic well-formedness constraints over $M$ .

The concrete syntax specifies the notation through which users interact with DSL instances. This paper focuses on textual DSLs whose concrete syntax is defined by a CFG $G$ . In the CLEVR case, a language engineer could define the CFG shown in Figure 2. The non-terminals of $G$ define textual forms for different syntactic categories of the language, such as edge, program node, and the type of a node.
We refer to these completed derivations of selected non-terminals as syntactic units. A text sequence $\boldsymbol{y}$ is syntactically valid if it belongs to the language generated by $G$ , i.e., $\boldsymbol{y}\in L(G)$ .

The abstract syntax defines a structural representation of DSL instances and is commonly specified through a metamodel [15]. A metamodel $M$ defines the types of elements that may appear in an instance model, including classes, attributes, references, containment references, multiplicities, and inheritance relations, often using a metamodeling language such as EMF Ecore [38]. The right side of Figure 2 shows the metamodel of the CLEVR DSL. We use $I\models M$ to denote that an instance model $I$ conforms to the metamodel $M$ .

A set of semantic well-formedness constraints $\mathcal{C}$ complements the metamodel by specifying semantic rules that cannot be expressed by the grammar or the metamodel alone [16].
These constraints are commonly specified using a constraint language [14, 39]. Formally, a constraint $c\in\mathcal{C}$ is a predicate over an instance model: $c:\mathcal{I}_{M}\rightarrow\{\mathrm{true},\mathrm{false}\}$ . $\mathcal{I}_{M}$ represents the set of instance models conforming to $M$ and the output shows whether the constraint is satisfied. Figure 2 shows three out of the 17 constraints (single-root structure, type-correct dataflow, and acyclicity) of the CLEVR DSL.

To connect a text sequence to an instance model, language engineers typically define transformation rules from concrete syntax constructs, such as selected grammar non-terminals, to metamodel elements. Given such rules, a DSL instance written in the concrete syntax can be transformed into an instance model, for example, through parsing and model transformation techniques [40, 41]. The coloring in Figure 2 illustrates an example of such a correspondence between the grammar and the metamodel. A DSL instance is valid only if the resulting instance model $I$ is consistent with respect to $(M,\mathcal{C})$ , i.e., it conforms to the metamodel and satisfies all well-formedness constraints: $I\models(M,\mathcal{C})\iff I\models M\land\forall c\in\mathcal{C},\;c(I)=\mathrm{true}$ .

Fig. 2: Example DSL for CLEVR programs [37]

## II-3 Partial models

Partial models represent incomplete instances of a metamodel [42]. Instead of fully specifying all elements, a partial model records what is currently known and leaves the remaining information unspecified [16, 43, 39]. Following prior work, we view a partial model as an interpretation of metamodel-level facts, represented as predicates whose truth values may be known, unknown, or inconsistent. In the CLEVR DSL, a partial model may already contain facts such as $\textsc{Node}(n_{1})$ , $\textsc{Node}(n_{2})$ , $\textsc{Edge}(e_{1})$ , $\textsc{source}(e_{1},n_{1})$ , and $\textsc{target}(e_{1},n_{2})$ , while other facts, such as the node type of $n_{2}$ or the remaining outgoing edges of $n_{1}$ , remain unknown. A complete instance model can be obtained by refining the partial model, i.e., by adding new facts until the objects, references, and attribute values are fully determined.

Refinery is a graph solver for generating and analyzing domain-specific graph models from partial specifications [36]. In this paper, we use Refinery as the backend solver for reasoning about the partial models constructed during decoding. The design of MeMoDecode is compatible with any backend that can reason soundly about partial models.

## II-4 Large language models

LLMs are deep neural networks that typically follow the decoder-only Transformer architecture [44]. They are trained on massive collections of textual data using the language modeling task, which consists of predicting the next token given a sequence of preceding tokens.
In practice, the generation follows an autoregressive process: an LLM receives as input a prompt $\boldsymbol{x}$ and produces a probability distribution over all tokens in its vocabulary, $\mathrm{LLM(\boldsymbol{x})}=P(\cdot|\boldsymbol{x})$ . Based on this distribution and a chosen decoding strategy,
the next token $t\sim P(\cdot|\boldsymbol{x})$ is selected by a sampler and appended to the prompt. The updated sequence is fed back into the LLM, and the process repeats until a predefined termination condition is reached, such as generating an end-of-sequence token, to create an output sequence $\boldsymbol{y}$ .

## II-5 Decoding strategies for LLMs

A decoding strategy determines how the next token is selected from the probability distribution $P(\cdot|\boldsymbol{x})$ predicted by an LLM from a prompt $\boldsymbol{x}$ .

Unconstrained decoding
strategies select tokens from the probability distribution produced by the LLM directly, without considering DSL-specific validity constraints. For example, temperature sampling adjusts the sharpness of this distribution by scaling the next-token logits before normalization. Other commonly used strategies include greedy decoding, beam search [45], top- $k$ sampling [46], and top- $p$ sampling [47].

Constrained decoding.
In many applications, the generated sequence is required to satisfy constraints beyond those captured by the language model distribution. Constrained decoding refers to decoding methods that restrict token selection using an external constraint specification. Given a set of constraints $\Phi=\{\phi_{1},\ldots,\phi_{k}\}$ , the goal is to generate an output sequence $\boldsymbol{y}$ such that $\boldsymbol{y}$ satisfies every constraint in $\Phi$ , while still using the LLM probabilities to guide token selection.

When the constraint specification is a CFG $G$ , the constraint is that the final output must belong to the language generated by the grammar, i.e., $\boldsymbol{y}\in L(G)$ . Such methods are commonly referred to as grammar-constrained decoding [26, 27, 28, 29, 30, 31]. The core idea is to maintain a parser state induced by the output and, at each decoding step, mask tokens that would make the output impossible to extend into a syntactically valid sequence [26, 28]. As a result, these approaches enforce concrete-syntax validity during generation, but do not by themselves ensure that the resulting instance model is consistent.

Beyond grammar-constrained decoding.
Several approaches augment grammar-constrained decoding with additional semantic reasoning mechanisms.
These approaches typically refine the token mask by incorporating complementary information, such as semantic pruners or static analyzers, thereby restricting generation with additional constraints [32, 33, 34]. However, they either lack sufficient expressive power to capture complex structured semantic properties [32] or focus on a narrow class of constraints [34, 33]. For example, ChopChop [32] employs semantic pruners. Given a program space, a semantic pruner returns the subspace of programs that satisfy a particular constraint, such as type consistency. Such pruners cannot fully express all types of constraints.
Other approaches [33, 34, 48] focus only on specific language semantic properties rather than general DSL specifications.

IterGen [35] takes a different approach by building on SynCode [29] with an iterative backtracking mechanism that revises previously generated tokens upon constraint violations. It introduces three operations: forward (generate until a syntactic unit is reached), backward (rewind to a previously generated syntactic unit), and view (retrieve the strings associated with a syntactic unit), enabling programmatic inspection and enforcement of semantic constraints dur
conclusion:
DSL correctness goes beyond syntactic validity.
RQ1-RQ3 show that syntactic validity alone is insufficient to ensure correctness of generated DSL instances. Grammar-constrained decoding is effective at enforcing the concrete syntax, but it can still generate inconsistent instances and, in some cases, even achieve lower consistency than unconstrained decoding. By verifying the generated outputs at the metamodel level, MeMoDecode provides an additional layer of correctness beyond syntax. This leads to systematic improvements in consistency and, for alignment metrics that treat invalid instances as unusable, also improves alignment with the intended output.

LLM capacity and guarantee.
RQ1 and RQ3 show that larger LLMs can improve both consistency and alignment. However, they still fail to produce consistent DSL instances in many cases. Even GPT-5.5 generates inconsistent instances on three of the four benchmarks, reaching only 82.9% consistency on CLEVR. These results suggest that while LLM scaling reduces the frequency of inconsistent instances, it does not eliminate the need for formal verification, especially when the generated results are intended for downstream SE applications.

Runtime overhead and retry.
RQ4 shows that the main runtime overhead of MeMoDecode comes from the additional LLM inference introduced by regenerating tokens after rejected syntactic units, while metamodel-level verification accounts for only a small fraction of the total runtime.
Therefore, future work should focus on more efficient retry and recovery strategies, such as finer-grained backtracking, adaptive retry budgets, verifier-guided resampling, or decoding-time repair mechanisms that reduce the need for regeneration.

Limitations and future work.
While MeMoDecode improves over both baseline decoding approaches, several limitations remain for future work. First, this paper focuses on unfixable constraints, while accepting partial models with fixable violations.
Future work could explore how to use these fixable violations as decoding-time heuristics.
Currently, MeMoDecode focuses only on the final output generated by the LLM. Future work could extend the framework to reasoning LLMs, where verification may guide not only the generated DSL tokens but also intermediate reasoning traces. Finally, MeMoDecode could be integrated with DSL frameworks such as Xtext [55] and JetBrains MPS [67] to streamline DSL development with verified LLM-based instance generation.

title: SAKURA: Serving Attention Key-Value State Under Rate Adaptation for Private Image Editing on Phones
abstract: Diffusion transformers are widely used in image-editing services. To preserve both efficiency and privacy, existing systems commonly rely on cloud-device collaboration. Keeping request-specific inference on the device avoids sending personal images and prompts to the cloud. These workloads often use common templates, such as in face swapping and virtual try-on, enabling KV state to be precomputed and reused across requests. However, this reusable state is large and scales with the number of templates, making it impractical to store all of them on mobile devices. Storing them in the cloud addresses this capacity issue, but cache transfer is placed onto the inference path and can even be slower than on-device computation, especially under fluctuating mobile networks. We introduce SAKURA, a cloud-edge architecture that delivers reusable attention state to mobile devices under a bandwidth budget. It first uses a fine-grained token-importance-aware compression method to preserve image quality under limited transfer budgets. At runtime, SAKURA adaptively selects the cache representation for each upcoming shard based on network bandwidth. To enable efficient execution, we develop a pipelined runtime that overlaps cache transfer and reconstruction with on-device execution. We evaluate SAKURA using three editing tasks and two diffusion models, using a Snapdragon 8 Elite Gen 5 phone. SAKURA reduces latency by 1.82x and 3.27x over CacheGen adapted to DiT and on-device generation, respectively. It also reduces cache storage by 3.06x over uncompressed cache, while preserving image quality.

body_start:
Abstract.

Diffusion transformers are widely used in image-editing services.
To preserve both efficiency and privacy, existing systems commonly rely on cloud–device collaboration.
Keeping request-specific inference on the device avoids sending personal images and prompts to the cloud.
These workloads often use common templates, such as in face swapping and virtual try-on, enabling KV state to be precomputed and reused across requests.
However, this reusable state is large and scales with the number of templates, making it impractical to store all of them on mobile devices.
Storing them in the cloud addresses this capacity issue, but cache transfer is placed onto the inference path and can even be slower than on-device computation, especially under fluctuating mobile networks.

We introduce SAKURA, a cloud–edge architecture that delivers reusable attention state to mobile devices under a bandwidth budget.
It first uses a fine-grained token-importance-aware compression method to preserve image quality under limited transfer budgets.
At runtime, SAKURA adaptively selects the cache representation for each upcoming shard based on network bandwidth.
To enable efficient execution, we develop a pipelined runtime that overlaps cache transfer and reconstruction with on-device execution.
We evaluate SAKURA using three editing tasks and two diffusion models, using a Snapdragon 8 Elite Gen 5 phone.
SAKURA reduces latency by 1.82 $\times$ and 3.27 $\times$ over CacheGen adapted to DiT and on-device generation, respectively.
It also reduces cache storage by 3.06 $\times$ over uncompressed cache, while preserving image quality.

## 1. Introduction

Diffusion transformers (DiTs) have become a leading architecture for
high-fidelity image generation and editing
(Peebles and Xie, 2023; Esser et al., 2024; Chen et al., 2024b; Black Forest Labs, 2026). A widely deployed class of editing
applications personalizes only part of a provider-supplied image
while preserving the surrounding content. Virtual try-on (Kim et al., 2024; Wan et al., 2026; Zhao and Peng, 2026), face swapping
(Baliah et al., 2025; Yu et al., 2025; He et al., 2026), and localized image editing
(Jiang et al., 2026; Mao et al., 2024; Simsar et al., 2024) are representative examples.
Personalized editing is already offered by cloud services,
such as Google Shopping’s photo-conditioned virtual try-on and Amazon Nova
Canvas’s managed virtual try-on API
(Google, 2025; Amazon Web Services, 2025; Alibaba Group, 2026; Alibaba Cloud, 2026). These applications take
two kinds of different inputs: provider-owned templates can be
public and reused across users, whereas each request contains
privacy-sensitive user data such as personal photographs, reference images,
and editing instructions. Keeping request-specific inference on the device is
therefore attractive because these inputs and the intermediate states derived
from them need not be sent to a remote execution service. Recent advances in model compression, architecture optimization, and
heterogeneous mobile execution have made on-device diffusion inference
increasingly practical
(Li et al., 2023; Zhao et al., 2024; Chen et al., 2025).

When requests share a template and a fixed mask defining the
editable region, computation associated with the unchanged region can be
reused across requests. In a DiT,
the key/value (KV) state of these reusable tokens can
be precomputed for each template
and reused while the device computes only
the request-dependent state for the edited region
(Jiang et al., 2026; Li et al., 2026; Yu et al., 2024; Qin et al., 2025). Cross-request reuse can therefore substantially
reduce repeated on-device computation. Every template has a different reusable state and the aggregate footprint grows with the number of templates.

This creates a mobile-specific scalability gap between execution capacity and reuse capacity: a device may have enough compute and working memory to run each edit, yet lack the storage to retain caches across a large template catalog.
In our FLUX.2-klein-4B deployment (Black Forest Labs, 2026) at $512\times 512$ resolution, the reusable FP16 KV state occupies up to 1.46 GiB for a single template. A catalog with hundreds of templates would therefore require hundreds of gigabytes of persistent storage, far beyond what is practical to replicate on individual mobile devices.
Cloud-only execution avoids this storage constraint but requires sending private user requests to the
server.
We instead consider a different cloud–edge split: request-specific
inference remains on the device, while the cloud stores the much larger,
provider-owned reusable templates and supplies the required cache on demand.
Unlike conventional cloud–edge inference, which
offloads all or part of a request to remote compute (Han et al., 2016; Kang et al., 2017; Yan et al., 2024), this scheme uses the cloud for template storage.
The network carries reusable template state,
while user inputs and request-specific activations remain on the device.

Moving reusable state to the cloud resolves the device-side capacity problem,
but places cache transfer on the inference path. At the 545 Mbps median
bandwidth of the 5G trace used in our evaluation (Narayanan et al., 2020), transferring
the full FP16 cache takes approximately 23 s, even without device-side cache
reconstruction. In comparison, executing the complete model locally without
cache reuse takes about 13 s on our mobile platform. Naively fetching
the full cache is therefore slower than running the complete model locally.
Remote reuse must both reduce the transmitted bytes and hide cache transfer
behind local computation.

These requirements translate into two challenges. First, the cache must be
compressed aggressively enough to arrive before use while preserving editing
quality. At an approximately 10% mask ratio, only 2.3 s of local computation
is available in total to hide cache transfer; even uniform 2-bit quantization
requires at least 650 Mbps, above the median 5G bandwidth.
Moreover, reusable cache compression must be constructed offline, before
future edit requests are known. This is challenging because the importance of cached tokens depends on the request-specific query generated by the edited region.
Therefore, compression must determine which tokens to preserve without knowing the future request.
Second, cache transfer must adapt as mobile bandwidth changes during an edit.
A representation chosen early in execution may become too large when bandwidth
drops or unnecessarily compressed when bandwidth improves, requiring transfer
decisions to be revised as later cache state is consumed.

Token-importance-aware cache compression.
Our first key idea is to make request-dependent token importance usable for offline reusable cache compression.
Although the exact attention scores depend on the specific request, We observe that, for a fixed template and mask, the reusable tokens that matter most remain largely consistent across different edit requests at the same transformer block and denoising
step.
This consistency allows importance measured from representative requests offline (i.e., through profiling) to guide compression for future requests.
Accordingly, compression can preseve cached tokens that are consistently important with higher accuracy.

Bandwidth-adaptive streaming.
Our second key idea is to make cache transfer
decisions at fine granularity based on the network conditions.
Each shard contains the reusable state for a group of consecutive transformer blocks at one denoising step.
SAKURA can adjust its transfer decision before each shard is needed.
It combines recent network measurements with device execution progress to determine how much cache data can arrive in time, then selects the highest-quality available representation that fits this budget.
If an earlier transfer finishes ahead of use, the resulting lead time is carried forward to later shards.
This allows cache transfer to track bandwidth changes within an edit instead of turning them into execution
stalls.

We present SAKURA, a cloud–edge cache streaming system
that realizes these ideas through complementary offline and online
decisions. Offline, SAKURA uses transferable token importance to construct
an importance-weighted low-rank factorization, preserving high-impact tokens’
KV state more accurately under aggressive compression. The compressed cache can vary along two dimensions: how much low-dimensional
structure is retained and how precisely it is encoded. These choices are
organized into a nested representation, allowing multiple compression levels
to share the same offline-constructed cache and enabling runtime adaptation
without repeating compression.
Online, SAKURA adaptively selects the representation of each upcoming cache shard based on current network conditions and device execution progress, ensuring that the shard can be transferred before it is needed for computation.
To enable efficient mobile execution, we develop a heterogeneous mobile runtime that pipelines cache
reception on the CPU, reconstruction on the GPU, and model execution on the NPU, overlapping the communication and reconstruction behind on-device computation.

This paper makes the following contributions:

• 

To the best of our knowledge, we present the first cloud–edge system that enables DiT cache reuse for mobile image editing, where reusable template cache states are stored in the cloud and streamed to the device upon request.

• 

We design a token-importance-aware cache compression scheme that exploits the stability of importance of the cache state across requests.
We also design a cache representation that supports fine-grained adaptation across precision levels without storing a separate version for each level.

• 

We develop an adaptive runtime that adjusts cache transfer to bandwidth fluctuations and overlaps cache transfer and reconstruction with on-device diffusion computation.

• 

We evaluate SAKURA on three editing tasks and two diffusion models using both 5G traces and WiFi.
On a Snapdragon 8 Elite Gen 5 phone, SAKURA reduces generation latency by 1.82 $\times$ and 3.27 $\times$ compared with CacheGen (Liu et al., 2024a) adapted to DiT and on-device generation, respectively.
It also reduces cache storage by 3.06 $\times$ compared with uncompressed caching while preserving image quality.

## 2. Background and Motivation

## 2.1. Cross-Request KV Reuse for Image Editing

Diffusion transformers (DiTs) generate images through multiple denoising steps, each executing the same stack of transformer blocks. Within each block, token-wise operators process tokens independently, while self-attention aggregates global context through Query (Q), Key (K), and Value (V) representations (Sun et al., 2026; Vaswani et al., 2023).

Masked image editing modifies only a target region while leaving the rest of a
template unchanged, creating substantial cross-request reuse opportunities
(Jiang et al., 2026; Li et al., 2026; Yu et al., 2024; Qin et al., 2025). As illustrated in
Figure 1, token-wise operators only need to process
tokens inside the editable mask. For self-attention, the model computes Q, K,
and V for these masked-region tokens, combines their K and V with cached K and
V from the unchanged template tokens, and evaluates attention only for queries
from the masked region.
Such localized editing is common in applications including virtual try-on (Kim et al., 2024; Wan et al., 2026; Zhao and Peng, 2026), face swapping (Version Systems Private Limited, 2026; Canva, nd), and inpainting (Xie et al., 2025a; Manukyan et al., 2024).

This reuse enables sparse request-time execution, but requires a large reusable cache. Because the hidden states of unchanged tokens differ across denoising steps and DiT blocks, skipping their computation requires preserving the corresponding K and V tensors for every step and every block. Thus, each template effectively maintains reusable KV state indexed by (denoising step, DiT block). For example, caching this state for a single $512\times 512$ template in a lightweight 4B FLUX2 model (Black Forest Labs, 2026) requires 1.46 GiB, and the footprint grows with the template library.

Recent mobile diffusion systems demonstrate that modern mobile devices have
sufficient compute capability for on-device diffusion inference
(Feng et al., 2026; Li et al., 2023; Zhao et al., 2024).
However, this improvement in compute capability does not eliminate the storage
cost of maintaining a large library of per-template KV caches locally.
At the same time, keeping request-time inference local avoids transmitting privacy-sensitive user inputs and request-derived intermediate states to the cloud (Sun et al., 2021; Nayan et al., 2024). This creates a mismatch between compute capacity and reuse-state capacity: the device can execute the sparse request-specific computation, but cannot retain all reusable state needed to enable it. Supporting cross-request reuse at scale therefore requires separating request-time computation from reusable-state storage.

## 2.2. Cloud–Edge Placement of Reusable State

The mismatch motivates a cloud–edge separation of computation and reusable state. As shown in Figure 1, the edge performs all request-specific inference, while the cloud stores the reusable per-template KV library and supplies the required entries on demand. This organization exploits the different roles of the two components: request-specific computation remains local, while reusable state, whose aggregate footprint grows with the template library, is placed in a remote tier with large capacity.

This setup differs from conventional cloud–edge inference, where the cloud primarily serves as an execution resource. Prior systems either offload an entire request or partition model execution across the device and server (Han et al., 2016; Kang et al., 2017), with intermediate activations or generation stages crossing the network (Kang et al., 2017; Yan et al., 2024; Xie et al., 2025b; Wei et al., 2025). In contrast, the cloud in our system acts as a remote storage for state: computation does not migrate across the network; only reusable KV state is transferred to the device.

This separation solves the device-side storage problem, but shifts the bottleneck to cache transfer. On our mobile platform, full-model execution without reuse takes 13 s, whereas transferring the full FP16 cache over the 545 Mb/s median throughput of our 5G trace (Narayanan et al., 2020) takes approximately 23 s. Naively fetching the full cache is therefore slower than local recomputation. Making remote reuse practical requires both reducing this transfer overhead and ensuring that the required cache state reaches the device in time for execution. We next examine the system challenges behind these requirements.

## 3. Challenges and High-Level Ideas

In this section, we describe two key challenges in enabling streaming KV acache for on-device diffusion editing and then introduce our high-level ideas.

## 3.1. Quality-Efficient Cache Representation

Due to limited mobile network bandwidth, only a limited cache size can be transferred before the reusable cache is consumed in the diffusion edit process.
As such, the cache compression must be quality-efficient: for a given cache size, it should preserve the reusable information that contributes most to output quality.
Using the same FLUX2 example in §2, execution with cache reuse has a median aggregate transfer window of only 2.3 s at a 10% mask ratio.
Even an aggressive 2-bit quantization still requires 650 Mbps of bandwidth, while leaving the quality non-ideal (results in §6.3).
This motivates selectively preserving the cached information with high image quality impact under a fixed transfer budget.

Cross-request DiT reuse introduces a new token importance problem.

Prior work has shown that token importance can reduce KV or computation.
LLM systems exploit this for request-time retention, eviction, or fetching (Zhang et al., 2023b; Li et al., 2024b; Lee et al., 2024), while DiT serving systems use such signals for token routing, merging, pruning, or reuse within a denoising process (You et al., 2025; Wu et al., 2025; Gupta et al., 2025).
These approaches determine important tokens based on the ongoing request.

Cross-request DiT reuse is a new challenge: a reusable cache is constructed once for a template and must serve future unknown edit requests. 
Consequently, token-importance-aware compression cannot simply reuse important tokens measured
from the current request. Instead, it requires a template-level signal that remains
valid across future edit requests.
This raises two questions: (1) whether some reusable cache tokens matter more than others to the final edit,
and (2) whether the same tokens remain important across different edit requests.

In this work, we show that remote reuse of DiT template caches can make
on-device image editing practical without replicating large cache collections
on the device or offloading private request data to the cloud.
SAKURA combines token-importance-aware offline compression with fine-grained,
bandwidth-adaptive cache streaming and a pipelined mobile runtime, allowing
cache transfer to track both network conditions and device execution.
Our evaluation demonstrates that SAKURA simultaneously improves latency, storage efficiency, and output quality: it is 1.55–1.82 $\times$ faster and 1.54–2.37 $\times$ more storage-efficient than prior KV-streaming systems, while also outperforming fully local execution by 3.27 $\times$ and reducing full-FP16 cache storage by 3.06 $\times$ .
