body_start:
Abstract

A common application of the process mining discipline is to connect observed event data with Petri nets, which are bipartite, directed graphical process models with rich formal underpinnings. Recent work learns vector representations of Petri nets to retrieve process models and relate them to event logs, but leaves implicit two key aspects hidden within the net’s structure: directed cycles (process loops) and invariants recorded by the net’s incidence matrix. We expose both of these to message-passing graph neural networks, through a positional encoding built from return probabilities of directed place-transition walks (PNRWPE), and through same-type messages gated by diffusion kernels of the incidence matrix (DA-PNGNN). Our constructions raise macro balanced accuracy in predicting the generation factors of the 96 Process Discovery Contest 2023 models from 0.751 to 0.796 with PNRWPE, which nearly doubles accuracy on process loops, and to 0.830 with DA-PNGNN, which, without retuning, also improves net-to-tree retrieval top-1 accuracy on the self-supervised ProcRosetta benchmark by 4.1 to 5.9 points.

## 1 Introduction

Petri nets are a commonly used formal model of discrete-event dynamical systems supporting the analysis of concurrent computation [17]. This has made them popular in the process-mining literature, which constructs, checks, and simulates them routinely [22]. Other process-mining tasks, such as retrieving similar models from a collection or relating a model to the event logs of the same process, can be approached by learning vector representations of the nets themselves. Existing work has learned such representations for retrieval and classification [6], and a recent study [4] has built a multimodal neural model that aligns the process net with the process tree that generated it [22] and the associated event logs.

A Petri net is, stripped to its bare bones, a directed bipartite graph whose two node partitions (or types) have semantic roles, and whose incidence matrix carries an algebra of conservation that Petri net theory has studied for decades [17]. Message passing is the de facto paradigm for learning on graphs [11]. It relies on repeated local aggregation of learned node features along the edges of the graph. It is therefore a natural tool for learning representations of a Petri net, and simple adaptations of message-passing networks have been shown to be beneficial [4]. We argue that current modeling approaches are not making complete use of specific structural inductive biases that a Petri net structure can provide. Concrete examples are notions of where a node sits relative to directed cycles, and whether paths between node partitions that lead to potential token conservation exist. This raises the central question that motivates our work: can the structure that Petri net theory makes explicit improve learned representations of process models?

In this work, we answer this question by proposing two constructions that extract higher-order structural information from a Petri net for use in message passing. The first concerns positional encodings (PEs). Since graphs are structured domains, a sense of position lets a node encode its graph-based distance to other nodes, or its membership in substructures that matter for a downstream task [8]. A positional encoding implements this as a deterministic vector describing a node’s structural role, which can be fed as input to any neural model over the graph, and a popular instantiation is the random-walk positional encoding (RWPE) [9]. We extend this encoding to Petri nets, obtaining the Petri net random-walk positional encoding (PNRWPE), by building it on the return probabilities of an alternating place-transition walk, a construction similar in spirit to the one used by transformers for directed graphs [10]. Since directed returns collapse on acyclic nets, we also derive a variant with uniform teleportation between opposite node types, which acts as a directed, bipartite PageRank [2]. Both encodings are equivariant to node reordering and can be cheaply computed for a new net.

The second construction is a modification of the message-passing procedure itself. The incidence matrix of a net records how each transition consumes and produces tokens, which lets us define a diffusion operator whose steady state lies in the place- or transition-invariant subspaces of the net [17]. Its powers yield pairwise kernels between nodes of the same type that suppress violations of linear token balance, and we use these kernels to learn same-type messages in addition to the ordinary ones. The resulting higher-order message passing produces representations that are informed about the state and structural conservation properties of the Petri net, an inductive bias unique to this graphical model. This construction is compatible with any message-passing architecture and can be used together with PNRWPE. We call the resulting architecture the diffusion-augmented Petri net graph neural network (DA-PNGNN).

We derive both constructions from first principles and evaluate them on two benchmarks from recent work: supervised prediction of the generation factors of the Process Discovery Contest (PDC) 2023 process models [6], and the self-supervised multimodal objective of ProcRosetta [4]. Both constructions provide improvements and the diffusion kernels do so on both benchmarks: on PDC 2023 they raise macro balanced accuracy from 0.751 to 0.832 when used together, while on ProcRosetta DA-PNGNN improves net-to-tree retrieval by up to 5.9 top-1 accuracy points. We run several control experiments that isolate the contribution of each component, study the effect of the receptive field during message passing, and also report the computational cost of the main architectural variants. The rest of the paper is organized as follows: Section 2 provides some background and fixes notation, Sections 3 and 4 derive the two constructions, Section 5 reports the complete experimental protocol and results, and Section 6 discusses what the evidence supports and our final conclusions.

## 2 Preliminaries

This section provides a brief account of the two ingredients that our constructions build on. Section 2.1 summarizes message passing and random-walk positional encodings on ordinary graphs, and Section 2.2 introduces the matrices that describe a Petri net. We denote matrices by upper-case letters ( $A$ , $\Phi$ ), vectors and scalars by lower-case, with the role of each symbol clear from the context. For a matrix $A$ , $A_{ij}$ is its $(i,j)$ -th entry, $(A^{k})_{ij}$ the corresponding entry of its $k$ -th power, $A^{\top}$ its transpose, and $\operatorname{diag}(A)$ the vector of its diagonal entries. Conversely, $\operatorname{diag}(v)$ is the diagonal matrix built from a vector $v$ . The symbol $\mathbf{1}$ denotes the all-ones vector or matrix and $I$ the identity matrix. Their shape is given as a subscript and is otherwise to be understood from the context. $\mathbb{N}_{0}$ denotes the nonnegative integers, $\mathbb{R}$ the reals, $\ker$ the null space of a matrix, and $\det$ its determinant. Finally, $\left\lVert\cdot\right\rVert_{2}$ denotes the Euclidean norm for vectors and the spectral norm for matrices.

## 2.1 Graph neural networks

Graph neural networks (GNNs) are a subclass of neural networks that learn representations of graph data by locally aggregating information [20, 11]. The main goal of the architecture is to implement symmetries natural to graphs [1]. Consider, for simplicity, an unweighted and undirected graph $G$ with $n$ nodes, represented by a symmetric binary adjacency matrix $A\in\{0,1\}^{n\times n}$ . This setting can be easily extended to deal with more general connectivity structures, as we will do in this work. By associating a node signal $X\in\mathbb{R}^{n\times m}$ with the graph, we can describe a simple GNN as a learnable convolution of the node signal with $A$ as the shift operator. A generalization of this concept can be obtained by considering the message-passing framework:

 $x_{i}^{(\ell)}=\theta^{(\ell)}\left(x_{i}^{(\ell-1)},\bigoplus_{j\in\mathcal{N}(i)}\,\phi^{(\ell)}\left(x_{i}^{(\ell-1)},x_{j}^{(\ell-1)},e_{ji}\right)\right),$ 

(1)

where $x_{i}^{(\ell)}$ denotes the features of node $i$ at layer $\ell$ , $e_{ji}$ the (optional) edge features of the connection between nodes $j$ and $i$ , $\mathcal{N}(\cdot)$ the set of (1-hop) neighbor nodes, $\bigoplus$ a differentiable, permutation-invariant function (e.g., sum, mean), and $\phi,\theta$ denote differentiable and (optionally) nonlinear functions such as multilayer perceptrons. Note that $\phi$ is of crucial importance as it allows us to transform the node features before aggregation, thereby acting as a map that determines what the aggregate can record.

## Positional encodings and random walks.

Positional encodings complement the node signal $X$ with information
about each node’s relative position (or structural role) in the graph. We remind the reader that a canonical coordinate system cannot be fixed on a graph and therefore the naive notion of an absolute, global positional encoding cannot be employed. In a certain sense, a graph positional encoding can be thought of as attempting to provide information about the relative positioning of a node with respect to others. In this work, we focus on random-walk positional encodings [9]. For the undirected graph $G$ , let $d_{i}=\sum_{j=1}^{n}A_{ij}$ denote the degree of node $i$ . The random-walk transition matrix $Q\in[0,1]^{n\times n}$ is defined by $Q_{ij}=A_{ij}/d_{i}$ whenever $d_{i}>0$ . Given a maximum walk length $K$ , the RWPE of node $i$ is

 $r_{i}=\left[Q_{ii},(Q^{2})_{ii},\ldots,(Q^{K})_{ii}\right]\in[0,1]^{K}.$ 

(2)

The coordinate $(Q^{k})_{ii}$ is the probability that a random walk starting at node $i$ returns to that node after $k$ steps.
The relative position of the node is therefore captured through the return patterns at different walk lengths: high values throughout the components of this position vector imply the node lives in a dense cluster within the graph. In this scenario, the positional encoding will be similar for nodes in that cluster. The encoding can be incorporated directly into features fed into a GNN, for example through concatenation with $x^{(0)}_{i}$ in Equation (1).

## 2.2 Petri net structure

We consider finite Petri nets with place set $P$ , transition set $T$ , and nonnegative integer arc multiplicities $w$ . Let $n_{P}=|P|$ , $n_{T}=|T|$ , and $n=n_{P}+n_{T}$ . We assume $n_{P},n_{T}>0$ and allow for disconnected components or isolated nodes. Inhibitor, timed, and colored-net semantics require additional structure and lie outside the scope of this study. The matrices $E^{-},E^{+}\in\mathbb{N}_{0}^{n_{P}\times n_{T}}$ , with entries $E^{-}_{ij}=w(p_{i},t_{j})$ and $E^{+}_{ij}=w(t_{j},p_{i})$ , record token consumption ( $P\to T$ ) and production ( $T\to P$ ), respectively. In both cases we index using places as rows and transitions as columns. The Petri net’s structure can be represented by the following directed adjacency matrix, written in block form as

 $A=\begin{pmatrix}0&E^{-}\\
(E^{+})^{\top}&0\end{pmatrix}\in\mathbb{N}_{0}^{n\times n}.$ 

(3)

Notice the bipartition: there are no $P\to P$ or $T\to T$ arcs and $P\cap T=\emptyset$ . The incidence matrix is defined as $B=E^{+}-E^{-}\in\mathbb{Z}^{n_{P}\times n_{T}}$ . It encodes the net change of tokens at each place when a transition fires. This object is fundamental in Petri net theory, as it captures the structural relationships between places and transitions [17]. For a marking (token state) $m\in\mathbb{N}_{0}^{n_{P}}$ , a transition $t_{j}$ is enabled when $m_{i}\geq E^{-}_{ij}$ for every place $p_{i}$ . Therefore, an enabled firing sequence with transition-count vector $x\in\mathbb{N}_{0}^{n_{T}}$ satisfies $m^{\prime}=m+Bx$ , an important fact for the interpretation of our later derivations.

## 3 Petri net random-walk encodings

We now start by presenting the first of our constructions, the Petri net random-walk positional encoding (PNRWPE). Define

 $\displaystyle d_{P}$ 
 $\displaystyle=E^{-}\mathbf{1}_{n_{T}}\in\mathbb{N}_{0}^{n_{P}},$ 
 $\displaystyle d_{T}$ 
 $\displaystyle=(E^{+})^{\top}\mathbf{1}_{n_{P}}\in\mathbb{N}_{0}^{n_{T}}$ 

(4)

 $\displaystyle\Phi$ 
 $\displaystyle=D_{P}^{\dagger}E^{-}\in[0,1]^{n_{P}\times n_{T}},$ 
 $\displaystyle\Psi$ 
 $\displaystyle=D_{T}^{\dagger}(E^{+})^{\top}\in[0,1]^{n_{T}\times n_{P}},$ 

(5)

where $D_{P}=\operatorname{diag}(d_{P})$ and $D_{T}=\operatorname{diag}(d_{T})$ . The symbol $\dagger$ denotes the reciprocal of each positive diagonal entry and zero at a zero entry. The matrix $\Phi$ describes a walker that, when at a place, chooses to move to a transition in proportion to the corresponding arc weight, and $\Psi$ has a similar interpretation for the other direction. It is worth noting that $\Phi$ and $\Psi$ have row sums in $\{0,1\}$ . We would like to emphasize this last statement: a zero row stops the walk, which corresponds to the walker landing on a sink node. Define the walk transition operator as

 $Q=\begin{pmatrix}0&\Phi\\
\Psi&0\end{pmatrix}\in[0,1]^{n\times n}.$ 

(6)

The walker starts at a node and takes a random walk according to $Q$ . The return probability after $k$ steps is the probability that the walker is back at the same node after $k$ steps, given by the diagonal of $Q^{k}$ . Since the walk alternates between the two partitions, such a return can only happen after an even number of steps, because bipartite graphs have no odd cycles. Algebraically, this is easily seen from the fact that $\operatorname{diag}(Q^{2k+1})=0,\;\forall k\in\mathbb{N}_{0}$ . On the other hand, for even walks we have that

 $Q^{2}=\begin{pmatrix}\Phi\Psi&0\\
0&\Psi\Phi\end{pmatrix}\implies Q^{2k}=\begin{pmatrix}(\Phi\Psi)^{k}&0\\
0&(\Psi\Phi)^{k}\end{pmatrix}.$ 

(7)

We can thus focus on the two-step operators $M_{P}=\Phi\Psi\in[0,1]^{n_{P}\times n_{P}}$ and $M_{T}=\Psi\Phi\in[0,1]^{n_{T}\times n_{T}}$ , which describe the return probabilities for places and transitions, respectively. One step of $M_{P}$ follows a place-transition-place path, while one step of $M_{T}$ follows a transition-place-transition path. We are now left with a final problem, which is that of sinks, as they can simply stop the walk. To address this, we define an absorption correction that adds the missing probability mass to the diagonal of each two-step operator. This ensures that the return probabilities remain well-defined. For $a\in\{P,T\}$ , define $\zeta_{a}=\mathbf{1}-M_{a}\mathbf{1}$ and $R_{a}=M_{a}+\operatorname{diag}(\zeta_{a})$ . Since $M_{a}$ is substochastic, $\zeta_{a}\geq 0$ and furthermore $R_{a}\mathbf{1}=M_{a}\mathbf{1}+\zeta_{a}=\mathbf{1}$ . This correction keeps all the missing probability mass at the current node. A sink node will thus absorb the probability mass and the walker will remain at that node for all future steps. For a fixed horizon $K$ , the Petri net random-walk positional encoding is defined as the vector of return probabilities after $2,4,\ldots,2K$ steps

 $\displaystyle r_{p_{i}}$ 
 $\displaystyle=\big[(R_{P})_{ii},(R_{P}^{2})_{ii},\ldots,(R_{P}^{K})_{ii}\big],r_{t_{j}}$ 
 $\displaystyle=\big[(R_{T})_{jj},(R_{T}^{2})_{jj},\ldots,(R_{T}^{K})_{jj}\big].$ 

(8)

## 3.1 Acyclic nets

There is a practical use case that we must take into consideration for our positional encodings. If the directed graph representing the Petri net is acyclic, $M_{a}$ has zero diagonal. A walk can return under $R_{a}$ only by repeatedly using the added self-loop, which implies that $(R_{a}^{k})_{ii}=(\zeta_{a})_{i}^{k}$ . The encodings will therefore be highly correlated on acyclic nets even when their structures differ substantially, which might limit their discriminative power. In simpler terms, variation in return signatures will be concentrated around cycles and stopping points, which can be considered both a strong and a weak point of PNRWPE, depending on the specific application.

We therefore define an additional PNRWPE variant that permits occasional jumps to nodes of the opposite type. Such jumps create fictitious return routes even when the original net has no directed cycle. This alternative is essentially an application of the PageRank walk [2] adapted for place-transition alternation. At a place with outgoing arcs, the walker follows $\Phi$ with probability $\alpha$ and jumps uniformly to a transition with probability $1-\alpha$ . At a transition, it follows $\Psi$ or jumps uniformly to a place. A node with no outgoing arcs always jumps, which bypasses the expressivity constraint described above. We therefore define the $P\to T$ and $T\to P$ transition matrices as

 $\displaystyle\Phi_{\alpha}$ 
 $\displaystyle=\alpha\Phi+\frac{1}{n_{T}}(\mathbf{1}_{n_{P}}-\alpha\Phi\mathbf{1}_{n_{T}})\mathbf{1}_{n_{T}}^{\top}\in\mathbb{R}^{n_{P}\times n_{T}},$ 

(9)

 $\displaystyle\Psi_{\alpha}$ 
 $\displaystyle=\alpha\Psi+\frac{1}{n_{P}}(\mathbf{1}_{n_{T}}-\alpha\Psi\mathbf{1}_{n_{P}})\mathbf{1}_{n_{P}}^{\top}\in\mathbb{R}^{n_{T}\times n_{P}}.$ 

(10)

The deficit in parentheses is a column vector, and its outer product distributes that deficit across destinations. Note that the normalization uses the size of the destination partition, meaning that teleportation is only defined between partitions.

Following the same logic as in the previous section, we define the two-step operators $M_{P,\alpha}=\Phi_{\alpha}\Psi_{\alpha}$ and $M_{T,\alpha}=\Psi_{\alpha}\Phi_{\alpha}$ and use them to define the teleportation PNRWPE, for a fixed horizon $K$ , through

\Psi_{\alpha}&0\end{pmatrix},\;Q_{\alpha}^{2k}=\begin{pmatrix}M_{P,\alpha}^{k}&0\\
0&M_{T,\alpha}^{k}\end{pmatrix},\;\begin{aligned} r_{p_{i}}^{\mathrm{tel}}&=\big[(M_{P,\alpha})_{ii},(M_{P,\alpha}^{2})_{ii},\ldots,(M_{P,\alpha}^{K})_{ii}\big],\\[5.0pt]
limitations:
Our evidence rests on two synthetic families of nets, and it is worth being precise about what that supports. The two benchmarks measure different things: the supervised recovery of the parameters that generated a net, and the geometry of a self-supervised latent space shared with two other views of the same process. Whether either construction helps other self-supervised objectives, or process-similarity tasks evaluated by behavior rather than by generation factors, remains to be tested.

There are two additional caveats regarding DA-PNGNN that we want to name rather than bury. The first is that both benchmarks have unit arc weights, so the multiplicity distinction of Figure 1, which motivated the kernels, is never tested explicitly in our experiments. The kernels are computed from the weighted incidence matrix and would register that distinction, but whether doing so helps a model remains untested. The second caveat concerns scaling. Pair kernels need $O(n_{P}^{2}+n_{T}^{2})$ storage per exponent and dense matrix powers cost cubic time, which is cheap for nets of tens of nodes, such as ours, but not for industrial process models, where sparse structures or a low-rank factorization of $S_{a}^{k}$ would be needed. Figure 5 in Appendix D places every variant by its epoch time and memory: the linear gate costs 2.6 times the plain encoder’s epoch on PDC and 4 to 5% more on ProcRosetta, where the encoder is a small part of the joint model, while the tanh gate needs 2.4 to 17 times the memory.

title: Retrieval Augmented Generation Compositionality
abstract: Retrieval Augmented Generation (RAG) grounds large language models in external knowledge. Modern pipelines combine embedding, chunking, retrieval, reranking, query augmentation, context compression, and agentic verification, yet these techniques are typically evaluated one at a time. It remains unclear whether their isolated gains survive composition, whether retrieval quality and answer faithfulness favor the same design choices, and whether conclusions from small corpora hold at large scale. We pre-declare three hypotheses and introduce LASAGNA, an open-source framework for controlled RAG evaluation. We test 450 configurations across eight benchmarks and corpora ranging from 5K to 200K documents. Three findings emerge. First, individually strong techniques from different phases of a RAG pipeline do not necessarily compose: three retrieval techniques predict a +47% combined improvement but deliver only +17% when used together. Second, component gains stack differently for retrieval and faithfulness, and optimizing one can hurt the other. Third, the best composition changes as the corpus grows: the combination that wins on a small corpus may not remain best at large scale. These findings show that gains measured in isolation are not reliable predictors of realistic performance, and that new RAG techniques should be tested with the full surrounding stack. We call on researchers to do so and supply LASAGNA to simplify these experiments.

body_start:
Abstract

Retrieval Augmented Generation (RAG) grounds large language models
in external knowledge. Modern pipelines combine embedding, chunking,
retrieval, reranking, query augmentation, context compression, and
agentic verification, yet these techniques are typically evaluated
one at a time. It remains unclear whether their isolated gains survive
composition, whether retrieval quality and answer faithfulness favor
the same design choices, and whether conclusions from small corpora
hold at large scale. We pre-declare three hypotheses and
introduce lasagna, an open-source framework for controlled
RAG evaluation. We test $450$ configurations across eight benchmarks
and corpora ranging from $5$ K to $200$ K documents. Three findings
emerge. First, individually strong techniques from different phases
of a RAG pipeline do not necessarily compose: three retrieval
techniques predict a $+47\%$ combined improvement but deliver only
 $+17\%$ when used together. Second, component gains stack differently
for retrieval and faithfulness, and optimizing one can hurt the other.
Third, the best composition changes as the corpus grows: the
combination that wins on a small corpus may not remain best at
large scale. These findings show that gains measured in isolation
are not reliable predictors of realistic performance, and that new RAG techniques
should be tested with the full surrounding stack. We call on
researchers to do so and supply lasagna to simplify these
experiments.

## 1 Introduction

Retrieval-augmented generation
(RAG) (Gao et al., 2023b; Fan et al., 2024) combines choices across
many pipeline stages. Our study covers eight stages that span the
dominant design axes in modern RAG (Fig. 1b; full
catalog in Appendix K): embedding, chunking, index-time
enrichment, retrieval, query augmentation, reranking, context
compression, and agentic quality gates. Most new techniques are
proposed and evaluated one stage at a time, in isolation from the
surrounding pipeline, or from several representative pipelines that
would test whether findings generalize (Yu et al., 2024). Adding to the complexity, RAG systems
are evaluated for two goals (Saad-Falcon et al., 2024; Friel et al., 2024):
retrieving the right content (NDCG@10) and producing a faithful
answer from it (Es et al., 2024, RAGAS;). It is unclear whether isolated gains persist under composition. It
is also unclear whether the same design choices optimize both
retrieval quality (which documents are retrieved) and answer
faithfulness (whether the answer is grounded in those documents),
two goals RAG evaluation typically reports separately. We pre-declare three hypotheses. H1. Components often fail
to compose: isolated gains from single-component ablations do not
necessarily persist when components are combined. H2. A
simple RAG pipeline can be near-optimal in many settings, while
more elaborate configurations tend to specialize to narrower ones.
Most RAG ablations in the literature run at 5K to 50K documents,
whereas the applications RAG can serve run at corpora an order of
magnitude larger; H3. composition rankings shift with
corpus scale, so conclusions from small-corpus benchmarks may not
hold at larger scales. Prior work has explored combinations through
configuration sweeps and heuristic
search (Wang et al., 2024; Li et al., 2025; Rau et al., 2024; Jin et al., 2025; Kim et al., 2024; Fu et al., 2024; Chen et al., 2026); these
approaches can identify strong configurations but do not directly
measure interaction effects: whether the benefit of one component
depends on the other components in the pipeline. These interactions,
and how they change with corpus scale, remain largely unquantified.

Testing these hypotheses requires a framework that isolates pipeline
stages and supports reproducible evaluation across benchmarks. We
created lasagna, an open-source RAG framework, to provide
this (Fig. 1a, Section 3). Each
stage sits behind a fixed interface, so swapping one method cannot
silently change the implementation at another. Adding a new
technique is a single line of code; the framework tests it inside a
complete modern pipeline without reimplementing the surrounding stack.

We use lasagna to study RAG composition with a
167-configuration D-optimal
design (Fedorov et al., 1972; Atkinson et al., 2007) across eight
configurable stages of a modern RAG pipeline
(Table 10), eight benchmarks (Fig. 5),
and corpus sizes from 5K to 200K documents, complemented by 138
non-factorial ablation configurations across 24 targeted
experiments (Appendix F). Across the factorial, ablation suite, and scaling sweep, the
central finding is that techniques that perform well separately do
not consistently retain their gains inside a full pipeline, and the
pattern differs between retrieval and faithfulness. Retrieval gains
compose sub-additively: the three largest single-component
improvements sum to a predicted $+47\%$ NDCG@10 gain, but the
composed pipeline realizes only $+17\%$ (Section D.14).
Faithfulness gains compose near-additively: separately measured
improvements approximately transfer to the full pipeline
(Table 47). Pipeline and generator
also partly substitute: a stronger generator helps the lightest pipeline
far more than the heaviest, so a heavier stack buys
less when the generator is already strong (Section F.9).

Three practical implications follow. First, the components that
improve retrieval are not the same as those that improve faithfulness,
and optimizing one metric can hurt the other. Second, the four
complete RAG profiles expose a Pareto tradeoff on retrieval
quality, faithfulness, and response time, with no universal winner.
Adding an agentic loop to a strong retrieval stack yields only a
negligible faithfulness gain while hurting retrieval quality and
latency. Across three other benchmarks at 100K–200K documents,
lighter pipelines retain similar measured quality at
 $10$ – $20\times$ lower latency
(Sections 5 and D.8). Third, corpus
size shifts profile rankings: the design leading at small corpora
trails by $13.7\%$ NDCG@10 at 200K, with a rank flip visible from
25K (Fig. 4(a)). Small-corpus rankings should therefore
be rechecked at the intended scale.
Our contributions are:

1. 

How RAG components compose. A compositional study
of RAG across eight configurable stages, eight benchmarks, and
corpora scales from 5K to 200K documents: 167 configurations from
a D-optimal factorial plus 138 non-factorial configurations across
24 targeted ablations. The four operational RAG profiles that
emerge (speed, standard, balanced,
max-reliable) are calibrated to cost, latency, and performance.

2. 

lasagna. The open-source framework built to
conduct and reproduce this study. It provides a modular,
stage-isolated RAG pipeline and an evaluation harness that lets
researchers add a method and test it with the surrounding stack
(Sections C.1 and F).

## 2 Related Work

Modern RAG spans a layered design space with plausible interaction
points at every stage (full method catalog in Appendix K).
On retrieval, sparse baselines
(BM25 (Robertson & Zaragoza, 2009)) coexist with dense encoders
(BGE-M3 (Chen et al., 2024a), E5 (Wang et al., 2022)), learned
sparse encoders (SPLADE (Formal et al., 2021)), and
late-interaction models (ColBERT (Khattab & Zaharia, 2020)), fused
by reciprocal-rank fusion (RRF) (Cormack et al., 2009) or learned
hybrids.
Reranking spans cross-encoder scorers trained on
MS-MARCO (Nogueira & Cho, 2019), ensemble rerankers, and
diversity-driven selection (MMR; Carbonell & Goldstein, 1998). Context
compression is either token-budget aware
(LLMLingua (Jiang et al., 2023a)) or positional
(lost-in-the-middle-aware selection (Liu et al., 2024)).
Query augmentation rewrites the query before retrieval:
HyDE (Gao et al., 2023a) drafts a hypothetical answer,
RAG-Fusion (Rackauckas, 2024) fans out multi-query
variants, decomposition (Khattab et al., 2024) splits multi-hop
questions into sub-questions, and step-back
prompting (Zheng et al., 2024) abstracts before retrieving.
Index-time processing enriches chunks before retrieval with
document summaries (RAPTOR (Sarthi et al., 2024)), contextual
prefixes (Anthropic, 2024), or entity-graph indexes
(GraphRAG (Edge et al., 2024)). Generation-time control
adds correction and gating loops around the answer model
(CRAG (Yan et al., 2024), Self-RAG (Asai et al., 2024),
Speculative-RAG (Wang et al., 2025)). Each of these
stages has been shown to help in isolation on some benchmark, but
they compose along more edges than a single-component ablation can
enumerate. We study how these choices combine once
deployed together, and lasagna lets others ask
compositionality questions in the same environment by
registering a new component and evaluating it against a full modern
pipeline.

Table 1 positions lasagna against prior
work that studies RAG beyond isolated components. Best-practice
studies (Wang et al., 2024; Barnett et al., 2024) search greedily
for strong end-to-end configurations but do not estimate interaction
effects. Benchmarking libraries such as BERGEN (Rau et al., 2024)
and FlashRAG (Jin et al., 2025) support composition in a shared
codebase but do not enforce the stage isolation that controlled
interaction estimation requires, so measured differences cannot be
cleanly attributed to the component being varied
(a positional smoke run against both is reported in
Section G.4). Automated
configuration search (Kim et al., 2024) optimizes
over configurations but reports only the winning setting, not the
interaction structure that produced it, so the resulting guidance
does not transfer when any assumption changes. Evaluation
suites (Krishna et al., 2025) and domain
benchmarks (Xiong et al., 2024) supply metrics
and tasks but not a common pipeline in which those metrics can be
compared across controlled compositions. Generation-time
controls (Yan et al., 2024) strengthen the agentic layer but are
usually tested with retrieval fixed, leaving composition with a tuned
stack untested.

## 3 LASAGNA: A Compositional Framework for RAG

lasagna is an open-source framework for
evaluating new RAG components inside a complete modern pipeline.
A researcher proposing a new reranker, chunker, or agentic loop today
must either compare against a stripped-down baseline that does not
reflect a modern pipeline, or reimplement the surrounding stack. The
first biases the conclusion by mixing implementation differences
with algorithmic ones; the second is prohibitively expensive and
rarely attempted. lasagna provides a configurable
end-to-end pipeline (Fig. 1a) with a fixed
interface per stage that the framework enforces, so a new component
drops into one stage and is measured against the same surrounding
stack used by every reported configuration (full code patterns in
Sections H.2.2, H.2.3 and H.2.4).
The workflow spans nine processing stages: document processing,
chunking, index-time enrichment, embedding and indexing, query
augmentation, retrieval, reranking, context compression, and answer
generation with optional agentic verification.
Every pipeline component is a subclass of a typed abstract base class:
eight component types are supported (embedder, chunker,
reranker, retriever, document_processor,
query_enhancer, agentic_pipeline, and generator), each
stage’s inputs and outputs are typed dataclass contracts, and
behavioral tests check that swapping one implementation does not mutate
a neighboring stage’s state. A single
@registry.register("<stage>", "<name>") decorator suffices
to make a new component discoverable at YAML-config time.
The framework ships with 53 built-in components, the 30 methods across the eight factorial
dimensions (Table 10; full catalog in Appendix K),
six vector backends (Milvus, Pinecone, Qdrant, Weaviate, pgvector,
OpenSearch), and adapters for the eight benchmarks used here (five
BEIR retrieval sets and three long-form QA sets;
Section B.2). Five automated isolation tests
(Section H.1) check that toggling one component does not
silently change another, including that two sessions with opposite
settings each keep their own configuration; this supports attributing
the interaction estimates in Section 5 to the components we
vary rather than to cross-stage leakage. A new component becomes a publishable comparison
in three steps (Fig. 2): register with a decorator,
declare a factorial sweep in YAML, and run end-to-end to receive a
paired statistical test against the same surrounding stack that
produced every reported number. The complete study, factorial plus
138 non-factorial ablations plus the 5K–200K scaling sweep, cost
approximately $5,200 in cloud compute and 310 wall-clock hours
(Section A.7).

## 4 Experimental Design

Notation.

A dimension is one of the eight experimental factors
(Table 10); default_standard is the
framework’s stock RAG pipeline (a simple, lowest-cost setting on
each dimension) that serves as the starting baseline for our
experiments; a profile is one of the four operational RAG
compositions we distill from our factorial and ablation sweeps as
the best-observed configurations targeting distinct points on the
retrieval-faithfulness-latency envelope (speed,
standard, balanced, max-reliable; full
specifications in Section I.1); a track
is one of the two evaluation surfaces (retrieval or end-to-end). We evaluate on both tracks
because retrieval quality (whether the right documents are
retrieved) and answer faithfulness (whether the generated answer
is grounded in the retrieved context) measure distinct properties
of a RAG pipeline, and different applications weight them
differently. We report the joint quality-latency envelope as a
hypervolume $\mathrm{HV}(L_{\mathrm{ref}})=\mathrm{NDCG@10}\times\mathrm{Faith}\times\max(0,1-\mathrm{latency}/L_{\mathrm{ref}})$ 
 (Zitzler et al., 2003) at $L_{\mathrm{ref}}{=}30$  s (a
fixed response-time reference; Table 2); HV values under
other fixed references are in Table 39. We
report marginal effect sizes as $\eta^{2}$ ; larger values indicate
stronger associations with variation in the metric (full statistics
in Sections D.2 and D.11).

Factorial design.

The configuration space spans eight
experimental dimensions, with 2–5 levels each (Fig. 1b,
Table 10). The full factorial of
 $4{\times}4{\times}4{\times}3{\times}5{\times}4{\times}2{\times}4=30{,}720$ 
configurations would exceed $\sim$ 40,000 GPU-hours and
 $\sim$ $600,000 in LLM API costs (extrapolating from the executed
167-configuration budget of 247 GPU-hours and $5,200;
Section A.7), roughly two orders of magnitude beyond our
resources, so we draw a 242-run D-optimal subset via Fedorov
coordinate exchange (Fedorov et al., 1972), sized to keep all
main effects and all 28 dimension-pair interactions estimable
under our budget. Of the 242 planned runs, 167 were executed: 63
GraphRAG-enriched runs were dropped after an isolated a
conclusion:
We study how modern RAG techniques compose across pipeline stages,
metrics, and corpus scales using lasagna, a stage-isolated
framework, and $450$ configurations across eight benchmarks from 5K
to 200K documents. Gains measured one component at a time do not
necessarily persist in complete pipelines; retrieval quality and
answer faithfulness favor different choices; and the best composition
changes with corpus scale. New techniques should be tested in
representative complete pipelines, on both metrics, and at the
intended scale. We release lasagna to make such studies
practical and reproducible, and to establish compositional
evaluation as the reporting standard for new RAG techniques rather
than the isolated single-component ablations common today.

title: Bio-Inspired Auditory Processing: Coupling Parallel Resonate-and-Fire Dynamics with Ternary Recurrent Networks for Speech Recognition
abstract: Spiking Neural Networks (SNNs) promise energy-efficient inference through sparse, event-driven computation, yet remain constrained on continuous, context-dependent tasks such as automatic speech recognition (ASR). A key bottleneck is the Leaky Integrate-and-Fire (LIF) neuron, whose membrane decay erases information across pauses and phonetic boundaries while it must both extract features and retain long-range context. Inspired by cortical separation of nonlinear filtering and somatic integration, we introduce the Spiking Ternary GRU (stGRU): a ternary-weight gated recurrent unit performs temporal filtering, while downstream Resonate-and-Fire (RF) neurons generate the binary spike stream driving the next block's event pathway. This makes binary event transmission a native training constraint rather than a separate deployment-time activation quantization step; together with ternary weights, learned projections avoid dense floating-point matrix MACs. Trained end-to-end on LibriSpeech-960, Small, Medium, and Large stGRUs reach 8.09%, 7.04%, and $6.44 \pm 0.17\%$ WER on test-clean without an external language model. To our knowledge, these are the first matrix-MAC-free spiking networks without a learned ANN sequence decoder to achieve single-digit WER on LibriSpeech. The architecture also achieves 10.88% test CER on Aishell-1 (9.28% on dev) when trained from scratch. Internally, trained networks develop a depth-graded hierarchy: shallow layers act as fast acoustic filters, while deep layers form slower semantic integrators whose latent representations segregate into part-of-speech manifolds and word-level spike events. Deep-layer firing rates follow lognormal distributions with a sparsity gradient, mirroring hierarchical processing observed in human cortex in vivo. Our biologically grounded architecture combines competitive ASR with favorable modeled compute and memory cost.

Abstract

Spiking Neural Networks (SNNs) promise energy-efficient inference
through sparse, event-driven computation, yet remain constrained on
continuous, context-dependent tasks such as automatic speech recognition
(ASR). A key bottleneck is the Leaky Integrate-and-Fire (LIF) neuron,
whose membrane decay erases information across pauses and phonetic
boundaries while it must both extract features and retain long-range
context. Inspired by cortical separation of nonlinear filtering and
somatic integration, we introduce the Spiking Ternary GRU (stGRU): a
ternary-weight gated recurrent unit performs temporal filtering, while
downstream Resonate-and-Fire (RF) neurons generate the binary spike stream
driving the next block’s event pathway. This makes binary event transmission a
native training constraint rather than a separate deployment-time
activation quantization step; together with ternary weights, learned
projections avoid dense floating-point matrix MACs. Trained end-to-end
on LibriSpeech-960, Small, Medium, and Large stGRUs reach $8.09\%$ ,
 $7.04\%$ , and $6.44\pm 0.17\%$ WER on test-clean without an external
language model. To our knowledge, these are the first matrix-MAC-free
spiking networks without a learned ANN sequence decoder to achieve
single-digit WER on LibriSpeech. The architecture also achieves
 $10.88\%$ test CER on Aishell-1 ( $9.28\%$ on dev) when trained from
scratch. Internally, trained networks develop a depth-graded hierarchy:
shallow layers act as fast acoustic filters, while deep layers form
slower semantic integrators whose latent representations segregate into
part-of-speech manifolds and word-level spike events. Deep-layer firing
rates follow lognormal distributions with a sparsity gradient, mirroring
hierarchical processing observed in human cortex in vivo. Our
biologically grounded architecture combines competitive ASR with
favorable modeled compute and memory cost while exposing interpretable
internal dynamics.

## 1 Introduction

Figure 1: Acoustic alignment, internal population activity, and semantic manifold emergence in stGRU.
(Top) Input acoustic waveform (LibriSpeech test utterance) aligned with ground-truth word boundaries (color-shaded spans) and internal spiking representations across physical time (top axis) and discrete network timesteps (bottom axis). The central heatmap displays the $Z$ -scored activity of 128 superneurons (co-active neural clusters sorted via Rastermap Stringer et al. (2025)), with darker pixels indicating higher population firing. Red labels beneath the raster mark subword BPE token emissions predicted by the CTC readout layer (leading underscores denote new word onsets; consecutive identical tokens are collapsed into a single emission; CTC blanks omitted for clarity).
(Bottom) 2D UMAP projections of latent representations across network depth (layers 0, 6, 10, and 14). Internal states progressively disentangle into distinct semantic and syntactic clusters, color-coded by part of speech: verbs (red), nouns (blue), and pronouns (green).

(a) Proposed Architecture

(b) Energy Efficiency Frontier

(c) Memory Efficiency Frontier

Figure 2: Architecture and efficiency comparisons.
(a) stGRU block architecture.
(b) LibriSpeech test-clean WER versus estimated arithmetic
energy over the 19,440 s evaluation set.
(c) WER versus theoretical parameter storage in decimal MB.
The Large stGRU WER is a six-seed mean; energy estimates correspond
to the reported profiling run.

Spiking Neural Networks (SNNs) promise highly energy-efficient inference by leveraging sparse, event-driven computations Roy et al. (2019). Yet they remain fundamentally constrained on continuous, context-dependent tasks such as automatic speech recognition (ASR) Bittar and Garner (2022); Song et al. (2025); Wu et al. (2020).
The primary bottleneck lies in the standard Leaky Integrate-and-Fire (LIF) neuron Gerstner and Kistler (2002); Maass (1997), whose intrinsic membrane decay erases critical context across pauses and phonetic boundaries Bellec et al. (2018); Zenke and Ganguli (2018).
Consequently, while continuous ANNs achieve state-of-the-art ASR performance Gulati et al. (2020); Vaswani et al. (2017), their reliance on dense multiply-accumulate (MAC) operations incurs prohibitive memory and energy costs Horowitz (2014)-leaving a critical gap for energy-constrained applications.

Prior spiking ASR systems largely resorted to hybrid architectures pairing a spiking encoder with a dense, floating-point ANN sequence decoder, forfeiting the energy benefits of a truly edge-ready system Bittar and Garner (2022); Song et al. (2025); Wu et al. (2020). Deep event-driven architectures are further hindered by an $\mathcal{O}(L^{2})$ training bottleneck arising from sequential recurrent dependencies Neftci et al. (2019); Werbos (1990) and discontinuous spike resets Lee et al. (2016); Neftci et al. (2019). Together, these limitations motivate separating rich temporal filtering
from discrete event communication while keeping learned projections
matrix-MAC-free.

A complementary limitation appears in MatMul-free recurrent models:
ternary weights remove dense learned matrix products, but the MLGRU
backbone retains continuous activations, so deployment on low-precision
neuromorphic hardware requires a separate activation-quantization stage
Zhu et al. (2024). This motivates our central question: can the
activation constraint itself be learned while retaining gated
long-range temporal filtering?

We answer this by treating spiking as a trainable activation interface
for the event-driven pathway. In stGRU, a ternary MLGRU performs
nonlinear temporal filtering, while a downstream RF neuron emits the
binary spike stream that drives the next block’s event pathway.
In the ternary backbone, weights discretize what the network stores;
RF spikes discretize what its event pathway communicates. Crucially, the
spike constraint is present during optimization rather than imposed only
at deployment. This separation also mirrors cortical neurons, where
gated nonlinear processing precedes somatic integration
Gidon et al. (2020); Häusser and Mel (2003); London and Häusser (2005); Mel (1991); Mel (1992); Shai et al. (2014); Shai et al. (2015). This storage–communication duality is central to stGRU.
Our primary contributions are as follows:

Train-Time Dual Discretization & matrix-MAC-free ASR.

stGRU pairs ternary learned weights with an RF-generated binary event
stream, moving activation discretization into training rather than
leaving it solely to deployment. To our knowledge, it is the first
matrix-MAC-free SNN without a learned ANN sequence decoder to achieve
single-digit WER on LibriSpeech Panayotov et al. (2015):
Small, Medium, and Large stGRUs reach 8.09%, 7.04%, and
 $6.44\pm 0.17\%$ on test-clean without an external LM. Training from scratch on Aishell-1 Bu et al. (2017) yields 10.88%
test CER (9.28% dev), close to the VGG-BiLSTM baseline (10.7% test CER)
but below the strongest dense and hybrid systems in Table S5, providing cross-lingual evidence that the architecture transfers from English to Mandarin ASR.

Exceptional Performance-to-Model-Size Trade-off.
Operating at $1.95\text{ mJ/s}$ (Small) and $3.42\text{ mJ/s}$ (Large), stGRU operates far below continuous Transformers ( $8.80\text{ mJ/s}$ ) and Conformers ( $11.28\text{ mJ/s}$ ) Gulati et al. (2020); Horowitz (2014). For the Large Conv1D–MLGRU–ReLU baseline, ternarizing the weights changes
test-clean WER from 5.83% to 6.49%, an increase of 0.66 percentage points,
while the modeled arithmetic-energy rate changes from 33.48 to
4.10 mJ/s (seed 3407). Ternary INT2 weights reduce the Large models to 122.22 MB on
LibriSpeech and 167.84 MB on Aishell-1, yielding a favorable modeled
energy–storage trade-off.

Emergent ACC-like Error-Monitoring.
Layer L11 autonomously develops an ACC-like error-monitoring signature Alexander and Brown (2018); Bryden et al. (2019): incorrect words trigger elevated firing, peak sparsity (0.83), and heavy-tailed lognormal rate statistics ( $\Delta R^{2}=+0.091$ over Gaussian).

Decision Confidence & Autonomous ACC $\rightarrow$ PFC Handoff.
At L14, the coding regime inverts into a prefrontal cortex (PFC)-like commitment state Kiani and Shadlen (2009); Rutishauser et al. (2015): high-confidence correct words elicit peak firing, sparsity drops, and distributions shift to Gaussian. Together, these signatures suggest an autonomous ACC $\rightarrow$ PFC-like functional handoff Alexander and Brown (2018) emerging within a single artificial sequence model.

## 2 Related Work

While dense continuous models (Transformers, Conformers, CitriNet) define state-of-the-art ASR Hou et al. (2024); Majumdar et al. (2021); Radford et al. (2022), their reliance on dense multiply-accumulate (MAC) operations incurs prohibitive compute and memory costs Horowitz (2014). MatMul-free MLGRU combines ternary weights with continuous activations;
its Loihi 2 mapping therefore separately quantizes activations and
retains 16-bit precision after 8-bit quantization substantially degrades
accuracy Zhu et al. (2024).

Motivated by biological efficiency, Spiking Neural Networks (SNNs) have been adapted for speech via surrogate gradients Bittar and Garner (2022); Wu et al. (2020), TCNs Bai et al. (2018), and Spike-driven Transformers Yao et al. (2023); Yao et al. (2024). However, existing ternary spiking speech models remain heavily restricted: QT-SNN Wang et al. (2025) targets only isolated keyword spotting, whereas DyTr-SNN Wang et al. (2023) is evaluated solely on single-speaker LJSpeech without reporting WER and relies on a dense continuous 6-layer Transformer decoder. More broadly, leading SNN ASR baselines (GSU Hao et al. (2024), Spike-driven Transformer Yao et al. (2024), IML-Spikeformer Song et al. (2025)) depend on continuous 6-layer ANN decoders to maintain competitive accuracy Song et al. (2025). While their encoders use sparse accumulate (AC) operations, continuous decoders reintroduce a floating-point bottleneck and serialized execution, compromising edge viability.

stGRU bridges these two lines of work: it retains ternary MLGRU
filtering but trains an RF-generated binary event interface end-to-end,
making event discretization part of the model rather than a post-training
hardware conversion. Deferred scaling keeps learned backbone projections
matrix-MAC-free, while direct CTC decoding avoids a learned ANN sequence
decoder.

## 3 Methodology

## 3.1 Ternary Projections with Deferred Weight Scaling

We use ternary BitLinear projections
Ma et al. (2024); Zhu et al. (2024). For a full-precision
shadow-weight matrix $W\in\mathbb{R}^{m\times d}$ , let
 $\gamma_{W}=(md)^{-1}\sum_{i,j}|W_{ij}|$ and quantize by

 $\widetilde{W}=\operatorname{RoundClip}\left(\frac{W}{\gamma_{W}+\epsilon},-1,1\right),\qquad\widetilde{W}_{ij}\in\{-1,0,+1\}.$ 

(1)

The shadow weights are trained with a straight-through estimator
(STE) Bengio et al. (2013) and QAT warmup
(Appendix C.1).

Let $V$ denote the input presented to a projection after its shared
input normalization. The three ablation modes differ only in the
placement or omission of the weight scale:

 $\displaystyle Y_{\mathrm{naive}}$ 
 $\displaystyle=V(\gamma_{W}\widetilde{W})^{\top},$ 

(2)

 $\displaystyle Y_{\mathrm{proposed}}$ 
 $\displaystyle=(V\widetilde{W}^{\top})\gamma_{W},$ 

 $\displaystyle Y_{\mathrm{none}}$ 
 $\displaystyle=V\widetilde{W}^{\top}.$ 

The naive and proposed modes are algebraically equivalent for fixed
 $V$ , $\widetilde{W}$ , and $\gamma_{W}$ . Naive scaling folds $\gamma_{W}$ 
into the weights, producing a floating-point weight matrix.
Deferred scaling instead accumulates through ternary weights using
additions and subtractions, then applies $\gamma_{W}$ to the output.
The None mode omits this scale entirely. Thus the proposed mode
avoids dense floating-point matrix MACs in the learned projection,
but retains an output scaling operation. We write this operator as

 $\mathcal{T}(V,\widetilde{W},\gamma_{W})_{i}=\gamma_{W}\sum_{j=1}^{d}\widetilde{W}_{ij}V_{j},\qquad i=1,\ldots,m.$ 

(3)

The same scale placement applies to a temporal depthwise projection.
Let $V\in\mathbb{R}^{T\times C}$ be the input to that projection and
 $\widetilde{W}_{dw}\in\{-1,0,+1\}^{K\times C}$ its ternary kernel.
With a weight scale $\gamma_{dw}$ , we define

 $\mathcal{T}_{dw}(V,\widetilde{W}_{dw},\gamma_{dw})_{t,c}=\gamma_{dw}\sum_{k}\widetilde{W}_{dw,k,c}V_{t+k,c}.$ 

(4)

The temporal sum therefore uses additions and subtractions through
ternary weights; $\gamma_{dw}$ is applied after that sum. This avoids folding a floating-point scale into every kernel weight.
In the ablation (Table S8),
deferred scaling reduces the modeled energy rate by about
 $5\times$ relative to naive scaling, with comparable test-clean WER
(Small: 8.09% vs. 8.15%; Large: 6.14% vs. 6.44%).
Omitting the scale instead worsens test-clean WER to 9.44%
and 7.51%, respectively.

## 3.2 Parallel Spiking-Ternary Block Architecture

To bypass the prohibitive $\mathcal{O}(L^{2})$ training bottleneck of recurrent networks and discontinuous resets Werbos (1990), the Spiking-Ternary GRU Block decouples recurrent filtering from spike emission, enabling global parallel unrolling in $\mathcal{O}(L\log L)$ time while avoiding dense learned matrix MACs at inference.

Acoustic features are initially mapped by a pre-encoder into discrete spike trains $S^{(0)}_{t}\in\{0,1\}^{C}$ . At block $l$ , temporal features are extracted from the incoming discrete spike sequence $S^{(l)}\in\{0,1\}^{T\times C}$ via a depthwise-separable operator pair consisting of a 1D temporal depthwise convolution and a pointwise channel projection:

 $X_{dw}=\mathcal{T}_{dw}(S^{(l)},\widetilde{W}_{dw},\gamma_{dw}),\quad X=\mathcal{T}(X_{dw},\widetilde{W}_{pw},\gamma_{pw})$ 

(5)

where $\widetilde{W}_{pw}\in\{-1,0,+1\}^{C\times C}$ denotes the ternary pointwise weights and $\gamma_{pw}$ their scale.

We adapt the MLGRU of Zhu et al. (2024) with deferred-scaling
ternary projections, RMS-normalized gating, and a ternary output projection. For brevity, we denote gate-specific ternary projections as $\mathcal{T}_{k}(V)\triangleq\mathcal{T}(V,\widetilde{W}_{k},\gamma_{k})$ for $k\in\{c,f,g\}$ . For input representation $X_{t}\in\mathbb{R}^{C}$ , the gates are computed as $C_{t}=\text{SiLU}(\mathcal{T}_{c}(X_{t}))$ , $F_{t}=\sigma(\mathcal{T}_{f}(X_{t}))$ , and $G_{t}=\text{RMSNorm}(\mathcal{T}_{g}(X_{t}))$ , updating state and output via:

 $\displaystyle H_{t}$ 
 $\displaystyle=F_{t}\odot H_{t-1}+C_{t}\odot(1-F_{t})$ 

(6)

 $\displaystyle O_{t}$ 
 $\displaystyle=\mathcal{T}(G_{t}\odot\text{SiLU}(H_{t}),\widetilde{W}_{o},\gamma_{o})$ 

(7)

Because Equation 6 is strictly element-wise (no dense $Wh_{t-1}$ products), intermediate representations are computed globally across sequence length $T$ via an associative parallel scan Gu et al. (2021); Smith et al. (2022).

Channels are mixed via a ternary SwiGLU block stabilized by learnable ReZero vectors $\alpha\in\mathbb{R}^{C}$ Bachlechner et al. (2021) (Appendix C.2):

 $\displaystyle U_{t}$ 
 $\displaystyle=\text{SiLU}(\mathcal{T}(O_{t},\widetilde{W}_{\text{gate}},\gamma_{\text{gate}}))\odot\mathcal{T}(O_{t},\widetilde{W}_{\text{up}},\gamma_{\text{up}})$ 

(8)

 $\displaystyle Z_{t}$ 
 $\displaystyle=X_{t}+\alpha\odot\mathcal{T}(U_{t},\widetilde{W}_{\text{down}},\gamma_{\text{down}})$ 

(9)

To prevent vanishing gradients and stabilize variance across depth, the continuous residual stream $Z^{(l)}\in\mathbb{R}^{C}$ updates via:

 $Z^{(l)}_{t}=\text{RMSNorm}(Z^{(l-1)}_{t})+\alpha^{{}^{\prime}}\odot\text{RMSNorm}(Z_{t})$ 

(10)

The stabilized residual $Z^{(l)}_{t}$ serves as the input current to the Parallel Resonate-and-Fire (PRF) neuron Huang et al. (2024). Unlike standard LIF neurons which enforce sequential BPTT due to hard reset subtractions ( $V_{th}S_{t-1}$ ), PRF folds resets into a complex decay factor $\tilde{\gamma}=-\frac{1}{\tau}+i\theta$ . Under Euler discretization over timestep $\Delta$ , membrane integration unfolds linearly:

 $U_{t}=\exp\left(-\frac{\Delta}{\tau}\right)\left(\cos(\Delta\theta)+i\sin(\Delta\theta)\right)U_{t-1}+\Delta Z^{(l)}_{t}$ 

(11)

Because temporal integration is independent of output spikes, membrane potentials $U_{1:T}$ evaluate globally in the frequency domain via Fast Fourier Transform ( $\mathcal{F}$ ) Cooley and Tukey (1965); Gu et al. (2021) using decay kernel $K_{1:T}=(\Delta A^{0},\dots,\Delta A^{T-1})$ with $A=\exp(\Delta\tilde{\gamma})$ :

 $U_{1:T}=\mathcal{F}^{-1}(\mathcal{F}(Z^{(l)}_{1:T})\odot\mathcal{F}(K_{1:T}))$ 

(12)

Finally, the continuous potentials are folded back into the binary domain for the $(l+1)$ -th block by applying a Heaviside step function strictly to the real component:

 $S^{(l+1)}_{t}=\mathcal{H}(\Re\{U_{t}\}-V_{th})$ 

(13)

Surrogate gradients (Multi-Gaussian Yin et al. (2021)) train
this binary event interface end-to-end, so the next block is optimized
on the same discrete spike stream used at inference. The MLGRU recurrence
admits an associative scan and PRF integration an
 $\mathcal{O}(L\log L)$ FFT implementation; empirically, training is
3.1 $\times$ –3.4 $\times$ faster than the parameter-matched LIF variants
(Tables S7, S9).

limitations:
Our energy estimates use analytical operation counts and 45 nm CMOS
constants. QAT also retains full-precision shadow weights and their training
overhead: the forward weights become ternary after warmup, while the
straight-through estimator updates the continuous weights during
backpropagation. Furthermore, while our design eliminates all dense
 $\mathcal{O}(C^{2})$ floating-point matrix multiplications, the model is
not entirely multiplication-free: continuous element-wise multiplications
persist in recurrent gating, residual scaling, RMSNorm, and neuron
dynamics. These operations are element-wise rather than dense $O(C^{2})$ matrix multiplications, but deploying them on pure addition-only or integer-only edge silicon still requires specialized arithmetic units or approximations. Performance remains weaker on
test-other than on test-clean. Finally, mitigating
the capacity limits of 2-bit weights required wide channels and
temporal kernels of up to $K=63$ , despite the low precision of their
weights.
conclusion:
We introduced stGRU, an ASR architecture combining deferred-scaling
ternary projections, gated recurrent filtering, and resonant spiking
integration. At inference, its learned projections avoid dense matrix
MACs, while the Large model reaches $6.44\pm 0.17\%$ LibriSpeech
test-clean WER without an external language model and a separately
trained Aishell-1 model reaches 10.88% test CER. The modeled
arithmetic-energy and parameter-storage results show a favorable
efficiency trade-off, subject to the accounting limits above.

Conceptually, stGRU couples complementary low-precision constraints in the event-driven backbone:
ternary learned projections constrain synaptic weights, while RF neurons make the inter-block event stream binary during training rather than relying on a separate deployment-time activation-quantization step. Spiking thus serves not only as
neuronal dynamics but as an end-to-end optimized binary communication bottleneck. Despite this
constraint, deep layers still develop error-to-confidence selectivity
and structured sparsity, suggesting that efficient event-driven
communication can coexist with rich internal organization.

However, not much is known about how these abilities are influenced by larger-scale pretraining. In this paper, we train a family of MPIXEL models along three axes of variation: more languages, more scripts, and larger model capacity under fixed per-language compute. In evaluations on five tasks covering 83 languages, we find that scaling acts locally: each axis improves the added languages and scripts, while increased capacity mitigates the curse of multilinguality from pretraining on more languages. On typologically distant low-resource languages, our models outperform subword and character-level baselines across many writing systems. ## Scaling Multilingual Pretraining of Pixel Language Models

Ilker Kesen† Jenny Kunz‡ Kasra Malihi§ Desmond Elliott§
††thanks: Work done while at the University of Copenhagen.
Affiliation: †Humboldt-Universität zu Berlin ‡Linköping University §University of Copenhagen

headings: Scaling Multilingual Pretraining of Pixel Language Models
body_start:
Abstract

Pixel language models process text as rendered images instead of a finite vocabulary, which gives them strong cross-lingual transfer abilities.
However, not much is known about how these abilities are influenced by larger-scale pretraining.
In this paper, we train a family of mpixel models along three axes of variation: more languages, more scripts, and larger model capacity under fixed per-language compute.
In evaluations on five tasks covering 83 languages, we find that scaling acts locally: each axis improves the added languages and scripts, while increased capacity mitigates the curse of multilinguality from pretraining on more languages.
Transfer to unseen scripts improves with multilingual pretraining, but does not further improve with scaling.
On typologically distant low-resource languages, our models outperform subword and character-level baselines across many writing systems.
We also show that larger pixel models reserve more layers for visual processing, and that cross-lingual alignment weakens as more languages are added.
Overall, our findings characterize how multilingual scaling improves pixel language models.

## 1 Introduction

Pixel language models process text as rendered images rather than discrete tokens (Salesky et al., 2021; Rust et al., 2023). This makes them appealing for the long tail of the world’s writing systems (Joshi et al., 2020), with previous research demonstrating strong transfer abilities to unseen scripts (Kesen et al., 2025; Lotz et al., 2025).
However, there is an open question about whether such transfer can be improved by increasing (i) the number of writing systems, (ii) the pretraining languages, or (iii) by increasing model capacity.

Figure 1: mpixel performance when scaling the number of pretraining languages and model capacity.
Adding new languages steadily improves performance on seen scripts, albeit with a slight decrease on shared languages.
Higher capacity improves performance on shared and seen scripts.
On unseen scripts, neither additional languages nor capacity yields consistent gains.

We investigate this question in a carefully controlled study that separates these axes of multilingual scaling.
Our starting point is an 86M parameter model pretrained on English, Hindi, Traditional Chinese, and Ukrainian, following Kesen et al. (2025).
From here, we train two models to investigate the effect of increasing the number of writing systems.
The first is pretrained on eight-languages by adding four languages in the already-seen Latin script, whereas the other model adds four languages in previously unseen writing systems.
We also pretrain an mpixel model by combining the seen and unseen scripts with four further languages, resulting in a total of sixteen pretraining languages.
Finally, mpixellarge increases the model capacity to $307$ M parameters.

These pretraining variations allow us to study the following research questions.
RQ1: Along which axis does scaling multilingual pretraining yield greater cross-lingual transfer: increasing language diversity within an already seen script or increasing script diversity?
RQ2: Does scaling multilinguality along both axes continue to improve cross-lingual transfer, or do gains saturate with more pretraining languages?
RQ3: To what extent does increased model capacity improve cross-lingual transfer?
RQ4: Do pixel language models suffer from the curse of multilinguality (Conneau et al., 2020) as more languages are added, and if so, does increased model capacity mitigate it?

We answer these questions with empirical experiments on five downstream tasks: sentence classification, dependency parsing, named entity recognition, natural language inference, and English-only sentence classification using the GLUE benchmark (Wang et al., 2018).
We evaluate on 83 languages in total, grouped into pretraining languages, unseen languages in pretraining scripts, and languages in unseen scripts.
Among these, we prioritize low-resource languages, including some that are typologically distant from the pretraining languages of all baselines.
We also analyze the models’ representations by testing cross-lingual alignment with ABX discrimination tasks, and locate where scaling acts by probing linguistic information across layers at the sentence and word level.

Our contributions are summarized as follows:

• 

We introduce mpixel, a family of pixel language models11
 1

 Code and models:  ilkerkesen/mpixel pretrained on up-to sixteen languages at 86M and 307M parameters.
This includes the first pixel language models pretrained on right-to-left scripts.

• 

We show that increasing the number of pretraining languages and scripts mainly benefits the newly covered languages and scripts. Transfer to unseen scripts is established by multilingual training, but does not improve with further scaling.

• 

We show that pixel language models suffer from the curse of multilinguality, and that increased capacity mitigates it.

• 

We show that mpixel outperforms subword and character-level baselines on low-resource languages typologically distant from XLM-R pretraining languages.

• 

We find that 307M parameter mpixel model reserves more layers for visual processing, and that cross-lingual alignment weakens as languages are added but generalizes to unseen languages through shared script.

## 2 Pretraining Setup

Models.

We pretrain five models to support our study on scaling pixel language models.
These models vary in the number of pretraining languages, the diversity of those languages, and the number of trainable parameters, as outlined in Table 1.

Axes.

The models are scaled along three axes: language diversity within a seen script (mpixel4s $\rightarrow$ mpixel8l), script diversity (mpixel4s $\rightarrow$ mpixel8s), and model capacity (mpixel $\rightarrow$ mpixellarge).
Since new scripts necessarily arrive with new languages, the two data expansions are matched in language count and differ only in whether the additions introduce new scripts; contrasting them asks whether script diversity adds anything beyond language diversity (RQ1).
mpixel expands along both data axes at once (RQ2), mpixellarge varies capacity on this data (RQ3), and evaluating every variant on the four shared pretraining languages quantifies the curse of multilinguality and whether capacity mitigates it (RQ4).

Languages.

We use FineWeb and multilingual FineWeb2 corpora (Penedo et al., 2024; Penedo et al., 2025) for pretraining data.
When selecting pretraining languages, we only consider higher-resource languages, and deliberately exclude some high-resource languages for downstream task evaluations.
As mentioned earlier, we maximize the diversity in pretraining languages along two axes: language family and writing system.
For this purpose, mpixel8l extends mpixel4s with four Latin-script languages from diverse language families (Spanish: Romance, Danish: Germanic, Finnish: Uralic, Turkish: Turkic), varying language family while holding the writing system fixed.
mpixel8s instead extends mpixel4s with four languages in previously unseen scripts (Korean: Hangul, Thai: Thai, Greek: Greek, Standard Arabic: Arabic), varying both writing system and language family.
mpixelbase combines these extensions and adds four further languages: Vietnamese (Latin), Persian (Perso-Arabic), Bengali (Bengali), and Hebrew (Hebrew), further extending coverage along both axes.
For each language, we an equal amount of patches, which is roughly equal to 7.5 billion image patches.
We fix the maximum number of patches per example to $512$ .

Rendering.

As demonstrated by Lotz et al. (2023), rendering strategy is a crucial design choice for pixel language models, where packing character bigrams per patch decreases input redundancy and improves performance.
We design a new adaptive rendering strategy for multilingual processing.
By default, we prefer grapheme-aware bigrams grouping as the original bigrams rendering may separate diacritics from their base characters.
For CJK languages, where wide characters make most bigrams span multiple patches, we render one character per patch, which lowers input redundancy at the same sequence length.
For Arabic and Hebrew, the bigrams strategy can sever ligatures, and rendering in visual order distorts word structure.
We therefore use word-level rendering for these scripts, where each word is rendered as a contiguous unit in logical order.

Pretraining.

Our pretraining procedure builds on prior work.
Our model variants implement the Vision Transformer Masked Autoencoder architecture (ViT-MAE) (He et al., 2022) by following the previous pixel models.
The only hyperparameter we vary independently is the effective batch size, which we double for the 8-language variants and quadruple for the 16-language variants.
With 7.5B patches per language, 1M steps, and 512 patches per sample, this holds per-language exposure at ${\approx}4.3$ epochs, which a fixed batch size would otherwise halve with each doubling of the language count.
We therefore double and quadruple the batch size for the eight- and sixteen-language model variants.
As we increase the batch size, we also adjust the learning rate by following the square root scaling procedure (Li et al., 2024; Krizhevsky, 2014).
Unlike previous pixel models, we select checkpoints on a held-out task:
zero-shot bitext mining on FLORES-200 (Team et al., 2022) over each variant’s pretraining languages.
We exclude examples overlapping with SIB-200 (Adelani et al., 2024) to prevent leakage.
The rest of the pretraining recipe is identical with previous pixel models.

## 3 Experimental Setup

We compare against several bidirectional encoder-based language models, including sub-word tokenizer-based xlm-r (Conneau et al., 2020) and mbert (Devlin et al., 2019), character-level hash embedding-based canine (Clark et al., 2022).
In order to eliminate confounding factors of data quality, data size, and text rendering, we pretrained our own pixel and pixel-m

4

 Both models are pretrained on the same 30B-patch budget, which pixel $\dagger$ spends entirely on English, while mpixel4S splits the budget equally across its four languages.

Tasks & Benchmarks.

We evaluate models on sentence classification on 77 languages from SIB-200 (Adelani et al., 2024).
We focus on (i) languages seen during pretraining; (ii) languages in seen scripts during pretraining; and (iii) languages in unseen scripts (e.g., N’ko).33

We also test models on dependency parsing using Universal Dependencies (Nivre et al., 2020) under the same transfer scenarios; on named entity recognition across 12 languages44
 4

 We combine data from Universal NER (Mayhew et al., 2024; Blevins et al., 2026), Naamapadam (Mhaske et al., 2023), NER-UK (Chaplynskyi and Romanyshyn, 2024) and KLUE (Park et al., 2021); on natural language inference with XNLI (Conneau et al., 2018b) (translate-train-all); and on GLUE (Wang et al., 2018), which we use to investigate the curse of multilinguality in English.

## 4 Results

We first compare the mpixel models against the baselines in Table 2.
We find that xlm-r obtains the best overall averages on all tasks, with mpixellarge the second-best performing model.
We note that xlm-r and canine-s are pretrained on ${\sim}100$ languages, which means they have been trained on most of the languages in our seen-script and unseen-script groups.
We also note that xlm-r has seen much more data per language than mbert, canine-s, or the mpixel models.55
 5

 For English alone, the xlm-r pretraining corpus contains ${\sim}55$ B tokens.
On the other hand, our mpixel pretraining corpus is $\sim$ 2.5B English whitespace separated words.
We find that mpixel outperforms the character-level canine-s on all tasks except XNLI.
On UDP, mpixel achieves an overall better score than xlm-r on unseen scripts (Table 14).
However, this is largely driven by Coptic, which uses a writing system not included during xlm-r pretraining.

Figure 2: Performance of models on typologically distant low-resource languages in the SIB-200 benchmark.

Low-resource cross-lingual transfer.

For a controlled evaluation of low-resource cross-lingual transfer, we compare performance on languages unseen by all models.
Within our evaluation set, we use the DistaLs toolkit (Goot et al., 2025) to determine which languages are typologically distant from every model’s pretraining data.
Figure 2 shows the SIB-200 results on these languages.
mpixel outperforms xlm-r on all writing systems.
mpixel also outperforms canine-s on Latin and Bengali.
The vocabulary bottleneck explains this gap at two levels.
On seen scripts, the xlm-r subwords are well-trained for its pretraining languages, so they segment and represent distant languages poorly.
On the four scripts unseen by all models (N’ko, Ol Chiki, Tifinagh, Tibetan), the characters fall outside the vocabulary and are largely mapped to unknown tokens.
xlm-r performs close to random on these scripts, whereas canine-s and mpixel demonstrate their strengths.

Figure 3: Downstream performance vs. number of pretraining languages (86M models; $x{=}1$ is English-only). Lines are evaluation tiers fixed w.r.t. mpixel’s languages and scripts; each point is a mean over that tier’s items ( $n$ per panel, in legend order). At $x{=}8$ the point is the mean of mpixel8l and mpixel8s and the bar spans them.

Figure 4: Performances of the mpixel variants on the downstream benchmarks considering only four pretraining languages shared across models.

Figure 3 provides an overview of how downstream performance changes across the language and capacity scaling settings considered in our research questions (RQ1–RQ3).

RQ1: Expanding language and script coverage mainly benefits the languages and scripts it adds.

We compare mpixel8L and mpixel8S against mpixel4S, where the former adds four Latin-script languages, and the latter four languages in previously unseen scripts.
Figure 3 shows clear improvements when pretraining on four additional languages, albeit with smaller improvements on the seen-script group for SIB-200 and UDP, and overall mixed benefits for unseen scripts.
For both of the 8-language variants, gains concentrate on the added languages and on other languages sharing their scripts: Latin for mpixel8L and the newly covered scripts for mpixel8S (e.g., the Arabic script; Tables 10, 11, and 14)
NER and XNLI cover too few seen-script languages for a reliable comparison.
On unseen scripts, the changes are small and mixed for both variants:
neither addition therefore yields a consistent advantage on unseen scripts.

In order to isolate the effect of multilinguality from training volume and other pretraining confounds, we train our own monolingual pixel $\dagger$ with the same patch budget as mpixel4S.
In this matched setup, mpixel4S outperforms pixel $\dagger$ on unseen scripts in SIB-200 (see Table 10 in the Appendix).
The gains also extend to scripts visually unrelated to Devanagari, such as N’ko and Ethiopic, so script similarity alone cannot explain transfer.

RQ2: Scaling further along the language and script axes brings further improvements for seen languages and their scripts.

If we compare the 16-language mpixel against mpixel8L and mpixel8S, the overall averages improve on SIB-200, NER and UDP, as shown in Figure 3 (see Tables 10, 11, and 14 for detailed per-language breakdown).

The improvements concentrate on seen languages, where the added languages improve their own performance.
They partly extend to seen scripts, which improve on SIB-200 and UDP but decrease on NER and XNLI (Figure 3); nevertheless, NER and XNLI cover only a few seen-script languages.
On unseen scripts, the effect depends on the task.
On SIB-200 (Table 10), mpixel obtains the lowest score among the multilingual variants; on NER (Table 11), all mpixel variants stay within one point.
On UDP (Table 14), unseen scripts instead improve with each extension, and mpixel outperforms all other models, including xlm-r.

RQ3: Increased capacity only improves performance on seen languages and scripts.

We compare mpixellarge (307M) against mpixel (86M) pretrained on the same data.

limitations:
Like most of the previous work, the pretrained mpixel models lack language generation capability as they are encoder-only models.
Our scaling study covers few points per axis: four language counts (1, 4, 8, 16) and two model sizes (86M and 307M parameters), so our claims hold only within this range.
Due to compute constraints, our models are pretrained on far less data than xlm-r.
Moreover, each variant corresponds to a single pretraining run, so small differences between variants may fall within run-to-run pretraining variance, which we cannot quantify.
Our controlled setup fixes per-language compute rather than total compute, so variants with more languages see more total data, and results under a fixed total-compute budget may differ.
Each scaling axis is instantiated with a single set of languages, rooted in the four-language set of previous work for comparability, and our findings may be sensitive to these particular choices.
In particular, the first multilingual step adds new languages and new scripts at the same time, so we cannot separate their individual effects.
Finally, we design the adaptive rendering strategy based on input processing efficiency and correct visual rendering of right-to-left scripts, and we do not compare it empirically against existing rendering strategies such as bigrams.
Therefore, we do not know whether adaptive is the optimal rendering choice.
conclusion:
We presented mpixel, a family of pixel language models pretrained on up to sixteen languages and 307M parameters, scaled along three axes under fixed per-language compute: more languages in a seen script, more scripts, and more capacity.
We found that scaling acts locally: each axis mainly improves the languages and scripts it adds, while transfer to unseen scripts is established by the first multilingual step and does not improve with further scaling.
Pixel models exhibit the curse of multilinguality, and increased capacity mitigates it.
On low-resource languages typologically distant from the pretraining languages of all baselines, mpixel outperforms subword and character-level baselines on many writing systems.
Our analyses showed that larger models reserve more layers for visual processing, and that cross-lingual alignment weakens with more languages but generalizes through shared scripts.
Future work will investigate explicit control over the capacity spent on visual processing, alternative rendering strategies for right-to-left scripts, and broader coverage of low-resource languages as scaling acts locally.

title: Toward Recursive Self-Improvement in Physical AI
abstract: Recursive self-improvement (RSI) describes a system that improves not only its behavior but also the process by which it improves. Recent digital agents test this idea by rewriting their own code and checking each version with executable tests. Bringing these mechanisms into the physical world requires learning from partial observations through costly trials, while accounting for changing operating conditions and potentially irreversible consequences. We position RSI within robot learning and trace pathways from improving robot capabilities to improving the processes that generate them. We examine how physical experience can strengthen these improvement mechanisms and when the resulting gains can support further self-improvement of the mechanisms themselves. Gains carry forward only when feedback addresses remaining learning needs, the receiving component can use the change, its value survives changes in tasks or hardware, and continued practice remains safe and affordable. Existing studies, concentrated in manipulation, support behavioral improvement, benefits to later learning, and procedure improvement. Some systems also change the improver's knowledge or tools, but the physical studies reviewed here have yet to isolate gains attributable to recursion. We synthesize these findings into evaluation principles and research directions for machines that, trial by trial, safely improve the way they improve.
