conclusion:
This survey examined how robots that improve from physical experience can move toward recursive self-improvement, in which a system improves not only its behavior but also the process by which it improves. We positioned RSI within robot learning: reinforcement learning, self-training, continual learning, meta-learning, and AutoML say how updates are computed or what they must cope with, whereas a ladder of claims states what an experiment shows to have improved. Along that ladder, we reviewed how physical experience improves policies, world models, and knowledge, the learning procedures that produce them, and the improver that revises those procedures. What limits a robot’s next improvement (RQ1) is rarely visible in a terminal outcome; it is a hypothesis about missing experience, supervision, optimization, action generation, interfaces, or retention, to be tested by intervention rather than inferred from data volume or component accuracy. The changes that address it (RQ2) are kept in policies, world models, external knowledge, or the learning procedure, and they build on one another (RQ3) only under four conditions: feedback addresses remaining learning needs, the receiving component can use the change, its value survives changes in tasks or hardware, and continued practice remains safe and affordable. Physical constraints (RQ4) act through all four: incomplete sensing limits what a signal can distinguish; embodiment interfaces limit what a recipient can execute; wear, calibration drift, and hardware changes drive distribution shift; and reset, safety, and cost bound continued practice.

Existing studies, concentrated in manipulation, support behavioral improvement, later-learning benefits, and procedure improvement. Some systems also change their improver’s knowledge or tools, but no physical study reviewed here has yet isolated a gain attributable to recursion, which requires a controlled comparison against a version of the improver whose acquired knowledge is frozen. These answers remain provisional, because the four conditions are overlapping diagnostic lenses rather than independently validated constructs and much of the evidence comes from recent preprints with few training runs or trials.

## Conflicted Records: Typed Adversarial Contracts

for Auditable LLM Output Quality Enforcement

Kardelen Subasi

Jarosław A. Chudziak

body_start:
Abstract

LLM-generated records increasingly populate production information systems
where they are treated as data assets subject to the same quality
expectations as records from operational databases. A single such record
can simultaneously satisfy and violate a quality rule: a grounded fact
adjacent to a hallucination, a useful answer adjacent to a stereotype.
Classical data cleaning cannot resolve this because the two judgments are
incompatible over the same span; a single LLM judge cannot either, since
it shares the training biases that produced the conflict. Existing
interventions such as prompt engineering, chain-of-thought, and RLHF
reduce surface error rates but provide no audit trail and cannot
distinguish genuine remediation from blanket suppression. The question is
whether a deterministic check over structured inter-agent records can catch
the defects that referential checks alone miss.

We present BiasGuard-D: two adversarial roles drawn from distinct model
families exchange typed claim documents, a three-model quorum adjudicates
by majority vote, and a combined referential-plus-semantic invariant
validates the verdict. The semantic component fires on verdicts referential
checks miss; removing the iterative loop drops invariant satisfaction
sharply. The deliberation layer transfers from stereotype to hallucination
remediation on HaluEval QA with only role-framing changes, raising
right-answer recovery by 49 percentage points; the triage gate required a
cross-family second auditor to maintain recall on objective hallucination.
Every claim, vote, and instruction is stored as a typed record giving
operators a provenance trail auditable under emerging AI regulations.

Keywords: 
LLM Output Quality Enforcement Typed Adversarial Contracts Multi-agent Systems Bias Remediation Hallucination Detection Large language models Artificial intelligence.

## 1 Introduction

LLM outputs are no longer transient. They are persisted into search indexes,
written into knowledge bases, embedded in recommendation feeds, and surfaced
through customer-facing information systems where they act as data [17, 8].
As deployments scale into regulated domains, operators need more than a quality
score; they need to know why an output passes or fails a constraint,
which span triggered the verdict, and whether the remediation
instructions are internally consistent.

What makes this hard is that an LLM-generated record can satisfy and violate
a quality rule in the same sequence of text. A hiring recommendation may
accurately ground its reasoning in a candidate’s qualifications while
simultaneously making an age generalisation the input does not support. A
knowledge-base entry may pair a faithfully lifted fact with one the model
invented. In neither case are the two things in separate fields or even
separate sentences; they share the same characters. Classical data
cleaning, which reads a record and refines it, cannot resolve this, because
the two issues require opposite judgments about the same text.
A single LLM judge cannot either, since it shares the same training biases
that produced the conflict [15, 25, 26].

The question this paper asks is: can a deterministic check over
structured inter-agent records catch the quality defects that referential
checks alone miss, and do those records carry enough information to audit
pipeline quality without calling an additional model? We evaluate this across
three dimensions: whether a semantic check catches a recurring class of
contradictions that referential checks miss; whether stored records carry
enough structure to tell genuine resolution from suppression without calling
a further model; and whether the deliberation layer transfers across different
quality domains with only role-framing changes.

We address this by treating enforcement as a data-quality problem rather than
a single-judge problem: two adversarial roles with opposing biases produce
structured claims about specific text spans; a multi-family quorum adjudicates;
and a deterministic invariant validates the result before any downstream action.
Records with a consistent verdict pass with a full provenance trail;
contradictory verdicts are quarantined rather than auto-repaired, because
auto-repair would bring back the model judgment the architecture is designed
to avoid. The experimental study confirms all three evaluation questions and
surfaces a finding we did not anticipate: the iterative deliberation loop
matters far more than any individual model choice, and the audit trail is
what makes this visible.

This paper makes three contributions. We present a five-stage typed
adversarial contract pipeline in which two adversarial roles from distinct
model families exchange typed claim documents over bounded peer-to-peer rounds,
a three-model quorum adjudicates, and a combined deterministic invariant
( $\mathcal{I}_{\mathrm{ref}}\wedge\mathcal{I}_{\mathrm{sem}}$ ) validates
each verdict, making the full lineage from any instruction back to its
originating span queryable as data. An ablation shows that the iterative
deliberation loop accounts for most of the invariant-satisfaction gain:
removing the loop drops satisfaction by nearly 30 percentage points on the
BBQ Disability benchmark, while schema-level coordination metrics stored as
typed records make the degradation auditable without calling an additional
model. Finally, we provide cross-domain portability evidence showing that the
deliberation layer, data model, and invariant transfer from subjective
stereotype remediation to objective hallucination remediation by changing only
role-framing prompts; the triage gate required a cross-family second auditor
to maintain recall on objective hallucination, isolating the gate as the one
domain-sensitive component.

Figure 1: A conflicted record (input): co-located spans require opposite
actions (one contains demographic reasoning that must be reframed or dropped;
another is contextually grounded and must be preserved) that a single LLM
judge cannot resolve consistently and returns no verdict. BiasGuard-D returns
a typed per-span instruction record (output) with a full provenance trail.

Section 2 reviews related work and shows where existing
approaches fall short. Section 3 defines the problem and describes
the data model, pipeline, and invariant. Section 4 evaluates
the system on stereotype and hallucination benchmarks;
Sections 5 and 6 discuss the findings,
limitations, and what the provenance trail offers in practice. Source code,
configuration, and run artefacts are at https://github.com/ksubasi/biasguard-d.

## 2 Background and Related Work

BiasGuard-D sits at the intersection of classical data quality, LLM output
enforcement, and typed-contract agent orchestration. Each tradition contributes
something the system needs; none alone addresses the conflicted-record problem.

## Constraint-based data quality and repair.

The standard view of data quality treats records as entities that satisfy or
violate integrity constraints, and routing or repairing violators is a
long-studied problem [10, 14, 3, 5].
Our invariant is recognisable in this tradition: $\mathcal{I}_{\mathrm{ref}}$ 
is a foreign-key coverage check, and $\mathcal{I}_{\mathrm{sem}}$ resembles
near-duplicate detection in entity resolution. Classical repair theory selects
a minimal change to restore integrity, but a span instructed both to be removed
and preserved cannot be fixed this way; there is no ordering on
natural-language paraphrases that singles out a canonical repair.
BiasGuard-D quarantines on $\mathcal{I}_{\mathrm{sem}}$ failure rather than
attempting an auto-repair, because doing so would bring model judgment back
into the verification step. The novelty lies not in either predicate alone but
in applying them together over natural-language payloads.

## Quality enforcement on LLM outputs.

Retrieval-augmented and self-refining pipelines [17, 8, 1]
read, refine, and pass on records. This works well for straightforward quality
issues but fails on conflicted records because no stage can mark two co-located
spans as simultaneously valid and invalid. Recent multi-agent
debate [7, 18] introduces structured
disagreement but without typed message formats or deterministic verification.
Related work in the group has studied agent disagreement as a diagnostic signal
for moderation [23], applied dialectical
multi-agent refinement to structured classification [4],
and used community-driven agent frameworks for implicit bias
detection [12].
Training-time approaches (Constitutional AI [2] and
RLHF [20]) embed quality constraints into model
parameters; the resulting guarantees are statistical and opaque to an auditor.
A single-model pipeline that produces a cleaner-looking output provides no
evidence that the conflict was resolved rather than suppressed.
BiasGuard-D is runtime, record-level, and inspectable: every inter-stage
exchange is a typed record rather than a raw string.

## Typed adversarial contracts and provenance.

Typed inter-agent messaging descends from FIPA contract-net
protocols [11, 21], was revived in
LLM orchestration frameworks [24, 16], and has
acquired formal treatment in Hoare-style contracts [6].
Because every inter-stage record conforms to a fixed schema, the full lineage
from any instruction back to its source is stored and queryable without
re-running the models. Prior work supplies the message-passing machinery but
does not apply it to adversarial quality enforcement with a deterministic
check across different constraint types.

## 3 Problem, Approach, and Methods

## 3.1 The Problem

Making the problem precise requires moving from record-level pass/fail to
span-level decomposition. A record that must simultaneously preserve one span
and remove another cannot be handled as a unit: each span needs an identified
role, and the roles assigned by different judges need to be checked for
mutual consistency before any downstream action.

Concretely: an operator maintaining an AI-generated catalogue needs both
span-level granularity to approve or remove individual claims without
discarding the whole entry, and a provenance trail linking each instruction
back to its source span, auditable without re-running the pipeline.

Both scenarios impose the same requirement on the data model: span-level
typed claims with stable identifiers, a deterministic consistency check
that needs no model at verification time, and a stored lineage that survives
the full pipeline. The data model described next is designed around exactly
these three requirements.

## 3.2 The Data Model

Every correctness property of BiasGuard-D rests on the data model, so we
describe it before the pipeline. Record-level pass/fail labels are
insufficient for quality assessment: locating where errors occur requires
finer-grained units [13, 22].
Two design decisions follow from the problem.
First, fixing schemas up-front means stages can be swapped or upgraded without
ambiguity, which matters as models are deprecated. Second, grounding all
schemas in a single atomic primitive means the consistency invariant operates
on stable identifier sets rather than on natural-language content, keeping
verification deterministic and LLM-free.

The primitive is an AtomicClaim: one identifiable assertion about a
specific text span. Each claim carries a role-prefixed identifier
(C001 for the Stereotype Advocate’s first claim, D001 for
the Context Defender’s), the verbatim or compressed span it concerns, a
typed claim category drawn from five values (Factual,
Rhetorical, Framing, OptionPreference,
DecisionFlip), an optional list of provenance identifiers from a
reference passage, and a confidence score. The role prefix makes cross-role
provenance trivial to compute: finding where SA and CD claims overlap is a
string-prefix operation, not a semantic search.
Confidence is discounted multiplicatively each time the opposing role contests
a claim, so four contestations reduce it by roughly two-thirds rather than
collapsing it to zero; the trajectory is stored per round and flags cases where
a low-confidence claim is nevertheless upheld. Full field definitions and the
Python implementation are in the repository.

Everything else in the system is either an AtomicClaim or a typed
collection of them. Table 1 lists the six inter-stage schemas.
The two primary documents (StereotypeCase, ContextDefense)
are updated in place across rounds; the DeliberationVerdict carries
the output the invariant checks. Because every edge carries a typed record
with consistent identifiers, the full lineage of any instruction back to its
source span is recoverable by traversing stored records, with no
natural-language processing needed.

AtomicClaim or a collection of them.

## 3.3 Pipeline Architecture

With the data model fixed, the pipeline determines which stage produces which
schema and how stages connect to preserve provenance end to end.
BiasGuard-D runs in five stages orchestrated by LangGraph [16];
the orchestrator is interchangeable since every interface is typed, following
contract-based design principles for multi-agent
systems [6].

## Generator and same-family Auditor (Stages 1–2).

The Generator (Llama 3.1 8B via Groq) produces the incoming record from
structured input; the Auditor (same model, same family) emits a
VerdictContract carrying a delegate flag. Pairing the Auditor
with the Generator’s own family is deliberate: self-preference bias means a
same-family judge is less likely to flag its own family’s outputs [15, 25], so records
it does flag are ones where even a sympathetic reading finds a problem,
making it a high-precision, if lower-recall, triage gate. The deliberation pipeline is
invoked sparingly and only on records the same-family judge cannot explain
away; the recall cost is the precision-recall trade-off the architecture
already surfaces at the delegation threshold. Records where
delegate=false pass through unchanged; otherwise they enter
deliberation. For the cross-domain HaluEval condition a second cross-family
Auditor B (Mistral Small) is added; delegation is OR(A, B), raising
recall at the cost of additional false delegations on correct inputs.

## Bounded peer-to-peer deliberation (Stage 3).

The Stereotype Advocate (SA, GLM-4-Flash via Zhipu AI) and the Context
Defender (CD, Mistral Small via Mistral AI) produce their initial
StereotypeCase and ContextDefense in round one. In each
subsequent round each role reads the other’s previous document and re-emits
its own, reusing the prior round’s claim_id when a claim survives
semantically and assigning a fresh identifier when a substantively new claim
is raised. The stability check is deterministic and operates on identifier sets only: the
loop terminates when two consecutive rounds produce identical contested and
defended claim sets, or when a five-round cap is reached. The cap is set at
roughly twice the empirically observed mean convergence point (2.24–2.39
rounds across conditions; Table 6): if claim sets have not
stabilised by that point, continued exchange is unlikely to resolve the
underlying tension, and the invariant will surface the contradiction at Stage
5 regardless. The two roles update in parallel within a round, so
neither sees the other’s current-round output. Identifier mis-assignment by a
role delays stability by at most one round; it does not compromise the invariant.

## Quorum Arbiter and invariant check (Stages 4–5).

Three Arbiters drawn from three distinct provider families (Cohere Command R,
Claude Sonnet, and Llama 3.3 70B) receive the converged claim documents
in parallel and each emit an independent DeliberationVerdict. A
per-claim majority vote (at least two of three) produces the aggregated verdict,
which then passes through the combined invariant (§3.4). If
the invariant holds, the Generator is re-invoked with the upheld preserve,
reframe, and drop instructions; if either component fails, an
InvariantViolation record is logged and the pipeline emits a
conservative fallback. The quarantine path deliberately avoids auto-repair: a
verdict that fails the semantic check has gone through five stages of
deliberation without resolving its contradiction, and patching it over would
bring model judgment back into the verification step.

## Family heterogeneity as a data-integrity guarantee.

The five roles span five distinct model families (Table 2).
Same-family models show joint error correlations up to 60% regardless of
prompt diversity, and single-family multi-agent setups systematically
overstate coordination gains [15, 25]. If two adversarial roles share a family,
their claim sets may converge at the span level, making the exchange vacuous.

limitations:
Two limitations bear on the evidence. The LLM-as-judge step that produced the HaluEval hallucination-removal
labels is itself subject to the same biases the architecture is designed
to catch. We mitigate by giving the judge a strict comparison prompt with no
reference to intermediate records, but a fully independent human judge would
eliminate this concern entirely.

One limitation bears on the auditor design. The HaluEval condition uses a
two-auditor gate with OR delegation; 19 of 24 false delegations on
correct inputs fire because one auditor flags while the other passes. The
delegation strategy is a tunable threshold that does not touch the data
model, quorum, or invariant; the trade-off is examined in future work.

One further limitation bears on configuration. The Jaccard threshold has not
been tested on paraphrase-rich corpora; Table 4 shows the
quarantine rate is insensitive to $\theta$ across $[0.70,\,0.90]$ on the
current datasets, but a denser paraphrase space could push items into the
borderline band and raise the false-positive rate.
Most roles use free or prototyping tiers deliberately, to stress-test the
architecture under realistic resource constraints. The exception is
Claude Sonnet as one Arbiter: ablations replacing it with free-tier
alternatives (Qwen3-32B, Mistral Large) produced substantially lower
hallucination removal rates on HaluEval, showing that Arbiter capability
is a genuine dependency on objective grounding tasks. The BBQ stereotype
results, which do not rely on this slot, are unaffected. Identifying a fully free-tier Arbiter that matches Claude-level performance
on HaluEval and improving end-to-end latency are left as future work.
conclusion:
Three threads extend beyond the experimental numbers: where the architecture
matters in practice, what the cross-domain transfer demonstrated, and where
the current design falls short.

title: Lineage-Aware Search Control for LLM-Based Evolutionary Factor Mining
abstract: Formulaic alpha factor mining searches for symbolic expressions that transform market data into predictive signals. Recent LLM-based evolutionary factor mining methods use large language models as semantic variation operators. Under the conventional LLM-EA paradigm, stochastic variation and fitness-based selection can leave the search weakly directed and concentrated around a narrow set of structurally similar factors. We argue that these limitations arise because current methods mainly organize search at the individual and population levels, leaving lineage-level control underused. A lineage connects successive factor variants through evolutionary descent. We propose LineageEvo, which uses lineage in two coupled forms of search control: (1) lineage-conditioned LLM variation, which distills Lineage-Scoped Search Experience into operator-specific priors and fuses them with global operator priors, providing persistent, lineage-relevant guidance for LLM generation; and (2) lineage-stratified search allocation, which balances factor quality against lineage concentration by distributing the search budget across lineages during evolutionary search. Together, these mechanisms make semantic variation more direction aware and prevent branches from dominating the evolution, thereby promoting the discovery of predictive and diverse factors. We evaluate LineageEvo on CSI 500 and S&P 500 in terms of factor predictiveness, portfolio performance, search efficiency, and lineage- and expression-level diversity. LineageEvo achieves the strongest predictive performance on both markets, while LSPS produces a more balanced lineage distribution and a structurally broader factor pool. The results support lineage as a useful intermediate unit for controlling LLM-based evolutionary factor search.

## Introduction

Formulaic alpha factor mining aims to discover mathematical expressions that transform raw market data into predictive signals for future asset returns (Kakushadze 2016). Such factors support portfolio construction
and trading, yet the vast expression space and noisy,
non-stationary data make predictive and stable factors difficult
to discover.

Early factor discovery largely relied on human experts who designed signals based on financial intuition and empirical experience. To reduce such manual effort, automated factor mining methods have been developed, including genetic programming (GP), reinforcement learning (RL), and other machine learning approaches (Zhang et al. 2020; Yu et al. 2023; Chen et al. 2025). These methods expand the searchable factor space and enable systematic exploration beyond hand-crafted factors. However, they still rely
mainly on fixed grammars, handcrafted operators, or scalar
rewards, limiting semantic reasoning and adaptive reuse of search
experience.

More recently, LLM-based factor mining has emerged as a
promising paradigm, using pretrained models to generate and
refine symbolic formulas through agent-based generation, tree
search, and graph-aware evolution
(Wang et al. 2023; Tang et al. 2025; Shi et al. 2025; Guo et al. 2026; Luo et al. 2026a).
Large-scale pretraining provides semantic priors over financial
concepts, mathematical expressions, and programming patterns,
supporting factor hypothesis generation and formula refinement.
Among these approaches, LLM-based evolutionary algorithm
(LLM-EA) factor mining is particularly appealing because it
replaces purely syntactic genetic operators with LLM-based
semantic mutation and recombination
(Liu et al. 2023; Luo et al. 2026b; Ren et al. 2025; Han et al. 2026). However, two
search-control challenges remain. First, LLM-based operators are flexible but weakly controllable, as the mapping from prompt context to offspring is implicit and difficult to steer persistently (Liu et al. 2023; Yin et al. 2024). Second, under limited budgets, fitness-based selection can lead to takeover, where currently strong individuals or branches receive disproportionate search opportunities, reducing diversity and risking premature convergence (Sudholt 2018; Gabor et al. 2018).

These challenges persist because current LLM-EA factor mining
methods mainly organize search at the individual and population
levels, while making limited use of lineage-level state. At the
individual level, LLM operators modify selected parent factors;
at the population level, evolutionary selection favors
high-scoring candidates. Between them, a lineage is a
descent-defined factor family whose membership follows primary
evolutionary inheritance. Unlike an isolated individual or an unstructured population, a lineage preserves the continuity of local search across successive variation events, making it a natural stateful unit for both persistent operator guidance and search allocation. Conventional
evolutionary algorithms have used genealogy and lineage
information for diversity preservation, selection, and
inheritance analysis (Burke et al. 2003; Gabor et al. 2018; Burlacu et al. 2013).
However, using lineage as a shared scope for operator priors
and search allocation remains underexplored in LLM-EA factor mining.

To address these issues, we propose LineageEvo, a
lineage-aware LLM-EA framework for formulaic factor mining.
LineageEvo represents evolutionary descent in a lineage
DAG and uses lineage in two coupled forms of search control.
First, it organizes Lineage-Scoped Search Experience (LSSE) into
operator-specific lineage priors and fuses them with global
operator priors to condition LLM-based mutation and crossover.
Second, Lineage-Stratified Parent Selection (LSPS) allocates
search opportunities at the lineage level before selecting
parent factor(s), while a separate elite archive preserves
high-quality discoveries. This design gives LLM variation a persistent local context and
distributes subsequent search more evenly across evolutionary
branches.

Experiments on CSI 500 and S&P 500 demonstrate the effectiveness
of LineageEvo across markets. Compared with the strongest
baseline for each metric, LineageEvo improves IC by
28.3% and 12.6%, and ICIR by 9.9% and 35.8% on CSI 500 and
S&P 500, respectively, while achieving the strongest portfolio performance on both
markets. Ablation results
confirm the complementary roles of lineage-specific and global
priors, while LSPS increases lineage entropy from 0.405 to 2.154
and average AST distance from 0.509 to 0.747, preserving a broader
and less concentrated factor pool. The search curve further shows
that LineageEvo reaches a strong factor set rapidly,
indicating efficient evolutionary search.

Our contributions are summarized as follows:

• 

We identify lineage-level search control as underexplored in LLM-EA factor mining and use it to connect
individual-level semantic variation with population-level
selection.

• 

We propose LineageEvo, which represents
descent-defined factor families in an evolutionary DAG and
organizes Lineage-Scoped Search Experience into
operator-specific lineage priors for LLM variation.

• 

We introduce lineage-stratified search allocation through
LSPS, which balances lineage quality against lineage concentration, and decouple search allocation from solution
preservation through a separate elite archive.

• 

Experiments on CSI 500 and S&P 500 show that
LineageEvo outperforms eight representative baselines
in factor performance, while preserving greater lineage
and structural diversity.

## Related Work

## Traditional Automated Factor Mining

Traditional automated factor mining mainly formulates alpha discovery
as symbolic search. AutoAlpha applies GP-style variation and
quality-diversity search, AlphaGen uses reinforcement learning,
and AlphaSAGE improves structure-aware exploration
(Zhang et al. 2020; Yu et al. 2023; Chen et al. 2025). These methods broaden
automated search, but still largely depend on predefined grammars, handcrafted operators, or scalar rewards, making it difficult to incorporate domain semantics or adaptively reuse search experience beyond predefined operators.

## LLM-Based Factor Mining

Recent work introduces LLMs into factor mining as semantic generators, refiners, and search assistants. Alpha-GPT explores human–AI interactive alpha generation by translating investment ideas into candidate formulas (Wang et al. 2023), while AlphaAgent develops an autonomous agent framework with originality, hypothesis-factor alignment, and complexity control (Tang et al. 2025). Search-oriented methods further combine LLM generation with Monte Carlo Tree Search or graph-based retrieval to guide formula refinement (Shi et al. 2025; Guo et al. 2026). These methods make factor mining more semantic by leveraging LLMs’ pretraining-induced knowledge of financial concepts, mathematical expressions, and programming patterns to generate factors with richer rationales and more flexible structures. However, as suggested by AlphaBench, existing LLM-based factor mining methods may still under-exploit the exploration capacity of LLMs, motivating evolutionary frameworks that embed LLMs into iterative population-based search (Luo et al. 2026a).

## LLM-EA Factor Mining

LLM-EA search combines the semantic generation ability of LLMs with the population-based optimization mechanism of evolutionary algorithms. General LLM-EA studies use LLMs as evolutionary optimizers or hyper-heuristics, where LLMs generate, mutate, recombine, or reflect on candidate solutions within an iterative search loop (Liu et al. 2023; Liu et al. 2024; Ye et al. 2024). In factor mining, EvoAlpha adapts this paradigm to evolutionary alpha discovery with LLM-generated factors (Luo et al. 2026b); TreEvo evolves tree-structured thoughts to capture the hierarchical nature of alpha formulas (Ren et al. 2025); and QuantaAlpha explores trajectory-level mutation and crossover to reuse effective mining experience (Han et al. 2026). These methods move beyond isolated LLM generation by introducing evolutionary variation and selection into factor search. However, they still face two fundamental search-control challenges: LLM-driven variation can be flexible but weakly controllable, while fitness-based selection can cause dominant branches to monopolize the search process.

## Genealogy and Lineage in Evolutionary Algorithms

Evolutionary computation has previously used genealogy and
lineage information for diversity preservation, inheritance
analysis, and selection
(Burke et al. 2003; Gabor et al. 2018; Burlacu et al. 2013). These studies establish lineage
as an evolutionary abstraction. Building on this
foundation, LineageEvo uses each lineage as the shared
scope for accumulating operator-specific priors
and allocating subsequent search opportunities in LLM-EA factor
mining.

Figure 1: 
Overview of LineageEvo. LSPS
first selects a lineage and then selects parent factor(s);
lineage-specific and global operator priors are subsequently
retrieved and fused to condition LLM-based variation. Valid
offspring are evaluated, and the feedback path updates the
lineage DAG, prior states, active population, and elite archive.

## Method

We propose LineageEvo, a lineage-aware evolutionary
framework for formulaic alpha factor mining with LLM-based
semantic variation. Its central idea is to associate accumulated search experience and
future search opportunities with each lineage. LineageEvo uses lineage as a
stateful intermediate search unit between individual-level LLM
variation and population-level evolutionary selection.
Specifically, lineage serves two complementary roles: (1) it defines
a local scope for accumulating operator-specific search
experience, and (2) it provides a unit for allocating a
limited evaluation budget.

Figure 1 summarizes one iteration of
LineageEvo. Starting from an evolutionary state organized by lineage, Lineage-Stratified Parent Selection (LSPS) first allocates
a search opportunity to a lineage and then selects parent
factor(s) from the active population. The corresponding
lineage-specific and global operator experience is retrieved and
fused into soft guidance for LLM-based mutation or crossover. A
deterministically validated offspring is subsequently evaluated,
after which the lineage graph, prior states, active population,
and elite archive are updated. This division of responsibilities
keeps the LLM focused on semantic variation, while deterministic
components govern validation, evaluation, inheritance, and
search-state transitions.

## Problem Setup and Lineage Representation

Let $\mathcal{X}$ denote the market feature space and
 $\mathcal{F}$ the symbolic expression space induced by a factor
grammar. A formulaic alpha factor $f\in\mathcal{F}$ maps the
historical observations of stock $i$ to a cross-sectional signal:

 $z_{i,t}^{f}=f\!\left(\mathcal{X}_{i,\leq t}\right),$ 

(1)

where $z_{i,t}^{f}$ is the factor value at date $t$ . Rather than seeking a single best expression, the
goal is to discover a collection of factors that exhibit strong
predictive performance and temporal stability while maintaining
sufficient structural diversity during search. The resulting
factor pool supports downstream factor selection and combination.

LineageEvo ties lineage identity to the structural
inheritance induced by its variation operators. Mutation applies
a local modification to a leaf node or a small subtree of one
parent while preserving the remaining expression structure.
Crossover is asymmetric: the parent sampled from the first selected
lineage is fixed as the primary parent and provides the recipient
expression backbone. A subtree from the secondary parent replaces
a selected primary subtree, while the remaining primary structure
is preserved.

We record these inheritance relations using a directed acyclic
graph

 $\mathcal{G}^{t}=\left(\mathcal{V}^{t},\mathcal{E}_{\mathrm{pri}}^{t},\mathcal{E}_{\mathrm{sec}}^{t}\right),$ 

(2)

where $\mathcal{V}^{t}$ contains all valid factors evaluated by
iteration $t$ . The set $\mathcal{E}_{\mathrm{pri}}^{t}$ records
the inheritance of the expression backbone. A mutation offspring
has one primary edge from its parent, whereas a crossover
offspring has one primary edge from the backbone parent. The set
 $\mathcal{E}_{\mathrm{sec}}^{t}$ records the donor ancestry of
crossover, preserving the contribution of the parent that
provides the replacement subtree.

Let $\mathcal{R}^{t}\subseteq\mathcal{V}^{t}$ denote the set of
root factors. Since each non-root node has exactly one incoming
primary inheritance edge, its lineage root is recursively defined
as

 $\rho^{t}(v)=\begin{cases}v,&v\in\mathcal{R}^{t},\\[2.84526pt]
\rho^{t}(u),&(u,v)\in\mathcal{E}_{\mathrm{pri}}^{t}.\end{cases}$ 

(3)

The lineage associated with root $r_{k}$ is consequently

 $\mathcal{L}_{k}^{t}=\left\{v\in\mathcal{V}^{t}\mid\rho^{t}(v)=r_{k}\right\}.$ 

(4)

A lineage is therefore a descent-defined local search family
induced by structure-preserving variation. Lineage membership follows the
inherited expression backbone through primary edges, while
secondary edges retain cross-lineage donor ancestry. Because mutation modifies only a local component and crossover
preserves the primary backbone, nearby descendants are expected
to retain greater structural and DSL-level financial-semantic
continuity than factors from unrelated lineages, as verified in
Appendix. This continuity provides
the basis for using lineage as a scope for search experience and
resource allocation.

## Lineage-Stratified Search Allocation

Modules 1–2 in Figure 1 implement
lineage-level search allocation. Standard individual-level
fitness selection may repeatedly favor factors from already
dominant branches, causing early lineage takeover and reducing
exploration
(Sudholt 2018; Gabor et al. 2018). To mitigate
this effect, LineageEvo organizes its active population
by lineage:

 $\mathcal{P}^{t}=\bigcup_{k=1}^{m_{t}}\mathcal{P}_{k}^{t},\qquad\mathcal{P}_{k}^{t}=\mathcal{P}^{t}\cap\mathcal{L}_{k}^{t},$ 

(5)

where $\mathcal{P}_{k}^{t}$ contains the active factors belonging
to lineage $k$ , and $m_{t}$ is the number of active lineages.

LSPS uses a two-stage sampling procedure. It first selects a
lineage and then selects a parent factor within that lineage.
Both stages use a common robust quality score. Let $\mathcal{M}$ 
denote the optimization metric, either IC or ICIR, and define
 $T(f)=|\mathcal{M}_{\mathrm{tr}}(f)|$ and
 $V(f)=|\mathcal{M}_{\mathrm{val}}(f)|$ . For factors satisfying
 $T(f)+V(f)>0$ , the quality score is

 $q(f)=\alpha T(f)+\beta V(f)-\gamma\left|\mathcal{M}_{\mathrm{tr}}(f)-\mathcal{M}_{\mathrm{val}}(f)\right|,$ 

(6)

where $\alpha,\beta>0$ and
 $0\leq\gamma<\min\{\alpha,\beta\}$ . This guarantees
 $q(f)>0$ while penalizing both strength disagreement and
directional reversals.

For each lineage, we define a quality score and a lineage-balance
weight:

 $b_{k}^{t}=\max_{f\in\mathcal{P}_{k}^{t}}q(f),\qquad d_{k}^{t}=\frac{1}{|\mathcal{P}_{k}^{t}|+1}.$ 

(7)

The first term reflects the strongest active factor within the
lineage, while the second assigns greater weight to less
represented lineages. Their normalized mixture defines the
lineage-selection distribution:

 $\pi_{\mathrm{lin}}^{t}(k)=\lambda\frac{b_{k}^{t}}{\sum_{\ell=1}^{m_{t}}b_{\ell}^{t}}+(1-\lambda)\frac{d_{k}^{t}}{\sum_{\ell=1}^{m_{t}}d_{\ell}^{t}},$ 

(8)

where $\lambda\in[0,1]$ controls the trade-off between favoring
high-quality lineages and maintaining exploration across
lineages.

After selecting lineage $k$ , LSPS samples a parent in proportion
to its robust quality:

 $\pi_{\mathrm{par}}^{t}(f\mid k)=\frac{q(f)}{\sum_{g\in\mathcal{P}_{k}^{t}}q(g)},\qquad f\in\mathcal{P}_{k}^{t}.$ 

(9)

This two-stage probabilistic selection exploits stronger factors
while preserving alternatives at both the lineage and parent
levels.

In this paper, we proposed LineageEvo, an LLM-EA
framework that uses lineage as an intermediate organizational
unit for evolutionary factor mining. LineageEvo
combines lineage-conditioned priors for guiding LLM variation with Lineage-Stratified Parent Selection for
distributing search opportunities across lineages.
The resulting framework discovers highly predictive and stable
factors, achieves strong investment returns, and preserves a more

body_start:
Abstract

We present an AI-assisted mathematical addendum to Strategic Trip
Planning: Striking a Balance Between Competition and Cooperation (Amar,
2018). We reconstruct selected relationships between strategic choice,
cooperative stability, participant approval and enforcement. The
thesis’s Nash-to-core proposition is under-specified until outsider
opportunities are stated. We verify two-person implications under fixed
outsiders and explicit efficiency conditions. Under isolation, the
original example has an empty TU core; its funded counterpart uses an
explicit external subsidy. For a monotone resource model we characterize
the exact financing gap. A finite negotiation procedure implemented in
Lean is proved to terminate with participant approval, joint-cost
non-worsening and local optimality against permitted approved moves.
Supporting formalizations address bargaining geometry and regret-based
efficiency. A resource-game counterinstance shows why monotonicity alone
provides no uniform price-of-anarchy bound. Reproducible computations
compare a documented heuristic reconstruction with the verified
procedure on 44 source-based instances and 96 starting cases from four
additional synthetic network families. Acceptance-matched heuristic and
randomized pairwise-search controls contextualize the optimization
results. The mathematical ingredients are established results; the
contribution is a traceable reconstruction linking source statements,
explicit assumptions, checked proofs, executable code and retained
counterinstances. The study illustrates how AI-assisted investigation
can turn engineering intuitions from legacy research into precise
mathematical claims whose conditions and computational consequences can
be inspected and reproduced.

## 1. Introduction

Trip planning is individually motivated but jointly realized. A route
that is attractive when considered in isolation may become costly once
other travellers select overlapping resources. Conversely, a traveller
may accept a less-preferred route because it reduces conflict, improves
a joint outcome or forms part of an enforceable agreement. These
observations motivated my doctoral framework, Strategic Trip
Planning: Striking a Balance Between Competition and Cooperation
[1]. Its principal components were personalized route generation,
team formation and bargaining, with a later application to territory
sharing in social taxi networks.

My decision to revisit the thesis was inspired by OpenAI’s 6 October
2026 release of mathematical manuscripts and supporting proof artifacts,
including Lean formalizations for many of the proofs [10]. That
release prompted a personal question: could AI-assisted mathematical
investigation help me give the engineering intuitions developed in my
2018 doctoral work a fuller and more precise mathematical treatment? The
thesis’s mathematics had supported an engineering contribution; it had
not been developed as a separate contribution to mathematical theory. I
wanted to investigate how far its underlying ideas could be
reconstructed as explicit definitions, justified assumptions and
checkable theorems, and how the resulting treatment would behave on new
synthetic planning instances.

This motivation shapes the present work. Lean substantiates the formal
guarantees of the stated models and revised procedure, while new
reproducible simulations test their engineering behavior and compare
outcomes with exact finite benchmarks. Together, these methods give a
concrete route from engineering intuition to a mathematical formulation
whose assumptions, proofs and computational consequences can be
inspected. The aim is to substantiate the coordination outcomes that
motivated the original work and establish the conditions under which
they follow. The simulations provide finite-instance evidence; universal
guarantees come from the theorems and their explicit assumptions.

This paper is an addendum to my thesis and a case study in AI-assisted
reconstruction of legacy engineering mathematics. Its purpose is to show
which mathematical statements can be made precise, which assumptions
change their meaning, and how the resulting claims can be checked
against executable procedures. The principal result of the investigation
is the source-to-model-to-proof correspondence, together with the
evidence needed to assess its limits.

The starting point remains the observation in the thesis abstract:
“Mobility planning as it stands today is an individual decision-making
effort that takes place in an environment governed by the collective
actions of various competing travellers” [1, p.iv, PDF p.4]. The
framework accordingly accommodates “the travellers’ individual
behaviours, preferences, and goals in cooperative and competitive
scenarios” [1, p.iv, PDF p.4]. These statements motivate the models
developed here; they are not offered as claims about the present state
of transportation research.

The engineering objective is coordination among travellers who retain
their own agendas, rather than the optimization of a centrally
controlled fleet [1, Chapter 1, pp.3–4, PDF pp.23–24]. In the
original framework, traveller-centric trip planning supplies
personalized strategies, team formation determines who interacts, and
bargaining manages conflicts. The present paper develops the
mathematical structure underlying that architecture. It does not repeat
the original experimental study or require the original engineering
contribution to have been a contribution to mathematical theory.

This paper develops those ideas as a collection of compatible
mathematical models. Our aim is not to identify cooperation with one
equilibrium concept. We instead ask what must be specified for the
relationships between competitive choice, cooperative stability and
collective efficiency to hold. Four questions guide the treatment: what
actions and costs define the strategic game; what opportunities remain
available to a departing coalition; what the referee actually enforces;
and which costs a repeated-game learner minimizes.

The distinction concerning departing coalitions is decisive. A
unilateral Nash deviation holds opponents’ actions fixed. A cooperative
opportunity may hold outsiders fixed, remove them, allow them to respond
strategically or allow the deviating coalition to escape a pricing
mechanism. These conventions cannot be interchanged. Once they are made
explicit, several intended connections become provable. Other
connections require additional conditions or fail under a different,
equally well-defined convention.

The treatment connects three contributions. First, it specifies
coalition opportunities and financing so that strategic and cooperative
stability claims have precise meanings. Second, it implements a finite
negotiation procedure and proves acceptance, termination and the
resulting local improvement condition. Third, it compares a documented
reconstruction of the thesis heuristic with that executable procedure on
shared finite instances. The original two-traveller model supplies an
end-to-end example whose returned plans also satisfy the stronger
equilibrium and cooperative conditions. The enforcement and regret
results explain what additional mechanisms can certify about
implementation and repeated outcomes.

The new synthetic data are a substantive part of this contribution. The
thesis supplies the planning concepts, source examples and heuristic
structure; the present treatment makes the relevant assumptions
explicit, proves a specified coordination procedure and tests
implementations on newly generated inputs. This provides fresh evidence
that the coordination logic can operate beyond the original numerical
example. Reproducible generators, shared-instance comparisons and
exhaustive finite benchmarks allow that evidence to be inspected and
rerun. The resulting support concerns the engineering framework under
the stated reconstruction and model assumptions; the guarantees of the
revised procedure are identified separately from observations about the
reconstructed heuristic.

The formal development uses Lean 4.24.0 [8] and Mathlib v4.24.0
[9]. We retain an assumption ledger and an exact correspondence
between the planning concepts and formal declarations. The present
treatment specifies the counterpart rules and admissible financing
explicitly. These specifications are part of the revised model, whose
guarantees are proved below; the original thesis is preserved unchanged.

## 2. Strategic actions and cooperative
opportunities

Let $N$ be a finite nonempty player set. Player $i$ has a finite
nonempty action set $A_{i}$ , and $A=\prod_{i}A_{i}$ is the profile space.
Actions may represent routes, territories or explicitly discretized
departure choices. We write $c_{i}(s)$ for player $i$ ’s physical cost
and

 $C(s)=\sum_{i\in N}c_{i}(s).$ 

Here “physical cost” means the underlying unpriced planning cost,
distinguished from referee charges and observed learning scores. Its
interpretation may be travel cost or a declared preference score; the
formal model does not turn a subjective score into a measured travel
time. Summing personalized scores requires a declared common scale and
system objective. We assume that scale where aggregate costs or TU
payments are used.

The principal notation is:

Symbol

Meaning

 $s$ , $b$ , $s^{*}$ 

Current profile, feasible baseline, joint
comparator

 $c_{i}(s)$ , $C(s)$ 

Base player cost and its declared sum

 $v_{s}(S)$ , $v_{\mathrm{iso}}(S)$ 

Fixed-outsider and isolated
coalition opportunities

 $h_{i}$ , $F_{h}$ 

Participant acceptance ceiling and approved
profiles

 $\widehat{c}_{i}$ , $L_{i}^{t}$ 

Enforced cost and time-dependent observed
cost

 $R_{i}(T)$ , $B_{i}(T)$ 

All-action regret bound and cumulative
cost-distortion bound

The full-profile argument records resource externalities. A baseline
route score on $A_{i}$ alone does not specify them. A Nash equilibrium
satisfies

 $c_{i}(s)\leq c_{i}(a_{i},s_{-i})\qquad(\forall i,\ a_{i}\in A_{i}).$ 

A social optimum minimizes $C$ over feasible profiles. Pareto
efficiency means that no profile makes every player weakly better and at
least one player strictly better. These are separate properties. We do
not assume that independently choosing baseline favourites produces a
Nash equilibrium.

The source supplies finite nonempty action sets in Chapter 3, pp.39–42
(PDF pp.59–62), and distinguishes personalized and system utilities in
Chapter 5, pp.80–81. Its use of compact convex strategy sets in Chapter
4, pp.55–56 requires a representation beyond a finite list of distinct
deterministic routes. Finite probability distributions provide one
explicit representation. Independent product distributions describe
mixed strategies; arbitrary joint distributions allow correlation. No
deterministic trip constraint is silently replaced by an expected
constraint.

## 2.1 Transferable and nontransferable
stability

For a scalar coalition-cost function $v:2^{N}\to\mathbb{R}$ with
 $v(\varnothing)=0$ , a TU cost-core allocation satisfies

 $x(N)=v(N),\qquad x(S)\leq v(S)\quad(\forall S\subseteq N),$ 

where $x(S)=\sum_{i\in S}x_{i}$ . One fixed allocation is used for every
coalition. We follow the source’s cost orientation in (4.23), p.65, and
(6.3), p.126. Its earlier reward orientation reverses the inequalities.
Different personalized utilities alone do not justify transferable
utility. TU conclusions below concern a declared common cost/payment
scale and permit real transfers.

An NTU model instead retains attainable cost vectors. A nonempty
coalition blocks an attainable vector if it has another attainable
vector that strictly lowers every member’s cost. This formulation uses
no interpersonal transfer. A coalition’s aggregate cost may decrease
while one member loses; that is a potential TU improvement, but not
necessarily an NTU block.

## 2.2 Two explicit outsider
conventions

Fix a reference agreement $s$ . The fixed-outsider value is

 $v_{s}(S)=\min_{t:\ t_{-S}=s_{-S}}\sum_{i\in S}c_{i}(t).$ 

The admissible set is nonempty because it contains $s$ , and a minimum
exists in the finite game. For NTU opportunities, retain the vectors
 $(c_{i}(t))_{i\in S}$ under the same constraint. Equation (3) defines a
reference-dependent family of cooperative problems; it is not a
reference-independent characteristic function.

Under isolation, outsiders are removed from the resource environment and
coalition costs are recomputed. We denote the resulting minimum by
 $v_{\mathrm{iso}}(S)$ . This convention needs an explicit
coalition-level resource model, supplied in Section 4. A coalition that
leaves the referee’s jurisdiction may have yet another opportunity. Exit
rights are therefore part of a mechanism specification.

## 3. A precise equilibrium-to-core
bridge

Proposition 4.2.1 of the planning framework [1, p.52, PDF p.72]
connects strategic stability with cooperative stability. The source does
not uniquely specify the outsider opportunities needed to determine that
connection. We formulate two conditional counterparts: fixed-outsider
opportunities for two-person agreements, and financed isolation for
efficient Nash agreements in the monotone resource model. The following
characterization supplies the first proof.

Theorem 1 — Fixed-outsider characterization. Under (3), the
realized cost allocation $(c_{i}(s))_{i}$ belongs to the TU cost core if
and only if

 $\sum_{i\in S}c_{i}(s)\leq\sum_{i\in S}c_{i}(t)\quad\text{whenever }t_{-S}=s_{-S}.$ 

For NTU attainable vectors under the same outsider rule, the realized
vector belongs to the NTU core if and only if $s$ is strong Nash: no
nonempty coalition can change its actions, holding outsiders fixed, and
strictly improve every member.

Proof. A TU core inequality bounds the current coalition cost by
its minimum opportunity, and therefore by every admissible deviation.
Conversely, (4) bounds the current cost by an attained minimum. The
reference profile itself is admissible, giving the opposite inequality.
Applying this to $N$ establishes efficiency. For NTU, admissible
blocking vectors and improving joint deviations have exactly the same
witnesses. The TU and NTU conclusions use different improvement tests.
 $\square$ 

Theorem 2 (Proposition 4.2.1A) — Two-traveller fixed-outsider
counterpart. For two players:

1. 

Nash equilibrium plus Pareto efficiency implies the fixed-outsider NTU
core.

2. 

Nash equilibrium plus social optimality implies the fixed-outsider TU
cost core.

title: FogTTA: Online Test-Time Adaptation for Robust Transformer-based Object Detection in Foggy Weather
abstract: Object detection models for autonomous driving commonly experience substantial performance drops when deployed under adverse weather due to the domain shift between training data and real-world operating conditions. This degradation is especially evident when models trained on clear-weather images encounter foggy environments with reduced visibility and contrast. To address this challenge, we introduce FogTTA, an online test-time adaptation framework designed to improve the robustness of Transformer-based object detectors in fog. Using RF-DETR as the underlying object detector, FogTTA enables real-time adaptation to the streaming target domain without requiring source data or retraining. The framework follows a teacher-student design, where the deployed model serves as the teacher and generates pseudo labels from weakly augmented target inputs. These predictions are subsequently refined through non-maximum suppression and confidence filtering. The student model then learns from strongly augmented target sample using the Varifocal loss to mitigate pseudo-label noise. The teacher is updated via exponential moving averaging to ensure stable and continuous adaptation. Experiments show that FogTTA outperforms prior baselines, delivering improved detection accuracy and stability while maintaining real-time performance.

These predictions are subsequently refined through non-maximum suppression and confidence filtering. The student model then learns from strongly augmented target sample using the Varifocal loss to mitigate pseudo-label noise. The teacher is updated via exponential moving averaging to ensure stable and continuous adaptation. ## 1. Introduction

Object detection is a fundamental task in autonomous driving, where reliable perception under diverse environmental conditions is essential for safety [9]. Accurate detection and localization of surrounding objects are essential for safe autonomous navigation. Early detection models are based on convolutional neural networks (CNNs) and can be categorized into two-stage and one-stage approaches. Two-stage detectors, such as Faster R-CNN [18], achieve high accuracy through region proposal refinement but incur heavy computational costs. As real-time performance is critical for autonomous vehicles, one-stage detectors such as SSD [14] and YOLO [17] were developed to deliver efficient detection through a single feed-forward pass. CNN-based methods rely on local receptive fields and thus struggle to model long-range dependencies, which limits their adaptability to adverse conditions [6, 2].

Transformer-based architectures, on the other hand, leverage self-attention to capture long-range dependencies and global context across entire images. Early models such as DETR [2] demonstrated strong accuracy but suffered from high computational overhead and slow convergence. Subsequent detectors, including Deformable DETR [27], LW-DETR [4], and RT-DETR [26], improved speed and efficiency while maintaining competitive accuracy. RF-DETR [20] integrates DINOv2 into LW-DETR, which makes it a robust and efficient detector. However, models trained under clear-weather conditions still experience substantial performance degradation when deployed in foggy environments due to the domain shift.

Domain shift refers to the discrepancy between the distributions of the training (source) and deployment (target) environments [10]. In autonomous driving, this shift is critical when clear-weather models face fog, where reduced visibility and contrast hinder object detection [12]. Unsupervised domain adaptation (UDA) methods aim to mitigate this issue by aligning labeled source and unlabeled target data. However, as shown in Figure 1a, such methods [12, 11] assume access to both domains, which is impractical due to privacy and storage constraints. Source-free domain adaptation (SFDA) [23, 8] addresses this limitation by adapting pre-trained models to unlabeled target data without accessing source samples (Figure 1b), yet still requires offline retraining on the entire target set. In contrast, online test-time adaptation (TTA) [25, 15, 22] enables real-time adaptation to a stream of unlabeled target inputs during deployment (Figure 1c). Although more practical, TTA remains challenging due to the absence of supervision, the noise in pseudo labels, and the need to balance adaptation stability and responsiveness.

Figure 1. Illustration of domain adaptation paradigms for object detection: (a) UDA uses labeled source and unlabeled target data jointly; (b) SFDA adapts a source-trained model without source access; (c) TTA adapts online to streaming target data during deployment.

In this paper, we present FogTTA, an online test-time adaptation framework that enhances the robustness of Transformer-based object detectors under foggy conditions. Built upon RF-DETR [20], FogTTA adapts continuously to unseen target data without requiring source access or retraining. It employs a teacher–student design, where the deployed model (teacher) generates and refines pseudo labels through confidence-based filtering and non-maximum suppression (NMS), while the student learns from strongly augmented target views using the Varifocal loss [24] to handle pseudo-label noise. The teacher is updated via exponential moving averaging (EMA) of the student’s parameters to ensure stable and progressive adaptation.

The main contributions of this work are as follows:

• 

We propose FogTTA, an online test-time adaptation framework that enhances the robustness of Transformer-based object detection under foggy weather conditions without requiring source data.

• 

We utilized a pseudo-label refinement strategy that integrates NMS and the Varifocal loss to mitigate noise and uncertainty during adaptation.

• 

We validate FogTTA through experiments, demonstrating improved detection accuracy in foggy conditions while maintaining real-time inference performance of RF-DETR.

The rest of this paper is organized as follows. Section 2 reviews related work. Section 3 presents the proposed methodology. Section 4 describes the experimental settings, and Section 5 discusses the results. Finally, Section 6 concludes the paper and outlines future directions.

## 2. Related Works

## 2.1. Transformer-based Object Detectors

The introduction of DETR [2] marked a turning point in object detection. As the first Transformer-based detector, DETR differs from previous approaches by utilizing learnable object queries and an end-to-end pipeline that eliminates the need for post-processing. However, the original DETR design is not suitable for real-time applications due to its computational complexity and relatively high latency. Deformable DETR [27], a follow-up work, adopts deformable attention to focus on key regions, accelerating training and reducing memory usage. To further improve real-time performance, RT-DETR [26] replaces the Transformer encoder with an efficient hybrid encoder to decouple the intra-scale interaction and cross-scale fusion of multi-scale features, improving performance while preserving the NMS-free design for faster inference. LW-DETR [4] uses a convolutional projector to connect a plain ViT encoder and a shallow DETR decoder, yielding a light-weight detector suitable for real-time applications. Building on LW-DETR and DINOv2, RF-DETR [20] leverages neural architecture search to create a scheduler-free object detector that surpasses prior state-of-the-art approaches as well as real-time methods.

## 2.2. Cross-weather domain adaptation

To systematically study clear-to-foggy adaptation, Foggy Cityscapes [7] dataset synthesizes foggy scenes on Cityscapes [5] dataset and is widely used as a benchmark for weather-robust object detection tasks. Early work on cross-weather domain adaptive object detection mainly follows the UDA setting. DA-Detect [12] augments Faster RCNN with image-level and object-level domain classifiers plus an auxiliary domain to reduce the influence of domain shift. This framework is further extended [11] to foggy and rainy conditions with a Dynamic Masking Process that exploits contextual information. However, these methods require access to both source and target data during training, thereby limiting their practicality in real-world deployment. To avoid accessing source data, DDT with AEMA [8] introduces a Dual-Rate Dynamic Teacher (DDT) with Asynchronous EMA (AEMA) to balance fast adaptation to domain shift and long-term knowledge in a source-free setting. FRANCK [23] shows a query-centric source-free framework for DETR with objectness-based sample reweighting module, a contrastive learning bank, and an uncertainty-weighted distillation. Nevertheless, these methods all rely on offline adaptation on a pre-collected target set, which limits their applicability in online test-time scenarios.

## 2.3. Test-time Domain Adaptation

Recent work extends TTA and online adaptation ideas to object detection by adapting detectors during inference without source data. MemCLR [22] introduced a unified teacher-student framework that adapts the target domain in both offline and online settings. MLFA [15] aligns informative global-level and cluster-level features between source and target domains while minimizing target entropy for realistic TTA object detection. DDT [25] introduce Dynamic Dual Teaching (DDT) scheme that combines a source detector and a vision language model teacher with dynamic prediction fusion and consistency regularization to achieve better generalization ability. However, existing TTA detectors still struggle with noisy pseudo labels and unstable adaptation under severe fog conditions. To address these limitations, we develop a transformer-based TTA framework that performs reliable adaptation without accessing source data.

## 3. Proposed Method

## 3.1. Problem Formulation

Let the labeled source domain be denoted as $\mathcal{D}^{S}=\{(x_{i}^{S},y_{i}^{S})\}_{i=1}^{N_{S}}$ , drawn from the joint distribution $P_{S}(X,Y)$ , where $x_{i}^{S}$ and $y_{i}^{S}$ represent the input image and its corresponding annotation. The source domain corresponds to clear-weather driving conditions. A model $f_{\theta}$ is first trained on the source domain by minimizing the supervised detection loss:

(1)

 $\min_{\theta}\mathcal{L}_{\text{src}}(f_{\theta})=\frac{1}{N_{S}}\sum_{i=1}^{N_{S}}\ell(f_{\theta}(x_{i}^{S}),y_{i}^{S}),$ 

where $\ell(\cdot,\cdot)$ denotes the overall detection loss that combines classification and localization terms.

At deployment, the pretrained model encounters a stream of unlabeled target samples $\mathcal{D}^{T}=\{x_{j}^{T}\}_{j=1}^{N_{T}}$ , drawn from foggy-weather driving conditions following a distinct distribution $P_{T}(X)$ such that $P_{T}(X)\neq P_{S}(X)$ . The goal of TTA is to adapt $f_{\theta}$ online to the target distribution without access to $\mathcal{D}^{S}$ or its labels. Formally, the adaptation objective is expressed as:

(2)

 $\min_{\theta}\mathbb{E}_{x^{T}\sim P_{T}(X)}\left[\,\ell(f_{\theta}(x^{T}))\,\right],$ 

where $\mathbb{E}_{x^{T}\sim P_{T}(X)}[\cdot]$ denotes the expected loss over target samples drawn from the target distribution, and $\ell(f_{\theta}(x^{T}))$ represents the unsupervised adaptation loss computed from each incoming target image.

## 3.2. Model Overview

Figure 2. Model overview of the proposed FogTTA framework. (a) The model is trained on the labeled source domain using focal and detection losses. (b) The trained model is then deployed on the vehicle. (c) During deployment, the vehicle encounters a continuous stream of target data with a distribution different from the source domain. (d) The incoming target data are processed through the TTA pipeline. (e) Weak and strong augmentations of the target images are generated, where the deployed model serves as the teacher and processes weakly augmented inputs to produce refined pseudo labels. NMS is applied to the results, and the student model, which receives the strongly augmented inputs, is trained on these pseudo labels using the Varifocal loss. The teacher model is then updated via EMA of the student’s parameters.

Figure 2 illustrates the overall framework of our proposed TTA method for autonomous driving under foggy conditions. The process begins with a model $f_{\theta}$ pretrained on a labeled source dataset $\mathcal{D}^{S}$ that contains clear-weather driving scenes, as described in Section 3.3. During deployment, this pretrained model is installed on the vehicle and performs inference on a continuous stream of unlabeled target samples $\mathcal{D}^{T}$ captured under foggy-weather conditions. As the visual appearance of foggy scenes differs significantly from clear-weather training data, the model experiences performance degradation caused by the domain shift between $P_{T}(X)$ and $P_{S}(X)$ .

To maintain robustness under such domain shifts, the model is continuously adapted to the incoming target data in an online manner without accessing the source dataset. This process follows a teacher–student framework, where the pretrained model $f_{\theta}$ serves as both the inference and teacher network, and a student model $f_{\phi}$ , initialized with the teacher’s parameters, is used for adaptation. This architecture enables continuous online refinement as the environment evolves while ensuring that inference remains real-time through the efficiency of the RF-DETR backbone and is unaffected by the adaptation updates.

As detailed in Section 3.4, for each target sample in the stream, the teacher generates predictions that are treated as supervision signals for the student. The student is optimized using the Varifocal loss [24] (Section 3.5) to minimize the discrepancy between its predictions and the teacher’s refined pseudo labels, thereby learning target-specific representations from unlabeled data. After each adaptation step, the teacher model is updated using an EMA of the student’s parameters to integrate the latest knowledge from the target domain. Consequently, the teacher model, which also serves as the deployed inference model, remains continuously adapted to the evolving target data stream while retaining the knowledge learned from the source domain.

## 3.3. Training Source Model

The training objective of source $f_{\theta}$ on the labeled source dataset $\mathcal{D}^{S}$ follows the standard DETR [2] formulation and is optimized using a combination of classification and localization losses. Specifically, the overall loss is defined as:

(3)

 $\mathcal{L}_{\text{src}}=\lambda_{\text{cls}}\mathcal{L}_{\text{cls}}+\lambda_{\text{box}}\mathcal{L}_{\text{box}}+\lambda_{\text{giou}}\mathcal{L}_{\text{giou}},$ 

where $\lambda_{\text{cls}}$ , $\lambda_{\text{box}}$ , and $\lambda_{\text{giou}}$ are weighting coefficients that balance the individual loss terms.

The classification loss $\mathcal{L}_{\text{cls}}$ is computed using the focal loss [13], which addresses the foreground–background imbalance commonly observed in dense detection tasks. It is formulated as:

(4)

 $\mathcal{L}_{\text{cls}}=-\alpha_{t}(1-p_{t})^{\gamma}\log(p_{t}),$ 

where $p_{t}$ represents the predicted probability for the target class, $\alpha_{t}$ is a balancing factor, and $\gamma$ is the focusing parameter that down-weights easy samples.

For localization, the bounding box regression loss $\mathcal{L}_{\text{box}}$ and the generalized IoU loss $\mathcal{L}_{\text{giou}}$ [19] are employed to jointly optimize box position and shape alignment. The Hungarian matching algorithm [2] is used to associate each prediction with a corresponding ground-truth box before loss computation.

## 3.4. Test-Time Domain Adaptation

For each incoming image $x_{t}$ , the teacher network generates a set of object predictions

 $\mathcal{P}_{t}=\{(b_{i},p_{i})\}_{i=1}^{N_{t}},$ 

where $b_{i}$ and $p_{i}$ represent the predicted bounding box and its associated class probability vector. To improve stability, the teacher performs two inference passes on weakly augmented versions of $x_{t}$ , and the resulting predictions are merged and ranked according to their confidence scores.

Only the top $K$ detections are retained, and low-confidence predictions are filtered using a pseudo-label confidence threshold $\tau_{\text{pl}}$ . The refined pseudo-label set is defined as

 $\hat{\mathcal{Y}}_{t}=\{(\hat{b}_{k},\hat{y}_{k},\hat{s}_{k})\in\mathcal{P}_{t}\mid\hat{s}_{k}\geq\tau_{\text{pl}}\},$ 

where $\hat{s}_{k}=\max_{c}p_{k,c}$ denotes the highest class confidence. The value of $\tau_{\text{pl}}$ determines a trade-off between precision and recall in the pseudo labels. A higher threshold increases precision by filtering out uncertain detections, however decreases recall, which means missing pseudo labels. Conversely, a lower threshold increases recall by retaining more true positives, but may introduce additional false positives that amplify noise during adaptation. As illustrated in Figure 3, selecting an appropriate $\tau_{\text{pl}}$ is crucial to balancing stability and adaptability in the test-time learning process.

Figure 3. Precision and recall of pseudo labels with respect to the confidence threshold $\tau_{\text{pl}}$ .

A non-maximum suppression with an IoU threshold $\tau_{\text{nms}}$ is then applied to eliminate redundant detections. The resulting pseudo labels $\hat{\mathcal{Y}}_{t}$ are used to supervise the student model $f_{\phi}$ , which is initialized with the teacher’s parameters and optimized using the adaptation losses detailed in Section 3.5. After each adaptation step, the teacher parameters are updated using an EMA of the student’s parameters:

 $\theta_{t+1}\leftarrow\mu\,\theta_{t}+(1-\mu)\,\phi_{t},$ 

where $\mu$ is the EMA momentum coefficient. This update allows the teacher, which also serves as the deployed inference model, to remain continuously adapted to the evol
conclusion:
In this paper, we presented FogTTA, an online TTA framework designed to enhance the robustness of Transformer-based object detectors under foggy weather conditions. Building upon RF-DETR, FogTTA enables online adaptation without accessing source data by combining pseudo-label refinement, Varifocal loss, and EMA-based teacher updates. Experimental results demonstrated that FogTTA consistently outperforms all baseline methods in detection accuracy and stability compared to the source-only model, confirming the effectiveness of our approach for real-world autonomous driving scenarios.
For future work, we plan to extend FogTTA to broader adaptation scenarios, including cross-dataset settings and simulation-to-real transfer, to evaluate its generalization under more diverse domain shifts. We also aim to explore additional adaptation cues, such as temporal information and uncertainty estimation, to further improve robustness in challenging driving environments.
